Several blazes are tearing across the West Midlands, including in Stourbridge and Sandyford, Stoke-on-Trent.



Entire houses can be seen consumed by flames in Stourbridge.

In Castle Vale, Birmingham a woman was seriously injured as a blaze tore through several homes.





A 50ft blaze ripped through at least six gardens and hospitalised one woman in Tamworth, Staffordshire this morning.

The terrifying inferno tore rapidly through several back gardens.

News.title: Heatwave dramatically ends in record-breaking rainfall sparking floods & horror landslides with 300k evacuated in Japan
News.content:
A BRUTAL heatwave has given way to a terrifying deluge in Japan, with record-breaking rain unleashing floods and landslides and forcing around 300,000 people to evacuate.

Torrential rain battered eastern Japan on Thursday, triggering landslides, power cuts and transport chaos as officials issued their highest-level heavy rain warning for the region for the first time.



Shocking footage shows cars being swallowed whole by surging floodwater in a residential area of Kashiwa, Chiba, as the streets are transformed into a raging inland torrent.

A terrifying whirlpool also spiralled, collecting rubbish amid the swollen floodwaters, churning violently as the deluge tore through the area.



In another dramatic clip, a cyclist battles through the water, almost completely drenched and engulfed as they desperately pedal through the flooded streets.

“This is shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain,” a Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) official told a news conference.

“In areas hit by the localised rainfall, lives may be in imminent danger. Please secure your safety immediately,” the official said.

More than 100,000 households, mainly in Chiba but also in Ibaraki and Saitama, were urged to evacuate, according to the disaster management agency.

Hundreds were also left stranded at Chiba station after train services were suspended.

In a staggering deluge, around 100mm (3.9in) of rain hammered the area around Sakura city in just one hour before 9pm, reports say.



The agency’s top-level warning was issued across more than a dozen cities in Chiba, signalling a high likelihood of an imminent disaster.

The torrential downpour also knocked out power to more than 10,000 households, while authorities reported landslides, mudslides and flooded homes across the region.



“This happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise. The power is out so I’m worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days,” a woman in Chiba’s Ichikawa city told NHK.

The weather horror comes just days after Japan was scorched by a savage heatwave, with temperatures soaring above 40C (104F) in some cities.

More than 52,000 people have been sent to hospital with heatstroke and nearly 100 have died since the start of May, according to the latest data.

Disgruntled female office workers in Japan even expressed their irritation as their male counterparts get their legs out as part of a government heatwave health initiative.



Now the blistering heat has been broken by a relentless barrage of rain as a rare trio of Pacific storms batters East and South-East Asia.

Typhoon Chan-Hom swept across Japan’s main island of Honshu after making landfall on Tuesday, hammering Tokyo and surrounding areas with ferocious rain.

At least seven people suffered minor injuries, while a construction barrier collapsed along an expressway in Tochigi Prefecture and trapped a car, although nobody was hurt.

Dozens of flights at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport were cancelled as authorities warned of treacherous landslides and flooding.

In Shibuya, the commercial heart of Tokyo, ominous storm clouds suddenly unleashed a downpour on pedestrians before the skies cleared again.



The violent weather has also battered China, where Typhoon Dolphin swept into the country’s eastern and central regions after making landfall on Sunday.

Dolphin has since weakened, but the battered storm is still dragging heavy rain inland, with Beijing braced for a potentially catastrophic deluge.

More than 150mm (5.9in) of rain is expected across much of the capital between Tuesday evening and Thursday – more than a quarter of its average annual rainfall.



Some districts could see more than 200mm (7.9in) in just 24 hours, with flood warnings issued, train services suspended and reservoirs pushed beyond their flood-control limits.

The Philippines has also been hammered by more than a week of relentless monsoon rain, with at least 26 people killed and thousands displaced.

In some areas, more than a month’s worth of rain has fallen in just nine days, according to the country’s state weather bureau Pagasa.

Floodwaters have swept rubbish towards the mouth of Manila Bay, creating a horrifying sea of garbage.

The chaos comes as three typhoons — Dolphin, Chan-Hom and Peilou — formed in the region within days of one another, prompting Chinese state media to describe it as a rare “three-typhoon situation”.



All three have since weakened, but another storm is now brewing.

Typhoon No. 17, also known as Nangka, has formed near Japan’s southern islands and is being monitored by authorities in both Japan and the Philippines.

The storm is expected to maintain its strength as it churns across the Pacific in the coming days, according to a JMA forecast.

August is traditionally peak typhoon season across the north-western Pacific, but forecasters warn this year’s season could be particularly ferocious.

London-based Tropical Storm Risk has predicted the season could become one of the most active on record, with storms potentially becoming more frequent and powerful.



Japan’s weather nightmare is also threatening its biggest high-school baseball tournament, Koshien, which is being held near Osaka from August 5 to 22.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The tournament is renowned for its brutal summer conditions, with last year’s players forced from the field on stretchers after suffering heat exhaustion.

One scheduled game has already been postponed until tomorrow as the country battles the latest weather assault.

News.title: Lewes derailment sparks rush hour travel chaos as trains cancelled for hours in ‘major disruption’ & commuters stuck
News.content:
COMMUTERS are facing rush hour chaos with trains cancelled for hours after a derailment near Lewes sparked travel misery.

Dozens of passengers are feared to be trapped in overturned carriages following the horror in East Sussex, just before 4pm today.



The horror crash has sparked chaos and “major disruption” accross the entire Sussex coastal network during peak hours.

Busy routes including both ways from Brighton to London have all been affected.



Passengers who are travelling to and from London to Brighton will be able get on the following services at no additional cost, according to National Rail.

National Rail said that travellers could hop on Southern services between Brighton and London Victoria, Thameslink services between Brighton and London Victoria and Gatwick Express services between Brighton and London Victoria

The disruption is expected to last until at least 10pm tonight, said National Rail.

Most trains between Brighton and Lewes have been cancelled, said Southern Rail.

There is also no service at all between Haywards Heath and Lewes as well as between Seaford/Eastbourne and Lewes.

Southern Rail have advised passengers to delay journeys in this area until later on today.



Passengers have also been advised to plan ahead and take alternative routes to travel.

Commuters who wanted to travel through Lewes have been advised to get on the following services at no additional cost.

Passengers can get on the London Underground between all London terminals and various Brighton & Hove bus routes.



Travellers can get on the following bus services: 28 – Brighton (St Peter’s Church), Moulsecoomb (Brighton University), Falmer, Lewes (Post Office / Law Courts), Polegate, and Eastbourne – 29 / 29B / 29X – Brighton (St Peter’s Church), Moulsecoomb (Brighton University), Falmer, Lewes (Post Office / Law Courts), Uckfield, Crowborough, Eridge, and Tunbridge Wells.

Cops, paramedics and fire crews scrambled to the crash after the train derailed at around 3.54pm.

Pictures showed passengers climbing on top of the train and being ushered into a nearby field by emergency crews.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was “deeply concerned” following news of the derailment.

Writing on X, she said: “Deeply concerned of reports of a derailment involving a Southern train in Lewes, Sussex.



“Grateful to emergency services who are on the scene supporting those impacted.

“We are working quickly with the rail industry and local partners to assist passengers.”

British Transport Police said: “Officers are currently on scene close to Lewes railway station following reports of a derailed train at 3.54pm today.

“We’re responding alongside paramedics and the fire service and will provide more information as soon as we can.”

Officers from Sussex Police are also in attendance, the force confirmed.

News.title: First-of-its-kind chocolate bar is made for the first time in 94 years
News.content:
A GAME-CHANGING chocolate bar has been made for the first time in 94 years.

There are currently only six bars of this confectionery treat in the world.



A University of Reading student has made the first 100 per cent British chocolate bar in nearly a century.

Food security master’s student Maha Khan used UK-grown cocoa which she harvested, fermented, and processed herself for the chocolate.



Khan took on this challenge to mark the University’s 100th anniversary, naming it the Reading 100 Chocolate Bar.

It is thought to be the first chocolate bar made using British-grown cocoa since 1932, when Rowntree’s first UK-grown bar was made.

This confectionery treat was later gifted to the then six-year-old Princess Elizabeth, later Queen Elizabeth II.

The university is home to a unique collection of cocoa, with more than 300 types of cocoa plants on offer in the Berkshire city.

Usually, Britain must rely on supply chains thousands of miles away to sustain the nation’s sugar cravings, such as in Africa, South America and Asia.

So far, only six Reading 100 chocolate bars have been produced, but there are no plans by Khan to make this a large-scale commercial launch.



This means that it is unlikely you will spot it in the supermarket anytime soon.

Khan said at the time of the launch: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.

“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy.”

News.title: How long will the UK heatwave last? Latest Met Office weather forecast as temperatures hit 38C
News.content:
BRITONS have been enjoying the fifth official heatwave of the summer, with temperatures reaching 38C on Thursday.

The Met Office has issued an amber extreme heat warning for parts of southern and eastern England, as well as the Midlands – here’s how long the latest spell of hot weather is forecast to last.



How long will the heatwave last?

On Thursday afternoon temperatures reached 38.1C in Kew Gardens, West London, this afternoon, the Met Office confirmed.

It is the second time the UK has reached the figure this year, marginally pipping the previous high recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk, in June.



The Met Office added: “The only other time this has happened twice in one year was in 2022. It also makes it the 5th hottest day on record.”

Amber warnings for “extreme heat” are in place for a swathe of England from London to Sheffield, parts of Cheshire and Greater Manchester, into Gloucestershire and Wiltshire in the South West and Shropshire and Herefordshire in the west.



However, while many people have flocked to the beach, some regions have had cooler weather, with Scotland and Northern Ireland seeing wetter conditions.

A yellow warning has been issued for thunderstorms in Northern Ireland, which is in place until 6am on Friday.

While Thursday is expected to be the peak of the hot weather this week, some warmth will remain in the South and Southeast for another day.

Friday will remain hot across much of England and Wales – with London forecast to hit 33C – before a weak cold front brings cooler, cloudier climate in from the west.



The Met Office says there is also a chance of isolated afternoon thunderstorms in the southeast on Friday.

Temperatures will start to tail off from Saturday, which should see cooler air spread south from the northwest, the forecaster says.

However, it will still remain in the mid-to-high-20s for much of the south of England and Midlands, with highs of around 28C in London and on the southern coast.

The arrival of the weekend will continue the sunny spells in many areas, but there will also be scattered showers, which will be heaviest in the southeast.

Sunday is expected to be mostly dry with a plenty of sunshine, though rain may be reaching the northwest later.



Temperatures will dip a little further, remaining in the mid-20s in the Midlands and south of England – this should mark the end of the official heatwave.

The start of next week will bring increased rain, as well as some breezier conditions.

Wet and breezy conditions can be expected next week, as Monday is set to bring some more rain.

What is a heatwave?

A single hot afternoon does not automatically mean the UK is in a heatwave.

The Met Office defines a heatwave as an extended period of unusually hot weather.



In the UK, it is officially triggered when a location hits a specific temperature threshold for three days in a row.

These high temps often go hand-in-hand with high humidity, making the heat feel more intense.

Due to the diverse climate across the UK, heatwave thresholds vary by county.

For example, this could mean up to 28C in London and southern England, but only 25C in the North and Scotland.

Heatwaves usually strike in the summer when high-pressure systems settle over the country.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

This happens when the jet stream moves north, bringing long spells of dry and settled weather.

The highest temperature ever recorded for the UK was on July 19, 2022, when the mercury hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.

News.title: Brit mum, 38, who died after BBL surgery ‘had only visited Turkey clinic for lipo when doc offered cut-price op’
News.content:
OP HORROR Brit mum, 38, who died after BBL surgery ‘had only visited Turkey clinic for lipo when doc offered cut-price op’

A BRIT woman who died after BBL surgery had only visited the Turkish clinic for liposuction when she was offered the cut-price op, an inquest heard.

Hayley Dowell, 38, was asked ten minutes before her planned surgery whether she also wanted the Brazilian butt-lift to help enhance her “flat” bottom.



Tragically, the mum-of-three suffered medical complications at the private BHT Clinic in Istanbul and died on October 3, 2023.

Winchester Coroner’s Court heard Hayley was “very self conscious of her body” so travelled to Turkey for liposuction and a tummy tuck.



She had already undergone two breast augmentations in the UK prior to flying to Turkey, and she was curious about having further surgery.

While waiting for the op, a surgeon asked if he could take the fat he was removing from Hayley and use it to enhance her bottom.

She was given five minutes to consider the BBL proposal and the surgeon knocked £1,000 off the £7,000 price, it was heard.

Hayley’s husband Neil Dowell told the inquest he did not think she had signed a consent form to undergo the BBL prior to her operation.

He also claimed doctors at the Turkish clinic did not outline the risks of the procedure to his wife

Neil added: “She was very embarrassed of her body. We just assumed he was going to use fat from the lipo. She was excited about it.



What are Brazilian Bum Lifts and why are they so popular? Buttock enlargement surgery – known as a Brazilian bum-lift (BBL) – is used to make the bum look bigger, rounded and lifted. Surgeons transfer fat, inject filler or insert silicone-filled implants. It is the fastest growing cosmetic procedure but also one of the most dangerous, according to the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS). Many patients are travelling to the likes of Turkey or seeking out unregistered surgeons in the UK and are not given full information on the risks. BBLs carry the highest risk of all cosmetic surgeries – with more than one death occurring per 4,000 procedures.

“They deducted £1,000 from the procedure because she was already having the other procedure.

“We had five minutes to decide that. We are trying to sort it out. Checking our banks, saying you pay half and I will pay half.

“It was so quick. We had to make a quick decision. She was going down in 10 minutes after the woman left with the card machine.

“The surgeon never came back in. They came in with anaesthetic to make her a bit drowsy, and they took her away.”



Area Coroner for Hampshire, Portsmouth and Southampton, Nicholas Walker said Neil was told four hours into the surgery that it was going well.

But just before midnight, he was asked to go with medical staff because Hayley was very “unwell” and had suffered two cardiac arrests.

Neil was tragically told to say his goodbyes before Hayley passed away just before midnight.

Mr Walker said Hayley suffered a fat embolism – an issue that can arise after surgery and causes a potentially fatal blood flow blockage.

He said the pathologist’s evidence carried out in Turkey and agreed as likely in the UK found she died from micro fat embolism, which affected her lungs, from the liposuction operation.



The coroner indicated he was looking to produce a prevention of future deaths report.

Dr Sophie Chung, CEO of Qunomedical, said they were the “facilitators” of the surgery.

She said the firm no longer worked with the BHT Clinic and they no longer offer BBL surgeries through their company.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

When asked why the surgeon was still listed on the company’s website, Dr Chung said she was not aware but it was likely he had changed clinics.

The BHT Clinic declined to give evidence at the inquest, which continues.

News.title: Russia names glam suspected assassin ‘who blew up treacherous Ukrainian sub commander after his defection to Putin’
News.content:
RUSSIA has named the glamorous suspected assassin accused of blowing up a former Ukrainian submarine commander who defected to Vladimir Putin’s regime.

Margarita Reutt, 32, allegedly acted as a covert Ukrainian intelligence operative before planting a bomb inside a rubbish bin and remotely detonating it in Sevastopol.



The blast is said to have killed Robert Shageev, 49, a former Ukrainian submarine commander who had defected to Russia and was serving as a Russian Ministry of Defence officer.

Reutt allegedly confessed to carrying out the deadly bombing after being detained by Russia’s FSB.



The explosive device reportedly erupted at around 10am local time, ripping into the officer and leaving him severe injuries, according the the FSB.

The security service said: “As a result of the explosion, the man sustained injuries incompatible with life.



“It was established that the woman, born in 1994, carried out the bombing on the instructions of the Ukrainian special services.”

Mikhail Razvozhaev, Vladimir Putin’s governor of Sevastopol, claimed the FSB was “hot on the heels of the incident” before Reutt was detained.

He said she was suspected of carrying out a “cynical crime” against a Russian officer.

Razvozhaev added: “This is a cynical crime against an officer.



“The perpetrator – born in 1994 – is already giving evidence.

“The investigation has established that she was acting on the orders of the Ukrainian special services and shows no remorse for her actions.”

Reutt was reportedly spotted acting suspiciously in a residential district before ordinary Russians helped authorities track her down.

When interrogators allegedly asked whether she regretted the blast, she reportedly answered: “no”.

The 32-year-old was born in Yaroslavl and previously ran a travel agency which collapsed before she took a job as a biologist.



Her reported final employment was at a laboratory producing floral-infused vaginal suppositories.

She has also reportedly appeared on escort websites.

Reutt lived in the Russian resort of Sochi and allegedly told interrogators she had been “paid for the explosion in cryptocurrency”.



The extraordinary claims come after Reutt was reportedly fined in 2025 for “discrediting the Russian Armed Forces”.

Mash reported she had previously caused outrage aboard a Samara-Adler train when she allegedly shouted: “Serves you right, Russians!”, after news of a drone attack on a railway station.

She also reportedly said she was “ashamed to be Russian”.

Reutt is said to have travelled extensively around Russia and abroad, particularly to Egypt and Turkey.

After the alleged bombing, she reportedly planned to vanish overseas and had already bought a ticket from Sochi.



But her alleged escape plan was foiled when she was detained by Russian authorities and taken in for questioning.

The explosive claims come amid a growing string of alleged Ukrainian covert operations targeting senior Russian military figures deep behind the front line.

In December last year, a concealed car bomb tore through a quiet Moscow district and killed Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov, one of Vladimir Putin’s senior generals.

Sarvarov, who was responsible for training Russia’s armed forces, was killed shortly before 7am when the hidden explosive detonated beneath his vehicle in the Yasenevo district.

It was the third killing of a senior Russian military leader in 2025.



And the latest alleged hit follows another deadly blast at an elite Moscow restaurant packed with Kremlin-linked military figures.

A secret burial was reportedly held for Lt Gen Igor Yerusalimov, 53, at the high-security Troyekurovskoye Cemetery after he was killed in the restaurant bombing.

Yerusalimov was reportedly among five people killed when a homemade device detonated during a lavish birthday gathering for Colonel-General Alexander Chayko.



High-ranking officers, politicians and senior bureaucrats had gathered inside the exclusive Balzi Rossi overlooking Moscow’s Kudrinskaya Square when the bomb exploded.

The device was reportedly carried into the restaurant as a “birthday gift” by a female courier.

The woman carrying it was stopped by a security operative before the package detonated, killing her, the security officer and three others.

A separate report identified one of the dead as Major-General Valeri Plokhotnyuk, a senior Russian officer who was reportedly killed in the same blast on August 1.

Despite alleged attempts by Russian authorities to suppress news of his death, Plokhotnyuk was reportedly buried covertly at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, in an area reserved for elite military and security officials.



The bomb was reportedly believed to have been intended for Chayko, who escaped the blast unharmed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Plokhotnyuk was said to be the godfather of Chayko’s daughter Maria, 25, who was seriously wounded in the explosion.

Together, the alleged attacks paint a chilling picture of a shadow war playing out far beyond Ukraine’s front lines, with senior Russian military figures increasingly vulnerable to devastating strikes in their own territory.

News.title: Horror footage shows passengers gasp for breath after ‘aircon failure’ turns plane into furnace during SEVEN HOUR delay
News.content:
OVER 100 passengers on board a plane in New Delhi were left gasping for breath after the air-con failed.

The SpiceJet flight to Pune, India, was readying to leave the Indira Gandhi International Airport when the temperature inside the cabin soared.



Footage from inside the “hot and humid” cabin shows people yelling for help and frantically fanning themselves.

Traveller Leshpal Javalge told local media: “We were drenched in sweat… [there was] no AC or ventilation.



“There were pregnant women, children and elderly passengers onboard. Everyone was scared for their lives. Children began to cry.

“A pregnant woman started feeling breathless and was about to faint. We raised the alarm that she would die if she was not attended to immediately.”



He said the flight was scheduled to depart from New Delhi at 9.55pm on Tuesday but was delayed until 10.30pm.

As passengers entered the aircraft, they noticed the air-con was not working – but assumed it would take some time to start.

Half an hour passed and the cabin turned “extremely hot.”

Javalge added: “The aircraft was completely full and with the doors closed, the heat and humidity became unbearable.”



Passengers grabbed newspapers, magazines and safety cards from their seat pockets to fan themselves and others.

One person could be heard shouting in Hindi: “Tell them to open the gate! Otherwise I’ll break it down.”

Tensions skyrocketed when a few even attempted to open the jet’s main door themselves.



Eventually, their demands were met and they were allowed to deboard.

Another flight was arranged, which departed at around 5.30am the day after – more than seven hours after it was initially scheduled.

A SpiceJet spokesperson said: “On August 11, 2026, SpiceJet flight SG 105, scheduled to operate from Delhi to Pune, encountered a last-minute technical issue.

“An alternate aircraft was arranged, and the flight subsequently operated to Pune.

“SpiceJet deeply regrets the inconvenience caused to the passengers.”



This comes just weeks after another incident, this time on board an Emirates flight from Dubai, UAE, to Shanghai, China, during which 373 passengers were left trapped on the tarmac without air conditioning for 10 hours.

News.title: Savers issued warning as more than five MILLION accounts at risk of tax bill
News.content:
Savers issued warning as more than five MILLION accounts at risk of tax bill

The number of non-ISA savings accounts forecast to earn over £1,000 in interest has increased by 1,047%

View 2 Images The number of savings accounts potentially liable for tax has risen to 5.3 million (Image: Getty)

Over five million UK savings accounts are now at risk of being hit with a tax bill as savers are being urged to review their finances.

‌



Basic-rate taxpayers can earn up to £1,000 in savings interest each tax year before they start to pay tax on the interest earned.

‌



New analysis by Yorkshire Building Society reveals the number of non-ISA savings accounts forecast to earn over £1,000 in interest has increased by 1,047% in the last eight years.

‌



There were 462,000 accounts that would have earned more than £1,000 in interest and be potentially liable for tax in January 2018. This figure has now risen to 5.3 million.

View 2 Images If you are a basic-rate taxpayer, you can earn up to £1,000 in savings interest (Image: Miljan Živković via Getty Images)

Inflation, a higher interest rate environment and frozen tax-thresholds have contributed to millions more being liable to pay tax on their savings interest.

‌



Higher rate taxpayers can earn up to £500 in savings interest before they have to pay tax, while additional rate taxpayers do not receive any allowance. Any interest earned above these limits is taxed at your usual income tax rate.

The personal savings allowance was introduced in April 2016 and the majority of easy access accounts paid 1% or less - now the majority pay 3% or more.

If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

‌



This means that in 2016 basic-rate-tax payers would have been able to put away £100,000 in a typical savings account. In 2026, savers would only be able to save around £25,000 at rates of 4% without breaching their allowance.

If you are at risk of having to pay tax on your savings interest, you could choose to put your money away into an ISA account, where any interest earned is free from tax. You can put up to £20,000 a year into one ISA account or across different accounts.

Tina Hughes, Director of Savings at Yorkshire Building Society, said: “People doing the responsible thing — saving for a home, for emergencies or for the future — are now being punished by outdated rules. The Personal Savings Allowance urgently needs reform so it keeps pace with reality and supports savers, rather than catching them out.”

Article continues below

Rachel Springall, Finance Expert at Moneyfacts, said: “Savers are earning higher rates of interest, but they are also becoming ever more exposed to tax due to fiscal drag.

“The fact that there are millions of accounts becoming liable to tax over the past five years alone just shows how the Personal Savings Allowance has not moved on with the times and is in dire need of review to protect savers.“

News.title: Ukraine 'traitor' killed in bomb planted by 'female assassin'
News.content:
Ukraine 'traitor' killed in bomb planted by 'female assassin'

Turncoat former Ukrainian submarine commander who swapped sides for Russian navy - then went on to help bomb his home country -blown up in blast conducted by suspected 'female assassin'

View 4 Images Assassinated Russian sub commander Robert Shageyev

A turncoat former Ukrainian naval commander who defected to Russia has been reportedly assassinated - blasted to death by a bomb apparently planted by a female spy. Robert Shageyev, who once commanded Kyiv’s only submarine, switched sides after Russian troops invaded Crimea in 2014 and died in the port city of Sevastopol. He went on to join the Kremlin’s naval command structure and is thought to have been involved in bombing Ukraine ’s cities with cruise missiles fired from submarines and ships.

‌



The bomb that killed him, according to reports, was planted by a woman aged between 28 and 30 seen with a backpack and had been watching him. Shageyev was part of the Russian naval command structure that has fired cruise missiles at Ukraine, killing many civilians and blasting his homeland. It is thought a bomb was placed in a trash can outside a building he was in and it detonated as he walked by along with another person. Witnesses described to Russian press a woman who had been seen observing him before he died.

‌



View 4 Images Russian troops invade Crimea in 2014 (Image: AP)

‌



Russia burns and 12 dead as Ukraine launches huge strike 1,000 miles from Kyiv READ MORE :

Russia steps up aerial bomb attacks killing two little girls as Ukraine launches deep-strikes READ MORE :

The 49 year-old was in charge of Kyiv’s submarine Zaporizhzhia when he turned traitor, signing up with the Russian navy. Ukraine accused Shageyev of surrendering the submarine to Russian forces without a fight and subsequently swearing allegiance to the Russian military. It is believed he had continued his service with Russia ’s Black Sea Fleet and Ukrainian authorities notified him of suspicion of high treason in July 2022. It is also understood that after switching sides, Shageyev was appointed commander of a submarine division in Sevastopol Bay in 2015.

From 2017 to 2018 it is believed he was in charge of the Russian submarine B-262 Stary Oskol, a Varshavyanka-class submarine capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles. Shageyev participated in Russian strikes on Syria and later served in the Black Sea Fleet submarines equipped with Kalibr missiles which were used against Ukrainian cities. It is believed Russia has lost as many as 19 senior Army generals, mostly assassinated by Ukraine’s undercover operatives. Ukraine has appealed to US President Donald Trump sell it up to 10% of its badly-needed Patriot defence missiles before winter.

‌



View 4 Images President Volodymyr Zelensky (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine could destroy all of the Kremlin’s deadly ballistic missiles and save lives with just 10% of the US Patriots. Last night Russian forces launched 133 drones at Ukraine, hitting 15 locations and killing two more civilians in Odesa and wounding five in Dnipropetrovsk region and another in Zaporizhzhia. Zelensky is keen to acquire Patriots before winter as Russia will likely weaponise the bitter cold by targeting civilian energy supplies. But it is widely-reported the US has depleted its Patriot stocks by up to a third throughout its five month war with Iran, defending against Tehran’s firepower.

American weapons manufacturers have been told to speed up production of the Patriots, which are usually produced at a rate of around 650 a-year. President Zelensky said: "This year I’m asking American partners to sell me five per cent of missiles, what they have in their stocks. If they sell us five per cent we will go through the winter and save people’s lives. If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles.” In July, Ukraine intercepted just 29 of the 195 ballistic missiles fired by Vladimir Putin ’s military - many of them at civilians. Last month was the deadliest for Ukraine’s civilians since the full-scale invasion was launched in 2022.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Ukraine attacks Kerch, Russian-occupied Crimea (Image: social media; east2west news)

At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 per cent increase compared with the previous month. Zelensky argued: “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.” It is believed Moscow is producing 1,000 ballistic missiles a-year and now it is stepping up production and also buying in North Korean missiles. Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission, said of the Ukrainian casualties: “Every month this year the number of killed and injured civilians has increased. That trend accelerated sharply in July. The number of civilian casualties in July was the highest we documented in a single month since March 2022.”

Russia has suffered 1.4 losses of frontline troops to death or injury since war began, according to Ukraine. And Ukrainian forces have recently retaken 26 settlements and pushed Russian troops back across at least six areas of the frontline. The counter-attacks, led by air assault soldiers, have won back roughly 700 square miles of territory for Ukraine.

News.title: 'Our canals are a national treasure': Why Britain's historic waterways urgently need saving
News.content:
'Our canals are a national treasure': Why Britain's historic waterways urgently need saving

Journalist Paul Routledge has spent a lifetime wandering canal towpaths and uncovering the rich history of Britain's 2,000-mile canal network for his new book, For The Love of Canals. Here, he reflects on his nostalgia for these iconic waterways

View 6 Images Severe summer droughts and canal bursts have left narrowboats stranded and sections of the 2,000-mile network closed to conserve water, Paul (pictured here) warns (Image: Ben Lack Photography Ltd)

The year opened with too much water, and now there's not enough.

‌



More than fifteen millions litres burst from the Llangollen Canal in Whitchurch, Shropshire, inundating fields and stranding narrowboats in the mud. Eight months on from that Christmas catastrophe, engineers are still working to reopen the waterway, which plays a key role in moving fresh water for public supply.

‌



But this year of unprecedented heatwave and drought has forced operators Canals and River Trust to close two dozen sections and impose low-water restrictions on many parts of the 2,000-mile system to conserve water and protect navigation.

‌



In another emergency move, until the end of August cruising boaters have been released from the legal obligation to cast off and move every fourteen days.

Heatwave sees NHS England’s top doctor issue urgent warning to stay safe today READ MORE :

View 6 Images For The Love Of Canals by Paul Routledge, published by Mirror Books (£12.99), is out on August 27

Campbell Robb, chief executive of the CRT, warns of a "perfect storm” created by dry and hot conditions, with no rain for weeks on end, meaning that even where water is available, it can't be moved to where it's most needed.

‌



It was never supposed to be like this, even in Britain's notoriously fiickle weather. But our unique network of man-made waterways was built 250 years ago, when no one imagined we might one day have a Mediterranean climate. I am not a boater, but I have been walking our canal towpaths for decades, enjoying the peace and quiet – even in big cities – and the abdundance of wildife by the water's edge.

I'm also fascinated by the extraordinary history and architecture of this feature of our landscape that powered the Industrial Revolution and now serves as a home and a playground for many thousands of fellow-enthusiasts.

View 6 Images

‌



My towpath treks in all weathers, alongside waterways as diverse as the magnificent, 125-mile Leeds & Liverpool, the dried-up Somerset Coal Canal, and the idyllic Kennet and Avon, have now borne fruit in a book, For The Love of Canals , published 27 August by Mirrorbooks.

This love-affair began in childhood, when I would see tugboats on the Aire & Calder Navigation pulling long strings of “tom pudding” barges filled with coal from nearby collieries to power stations and export docks at Goole. I'm talking of the 1950's, when the canal was a word almost as dirty as the rubbish thrown into them. They were grubby highways of industry. Nobody wanted to live next to “the Cut”, as it was known to generations of working boatmen.

And as commercial trade dried up in the sixties, so did the waterways. Of the 6,000 miles of navigable water, more than two-thirds were lost in a few years : filled in, paved over for car parks and built on. We were in danger of losing a priceless heritage, the product of great Georgian and Victorian architects, builders and pioneering scientists who imagined their work would endure as long as the Pyramids.

‌



View 6 Images Canals once served as the "grubby highways" of Britain's Industrial Revolution

Men like James Brindley, regarded as the father of the narrow boat system – unique to the UK – who build the Birdgewater canal, the nation's first modern waterway, to bring coal to Manchester, and the 1.65-mile Harecastle Tunnel on the Trent & Mersey, the longest man-made tunnel on Earth when built and still in use after two hundre years.

And Thomas Telford – the only pioneer to have a new town named after him, in Shropshire – who built the incomparable Pontcsyllyte Aqueduct, soaring high above the valley of the river Dee, and now a Unesco World Heritage Site : a frightening experience for boaters and towpathers alike. Too scary for me!

‌



And Scots engineer John Rennie, star of the “Canal Mania” years of the late 18th century, who not only consructed canals but created Staffordshire's tranquil Rudyard Lake to feed one of them.

That so much of their – literally – ground-breaking work remains fully operational today is not only a testimonial to their remarkable skill, but a tribute to a preservation movement that has saved so many canal from closure, and restored many more to navigation.

Their campaign, combined with an ambitious programme of work by the CRT, continues apace. Thousands of volunteers toil away at weekends digging back where navvies once toiled. They have saved a national treasure, that keeps on giving - not least to television, with celebrity canal boat diaries air at prime time.

‌



View 6 Images Severe summer droughts and canal bursts have left narrowboats stranded and sections of the 2,000-mile network closed to conserve water (Image: Ben Lack Photography Ltd)

The canal is a Mecca for creative people, bringing together artists, photographers and writers like the poet Ian Macmillan who has contributed a foreword and a poem to my book, and for some years I was fortunate to live in one of the most attractive places on the mighty Grand Union Canal.

And therein lay a mystery, solved when I retraced my steps to the towpath of our former home, Dudswell Wharf, close to the inland Port of Berkhamsted, barely thirty miles north of London.

‌



We moved there in the early 1980's, to get away from the traffic on the busy A41 through the town (it's now by-passed), to a strange, half-timbered building that looks more like a farm building than a house.

View 6 Images

That's because it was, once. Our home was originally part of a hay and coal mechant's business alongside a deep lock in the canal. Local gossip said it was also part of a pub, The Swan. Indeed, our bedroom had been been a drinking den, not just a place for a newspaper man to lay his head after a hard day's toil in the pubs of Fleet Street, where I worked at the time.

‌



For several years, I walked the towpath every morning from this idyllic setting to Berkhamsted station to catch a train to Euston, and the office of The Times. It was a two-mile shlep in all weathers, dodging puddles to save my suit from the mud.

I was determined to relive that experience, and discover whether our old home was as I remembered it forty years before. It was. And not only was the wooden shelf above my bed where pints were once crossed to thirsty boatmen still there, but Ms Diana Holliday, the cellist lady to whom we sold the house in 1986 still lived there!

Little had changed, apart from a small conservatory with a view to the back garden where my hens once strutted, until the fox got them. The summer house built by my brickie brother John was now a music room. And my one-time neighbour Ned Hunt, just a school boy in those days, still lived in Lockside, the former pub and is a rival canal historians. They should rename it the Grand Coincidence Canal!

‌



As pledged, I did the towpath to "Berko” station. It took me more than twice as long as the old days, but then, I was twice as old and not rushing for a commuter train. The Grand Union is clearly in business, with many boatts moored amd others passing through the many locks. There's a new park, with a bench dedicated to Suzan, the late wife of my towpath comrade of the day, David Felton, another ex-Times journalist who took the pictures.

It was all very nostalgic, and great for the book. But it set me thinking: what of the future? This is a serious issue. Canal owner-operator CRT, a charity set up when the Tories wanted to privatise state-owned British Waterways in 1989, is strapped for cash and faces a downward spiral of government subsidy.

CRT boss Robb seeks greater long-term investment for the network : not just for leisure and stay-aboard boaters but for water transfer, drought and flooding resilience and enviornmental protection. The canal, he argues, should be “a core part of the nation's climate change resilience plan.”

‌



He's right. And not just climate change, but defence. The network was once a water-style Maginot Line against Nazi invasion in WW2, complete with concrete pill boxes that still survive.

A land invasion is unlikely, but the War on Iran shows that water, not just a useful transport link but vital for life as we know it, has been weaponised by both sides. That's why I suggest in the book that the canal network should be declared a National Strategic Asset, funded in part by the Ministry of Defence.

Our canals are not just iconic heritage. They are the biggest and most ubiquitous reservoir of water imaginable. Island Brtian needs them. Meanwhile, best foot forward on the towpath. There's no better was to see this wonderful country. A million footfalls every year – official – can't be wrong.

News.title: Kids find 'old club' while litter picking in stream and it turns out to be a bomb
News.content:
Kids find 'old club' while litter picking in stream and it turns out to be a bomb

Amelia Appleyard, 10, Rosie Appleyard, seven, Liam Green, eight, and Ryan Green, six, were left stunned when they pulled a rusty military bomb from a beck in Leeds, West Yorks., during a litter pick

View 8 Images Rosie with the old military bomb the children discovered while litter picking

Four children got the fright of their lives when a litter pick took a dramatic turn – after they hauled a rusty military bomb from a stream.

‌



Amelia Appleyard, 10, Rosie Appleyard, seven, Liam Green, eight, and Ryan Green, six, had been clearing rubbish from a beck in Leeds, West Yorks. , when they stumbled across the heavily corroded device.

‌



Liam initially thought the bizarre find looked like an "old club" and began waving it around – before his cousins' mum realised it could be something far more sinister.

‌



Amelia and Rosie's mum, Shauna, 34, said: "Liam pulled something out and he said look at this, it looks like an old club.

View 8 Images

"I thought, that looks a little bit suspicious, so I told him to hold that still because he'd been swinging it around."

‌



The four primary school pupils had set out to clean up the waterway, expecting to find little more than discarded plastic bags and bottles.

Shauna, who works in a school, took the mysterious object from Liam and showed it to the children's granddad.

8 View 8 Images Liam Green, eight, with the bomb he pulled from the stream 8 View 8 Images Amelia Appleyard, 10, holds the corroded military training bomb which police said had already been detonated

‌



She placed it to one side as the youngsters carried on with their clean-up – but couldn't shake the nagging feeling that they may have unearthed something truly dangerous.

She said: "I put it to the side and they pulled out more things, but it just wouldn't leave my mind."

Mum-of-two Shauna carried out a Google reverse image search – and was alarmed when every result suggested the rusty object could be a military bomb.

‌



She said: "Every angle I took of this object, it kept saying it was a potential military bomb.

View 8 Images Ryan Green, six, holds the rusty military training bomb

"It didn't come up with any other explanation of what it could be."

‌



With no way of determining whether the device was still active, the family contacted the police.

Officers swiftly arrived and inspected the object before confirming it appeared to be an old military training bomb.

View 8 Images The children were litter picking when they made the discovery

‌



Shauna said: "I was shocked and bewildered.

"Police were asking us all to stay back - that's when I knew it was as serious as I'd catastrophised in my head."

To everybody's relief, it had already been detonated.

‌



However, the heavily corroded and rusty relic was still not safe for the children to handle.

Rather than being unsettled by their remarkable find, Amelia, Rosie, Liam and Ryan were absolutely delighted – and peppered officers with questions about their discovery.

View 8 Images Amelia and Rosie's mum Shauna with the four youngsters following the discovery

‌



Shauna praised the police for taking the time to fully explain what the children had unearthed.

She said: "They were absolutely brilliant and they took the time to explain it to the children, showing them how they could see it had already been detonated.

"They were really kind and I think it's really good for the children to see that side of the police."

‌



View 8 Images Amelia Appleyard, Rosie Appleyard, Liam Green and Ryan Green with a police officer

The explosive discovery has since become the undisputed highlight of the youngsters' school holidays – even overshadowing an upcoming family trip overseas.

Shauna said: "It's been the highlight of the summer.

Article continues below

"We're going to France next week and we might as well cancel because I think we've topped the excitement of the holidays.

"They've been excited beyond words. They've absolutely loved it."

News.title: 102-year-old dementia patient's family demand 'justice' after he was 'pushed from band's stage at pub'
News.content:
102-year-old dementia patient's family demand 'justice' after he was 'pushed from band's stage at pub'

Great-grandfather Phillip Ormerod, 102, died after allegedly being assaulted at the Crow's Nest pub in Cwmbran on August 1, was a “pub character” who had been diagnosed with dementia, his son Robert Ormerod has said.

View 3 Images Photo provided by Robert Ormerod of his father Phillip Ormerod, celebrating his 100th birthday (Image: Robert Ormerod/PA Wire)

The family of a 102-year-old man who died after allegedly being "pushed" from a stage as a band were playing in a pub are demanding "justice" for his death.

‌



Widower Phillip Ormerod, who was a regular at the pub near his home in Cwmbran, south Wales, was said to have asked for the music to be turned down during the performance. But it is claimed Phillip, who had dementia, was pushed away and suffered critical injuries after tumbling backwards and hitting the floor. He later died in hospital.

‌



Speaking from his father's end-of-terrace home, son Robert said his father would walk almost half a mile to the Crow's Nest pub or nearby social club two or three times a week. The great-grandfather was known by the younger punters and would often have drinks bought for him.

‌



Retired civil engineer Robert said: "What happened is not nice. The pub has changed a lot over the years. It has become a youngster's pub. Me and my brother would visit our father regularly and clean the house.

"His eyesight had deteriorated and he had been diagnosed with dementia two or three years ago. He could be difficult with having dementia. He walked to the pub two or three times a week. He was a beer drinker and I suppose some people saw him as a bit of a character at his age."

Robert said he grew up in the home where his father lived since 1960. Dad-of-two Phillip, who had a career as a design draftsman, lived at the property alone since his wife died 40 years ago. Phillip had worked as toolmaker during World War II but later joined the Merchant Navy.

‌



View 3 Images Emergency services were called to the Crow's Nest in Cwbran (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Robert added: "It has changed a lot since I grew up here and of course a lot of my father's generation are no longer here. We just hope for some justice."

A neighbour, who lives on the close in Cwmbran, South Wales, said: "It is terribly sad. He was very independent and didn’t like to have help from anybody.

‌



"He would often get lifts home from the pub by people who wanted to make sure he got home safely. He had to wait until 4am for an ambulance after it happened. He was out every day, two or three times a day. He would have been 103 next month."

Emergency services were called to The Crow's Nest in Cwbra, at around 10.25pm on Saturday August 1.

Gwent Police said: "We're continuing to appeal for witnesses following a report of an assault at The Crow’s Nest pub in Cwmbran at around 10.25pm on Saturday 1 August.

‌



View 3 Images The Crow's Nest in Cwbran where the attack took place. (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

"A 102-year-old man was taken to hospital for treatment. The man, who can now be named as Phillip Ormerod from Cwmbran, has since sadly died while in hospital."

Senior Investigating Officer, DCI Shelley Comley said: “We understand the public interest in this incident but want to remind people that not only is this an active criminal investigation but there is a family at heart of it processing the loss of a loved one.

Article continues below

“Please consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments – particularly online commentary - could have on them and the ongoing investigation as a whole.”

"Anyone who was in the pub between 10pm and 11pm on Saturday 1 August and hasn’t yet spoken to police is asked to contact us"

The pub shared the police appeal, adding: "If anyone was in the pub that night and witnessed this please get in contact with the police."

News.title: Turkey trip boat carrying 115 bursts into flames as families leap into the sea
News.content:
Turkey trip boat carrying 115 bursts into flames as families leap into the sea

The boat caught fire off the coast of Fethiye in south west Turkey with passengers, including children, forced into the water

View 3 Images The trip boat burst into flames off the coast of Fethiye (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A massive fire has erupted on a tour boat in Turkey carrying around 115 passengers forcing them into the sea.

‌



The incident took place off Fethiyein the southwestern Mugla province on Thursday with people on board, including children, leaping into the water.

‌



Coast Guard teams and nearby boats moved in to evacuate those in the water, while health teams checked passengers after they were brought ashore.

‌



View 3 Images Flames and huge plumes of smoke coming from the boat (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Households urged to contact local council immediately when 1 issue happens with bins READ MORE :

Rotterdam port explosion kills at least one with several injured and helicopter scrambled READ MORE :

Local reports say that there were 11 passengers affected by smoke who were taken to hospital by ambulances after being taken to hospital but it is understood that none are in a serious condition.

The fire is believed to have broken out in the boat's kitchen at around 11am local time in Katrancı Bay but the exact cause is not yet known. Flames quickly spread through the vessel forcing the evacuation in the sea.

‌



The blaze caused extensive damage, and reports indicated that the vessel later began to sink.

Fethiye District Governor Fatih Akkaya went to the area after the incident and confirmed that no deaths had been reported, adding that passengers were brought to safety by Coast Guard vessels and other boats nearby.

The General Directorate of Maritime Affairs announced that an investigation has been launched as part of the inquiry into the cause of the incident.

‌



View 3 Images Everybody from the boat was rescued (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The nationalities of those on board have not yet been released but tourists from around the world including the UK flock to Turkey's pristine Aegean and Mediterranean coastline each year, with boat trips extremely popular.

Meanwhile a teenager has died and 211 people were rescued following a ferry fire in Bali on Wednesday during rough seas.

‌



Videos released by the National Search and Rescue Agency showed people wearing life jackets crowding an inflatable life raft in choppy waters during a rescue operation at sea, as thick black smoke billows from the ferry.

The agency said that as of early Thursday, rescuers evacuated 211 people from the burned vessel, including seven foreign tourists, and recovered the body of a 19-year-old Indonesian woman.

The Putri Yasmin ferry was traveling from Bali to the neighbouring island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara province when the fire broke out at about 4:15am Wednesday. The ferry was also transporting 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles.

Article continues below

The Search and Rescue Office in Mataram, the capital of West Nusa Tenggara province, received an emergency report almost half an hour later and immediately deployed personnel and rescue vessels.

News.title: Households urged to contact local council immediately when 1 issue happens with bins
News.content:
Households urged to contact local council immediately when 1 issue happens with bins

A self-proclaimed 'binfluencer' has shared two handy recycling bin tips, including what to do if your lid won't close and you still have days to wait until the next collection

View Image What should you do if your recycling bin is full to the brim? (Image: SolStock via Getty Images)

A binman has shared advice to all UK residents on what to do should their recycling bins fill up prior to collection day. Refuse collector, Ashley is no stranger to sharing advice on all matters concerning our rubbish and describes himself online as a 'binfluencer'.

‌



Earlier this week he informed his followers they should take action when there's no room left for tin cans and plastic and glass bottles in the recycling bin. While the simple solution might seem to be throwing them in with general waste, for Ashley that's a big no-go.

‌



"If your recycling bin is constantly getting full, I suggest you ring your local council," he recommended in a TikTok video. "Most councils - but not all - will probably give you another bin for recycling."

‌



It really is that straightforward as he went on to explain: "It's cheaper for them to take recycling away than it is to take general waste away... so put less in your general waste bin or just take it to a recycling centre."

Ashley concluded: "Well done for filling your recycling bin up - correctly I'm hoping. You'll probably get given another bin and then it is problem solved. What more do you want?"

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



How to Get an Extra Recycling Bin from Your Local Council

Wheelie Bin Solutions shared additional advice online: "if you’ve too much rubbish for your wheelie bin, then make sure you’re only throwing out actual rubbish.

"If some of the waste could be placed in another bin, donated or reused, then sort through your waste accordingly. Otherwise, check with your local council or waste management company or take your excess waste to a recycling centre."

Why You Should Never Put Black Bags in Recycling Bins

Meanwhile, Ashley also explained why black bin bags are often rejected during recycling collections, revealing it comes down to visibility.

‌



"We don't know what's in them... black bin bags, we can't see through them, and we're not going to open them and rummage through them," Ashley said.

The binman cautioned that, as collectors are unable to see what's inside, black bags are deemed contaminated - which can result in entire bins being left uncollected.

Ashley instead urged households to place their recycling items loosely in the bin, without using any black dustbin bags.

‌



"Put it all in loose," he added. "Do not put anything in a bag in your recycling bin because it has got a chance of being contaminated and they won't take it."

Responding to Ashley's clip, one TikTok user wrote: "In my local council you can have up to three tin bin and three cardboard bin. I currently have 8 bins."

A second person commented: "I flatten/squash everything and ordered a second bin in case it still won't fit."

Article continues below

While a third added: "This is true, I have three recycling bins."

News.title: Escaped snake spotted on the loose in Glasgow city centre biting shoppers
News.content:
Escaped snake spotted on the loose in Glasgow city centre biting shoppers

A bright orange snake was spotted on busy Argyle Street, located outside one of the St Enoch Shopping Centre entrances in Glasgow

Moment snake lunges at pedestrians in Glasgow city centre

A snake has been spotted trying to bite shoppers in Glasgow city centre, with people left "raging".

‌



The bright orange reptile was seen crawling on one of the city's busiest shopping thoroughfares, Argyle Street, located outside one of the St Enoch Shopping Centre entrances. The snake was captured in a TikTok video lunging at people's ankles as they walked by.

‌



Other pictures shared online show the snake covered by a cardboard box as a security guard stands near it. The reptile is understood to have been placed in the box to be handed to staff at the shopping centre, the Daily Record reports.

‌



View 2 Images An escaped snake tried to bite shoppers in Glasgow (Image: TikTok/@mcbainthepain)

Golden retriever defies vets to survive FIVE surgeries after he's bitten by a snake READ MORE :

Couple buy cute house in small town but then realise they aren't alone READ MORE :

The animal was eventually collected by the Scottish SPCA and taken to SSPCA's Glasgow Animal Rescue and Rehoming Centre in Cardonald. It remains unclear how the snake ended up in the city centre.

‌



Writing online, one witness said: "The snake was clearly f*****g terrified and could have hurt someone." Others took to social media to share their concern.

Another said: "I know I have an irrational fear of snakes but I always control it by knowing that it is highly unlikely I’d ever come across one randomly …now this!! I was genuinely in town today."

View 2 Images The bright orange reptile was eventually captured by the Scottish SPCA (Image: TikTok/@mcbainthepain)

Article continues below

A third said: "This has made me so raging. The wee soul is in fight or flight. I’d have phoned SSPCA."

An SSPCA spokesperson said: "I can confirm that an Animal Rescue Officer from the Scottish SPCA attended and collected the snake after a member of the public handed it into security at St Enoch Shopping Centre in Glasgow on August 12.

"It was then taken to our Glasgow Animal Rescue and Rehoming Centre in Cardonald where it is now being cared for by the team."

News.title: UK sees hottest day of the year as 38.1C recorded in Kew Gardens
News.content:
The UK has experienced its hottest day of the year and fifth hottest day on record, as a heatwave that gripped much of the country peaked at 38.1C on Thursday, the Met Office said.

Kew Gardens in west London recorded England's top temperature, provisionally surpassing the 38C recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The latest spell of extreme heat marks the UK's fifth heatwave this year, with the Met Office warning this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began.

An amber heat health alert, warning of significant detrimental impacts to health and social care services is in place across the whole of England until 21:00 BST on Friday.

News.title: Five key takeaways from results day 2026
News.content:
Results for A-levels, T-levels, BTecs and other vocational qualifications are out.

And this year, they've come at a time when all eyes are on what teenagers decide to do next.

Universities are keen to get them through the door. As they grapple with their finances, they know that every filled seat in a lecture hall comes with tuition fee funding.

The new prime minister, meanwhile, wants to carve out clear routes into technical jobs that can rival the well-established path of A-levels and a university degree.

For teenagers, considerations about the immediate and long-term cost of university, as well as the availability of other options, are all in the mix.

Here are the standout things you need to know.

News.title: Son pays tribute to dad, 102, who died after allegedly being assaulted in pub
News.content:
The son of a 102-year-old great-grandfather who died after allegedly being assaulted at a south Wales pub says he was a "pub character".

Phillip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following the incident at the Crow's Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

Gwent Police confirmed on Thursday that he had since died.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains under investigation.

Ormerod's son, Robert Ormerod, said his dad had been diagnosed with dementia and was a widower who lived alone.

News.title: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes by looking at the eclipse
News.content:
Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

News.title: Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged
News.content:
A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

The pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims on the first day of their trial in June.

Mihai, 31, and Dumitru, 30, were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

News.title: Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding
News.content:
Water companies have been given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra Â£3.4bn in coming years to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Nearly a third of the extra funding provisionally approved for 13 water companies in England and Wales is earmarked for making sure water services are maintained.

Some of the rest will be used to meet rising demand from housebuilding and data centres and to address pollutants known as "forever chemicals".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the proposal was "real money out of family budgets at a time when they are struggling with the cost of living", and an environmental group described the decision as "an insult".

Customers of five water companies - Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water, and South East Water - are facing additional bill rises over the next two years, on top of increases that were already announced in 2024.

The new increases will vary between firms.

Southern, for example, will charge Â£43 extra next year, while South Eastern will only charge Â£1 more in 2029. The increases will only come into effect if they are given final approval later this year.

The other eight water firms identified - Anglian Water, Dwr Cymru Welsh Water, Hafren Dyfrdwy, Northumbrian Water, Wouth West Water, United Utiliites, Yorkshire Water, SES Water - would recover their additional spending through customer bills after 2030.

Many consumers are angry at being asked to pay anything more against a backdrop of interruptions to supply sometimes lasting for days, and rivers, lakes and beaches too polluted to use safely.

But water companies argue that these problems can only be solved by boosting spending to replace pipes, build treatment plants and establish new reservoirs.

Climate change has also increased pressure on the water infrastructure by making heavy rains and heatwaves more frequent.

News.title: Voting under way in Clacton by-election
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Clacton by-election as a record number of candidates vie to become its next MP.

Fifty-one polling stations in the Essex resort, which includes the towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze, opened at 07:00 BST and will shut at 22:00.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Dating app Bumble divides users by ditching its signature 'women-first' chat rule
News.content:
Dating app Bumble has divided its users by dropping its signature rule which allowed only women to send the first message to a match.

When the app launched 2014, founder and boss Whitney Wolfe Herd said it distinguished itself from rivals like Tinder by allowing women to "make the first move".

But the thing that made Bumble famous will now be ditched following a trial which showed more engagement - and a survey among users which found 66% of women prefer men to send the first message.

Reaction across online forums has highlighted a divide among users about whether the update will get more people using Bumble - or if it makes it "just like any other dating app".

Previously, only same-sex relationships did not have to follow the women-first rule.

Another change coming to Bumble will extend the time-limit users have to initiate a conversation after matching.

Users will now have three days to begin messaging one another instead of 24 hours.

"While women making the first move was a radical idea, being women-first was never about prescribing just one way to connect," said Wolfe Herd.

"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides."

In an April 2015 interview shortly after Bumble's launch, Herd Wolfe told the Toronto Star it was a "stereotype to say women like to sit back and want men to come to them".

News.title: Dad to stand trial accused of murdering daughter Minnie Merriman
News.content:
The father of a nine-year-old girl who died after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in Arbroath is to stand trial accused of her murder.

Prosecutors allege Christopher Rice, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, killed Minnie Merriman, who died in Dundee's Ninewells Hospital on 3 August.

The 35-year-old, who was remanded in custody, made no plea during a second appearance in private via videolink at Forfar Sheriff Court. He was fully committed for trial.

Minnie's family previously paid tribute to their "beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo".

Emergency services were called to the Elliot Industrial Estate in Arbroath shortly after midnight on 3 August following reports that a child had been found injured.

Minnie was taken to Ninewells Hospital alongside four other people, but later died as a result of her injuries.

Police Scotland said they were not looking for anyone else in connection with Minnie's death and the other members of the family - who were camping in the area - are being supported by specialist officers.

News.title: Bishop appears in court over child rape charges
News.content:
A 70-year-old bishop has appeared in court for the first time accused of two counts of rape against a female under the age of 16.

David Oakley, the Bishop of Northampton, was charged in June following an investigation by Staffordshire Police.

He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court via videolink from his lawyer's office.

Oakley was not asked to enter a plea during the hearing as Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring sent the case to the Old Bailey.

Oakley was released on bail, with conditions not to contact the alleged victim, or her family, ahead of a plea hearing on 10 September.

The incidents allegedly took place in Staffordshire between February 2000 and February 2001, when Oakley was in his mid-40s working as a Catholic priest.

Oakley was born in Stourbridge, West Midlands, and ordained as a priest in 1980 before becoming Bishop of Northampton in 2020.

Oakley retains the title of Bishop but has withdrawn from public ministry.

The Catholic Diocese of Northampton - which covers Northamptonshire, Bedfordshire and Buckinghamshire â said in a previous statement that it recognised the case was "very distressing for all concerned".

News.title: Human bones found in south-east London garden
News.content:
Human bones found in the garden of a bungalow in south-east London are being examined by the Met Police.

Officers were called to Aperfield Road in Biggin Hill at about 15:30 BST last Friday, the force said.

The bones were sent for specialist examination which confirmed they were human. They are now undergoing further tests to establish their age and identity, police added.

The area around the home was cordoned off for six days, according to The Sun, external, with one resident telling the newspaper the property was being renovated.

"The builders discovered something on Friday and of course they completely had to stop work," they added.

A Metropolitan Police spokesperson added: "The crime scene is now closed and an investigation remains ongoing to establish the full circumstances."
