Richards (20-4-1, 13 KOs) is a world-ranked former British champion who fought Dmitry Bivol for the WBA light-heavyweight title in 2021. He won his two most recent fights in 2025, including a knockout win over Dan Azeez last December.

The fight will mark the first time hard-hitting, Serbian-born Kalajdzic (30-3, 22 KOs) has fought outside North America as a professional. The 35-year-old's last fight was a seventh-round knockout victory against Oleksandr Gvozdyk in February.

The Copper Box Arena bill will also feature a 10-round middleweight showdown between British boxers Cutler and Greene.

Cutler beat Stevie McKenna on points when they fought in December 2024, marking the only professional defeat for Ireland's KO king so far.

Image: Lee Cutler and Louis Greene clash at middleweight

Cutler's last fight saw him stop Aaron Sutton in his hometown of Bournemouth in three rounds, while Greene - a former Commonwealth super-welterweight champion - earned a points decision win over Daniel Buciuc in Dublin last week.

Decorated British amateur Kayla Allen is also fighting as part of her professional debut after becoming the first female fighter to sign with Zuffa Boxing.

Alex MacMillan, Leon Hughes and Fred Pullen, who is also turning professional, are also on the London bill.

Richards: My story isn't written yet - the time is now

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Having announced he'll face Radivoje Kalajdzic on Zuffa Boxing 11's undercard, Craig Richards believes he'll now be able to be able to get the big fights after linking up with the new promotional company.

Craig "Spider" Richards speaking on Sky Sports News:

"It's a very exciting fight. Everyone knows Kalajdzic can punch, I can punch, we've both been two fighters who haven't shied away from competition.

"We've been in with everyone, we've mixed it, we both probably want to push on now towards that world title and I feel like it's a great opportunity.

"UK vs USA - that mix always goes down well! I'm up for it, I'm excited and I think this is now going to be the best version of me going into the new chapter and I get to go and display what I'm about.

Image: Richards is looking for another shot at a world title

"I feel like my story is not written yet and I feel like I need to write it now.

"The problem we had before is that a lot of opponents were turning [a fight with] me down, saying 'he's a hard fight, he's a long night in the office'.

"Zuffa doesn't allow you to do that, and that means I can get some activity. I can go out there and make a statement."

Watch Johnny Fisher's next fight at London's Copper Box Arena, on Saturday September 26, live on Sky Sports. Get Sky Sports or stream boxing with no contract.

Sports.title: The Hundred awards: Broad, Hussain, Greenway give their player verdicts
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain and Stuart Broad give out their player awards for the 2026 men's Hundred campaign, while Lydia Greenway looks at the women's competition...

Best local player

Stuart Broad:

"Jos Buttler is into the eliminator with Manchester Super Giants. Batting three, he's scored vital runs at vital times.

"He's England's best-ever white-ball batter. He's the icon of that MSG franchise.

"He's a leader in that changing room and he's got a chance of lifting the trophy."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch all of Jos Butler's sixes from The Hundred match between Manchester Super Giants and Birmingham Phoenix

Nasser Hussain:

"Ben Duckett went straight to the final with Trent Rockets and avoided the eliminator. That's how well he's played.

"Top of the order, he plays spin, plays fast bowling, hits it in unusual areas. He's been brilliant in the field.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player 'He's toying with them!' | A brilliant 50 for Ben Duckett!

"Also, at the top of the order, the way he's set the tone for that middle order of the Trent Rockets, it's just nice to see Duckett playing with such confidence and such flair.

I mentioned his fielding as well, which we do have a section on, but he's been excellent. I'm very impressed."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Spectators look up at the sky as the solar eclipse can be seen during MI London's game with Birmingham Phoenix at Edgbaston

Lydia Greenway:

"I've gone for the leading wicket taker in the tournament, Tilly Corteen-Coleman. I think she's taken 13 wickets.

"The reason I picked her, she's just been really consistent. Not just this season but over the last couple of seasons.

"It's great to see her top of the tree with the wickets."

Best overseas player

Stuart Broad:

"Mitch Marsh has played some really eye-catching innings. He's batting at one of the best batting services in the country at Headingley, and he's been really entertaining.

"He's done exactly what you want an overseas player at the top of the order to do. He's led from the front. He's set the tone. He's guided his teams to win.

"His average is higher when they win than when they lose, which means he's playing a key role in winning games. Look at his strike rate, nearly 170.

"So I think he's been really crucial and a really clever signing."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Marsh hits MONSTER six out Trent Bridge ground!

Nasser Hussain:

"Mitch Marsh. Compare his consistency to someone like Harry Brook. Now, Harry's a very fine player, but a lot of his runs have come at Headingley on that belter of a surface.

"Mitch Marsh knows Headingley well, he's got Test runs there. He loves it, but he's also gone away from home at Trent Bridge, Manchester. He's got runs all around the country.

"I like the way he's a very simple person. He's a very simple player. You pitch it up, he belts it straight back past you. You drop your length back just a fraction and he'll pull you for six.

"I just love the way he keeps it very simple. And for an Aussie, he's a really nice top bloke."

Best value for money

Nasser Hussain:

"I've gone Calvin Harrison, because he came in late as a replacement player.

"Around about £31,000 was the replacement figure. And he's bowled beautifully. He's got eight wickets.

"He's fielded really well, we've seen some of his extraordinary catches, but I just think to come in at the last moment and play, he's a real talented cricketer.

"That's someone England should be looking at across formats. He bats very well - he hasn't had much chance with the bat because the Trent Rockets have been so good - but value for money, I'm going Calvin Harrison and what he's done for the Trent Rockets."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Calvin Harrison produces a sensational caught and bowled to dismiss Will Jacks in The Hundred game between MI London and Trent Rockets

Stuart Broad:

"I completely agree with Nasser. Calvin Harrison's been absolutely superb and now it's my time to be honest and say I've got this completely wrong with Adil Rashid, because he's on £250k to play!

"Yes, he's been very successful but as Nasser, I think, got newcomer wrong, I might have got value for money wrong because a quarter of a million pounds is quite a lot of money for eight games.

"He's been fantastic, Adil Rashid, as he was going to be.

"He's one of those players that I think every single team would have been talking about at the start of the auction. You know what you're going to get. He just delivers time after time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Adil Rashid once again showed how he can be a game changer with the ball as he took three SunRisers wickets in just five deliveries

"His leg spin, which is always crucial. We're in a dry spell, so it's going to spin a little bit more.

"He's one of those players that could have gone for a lot more. When you're talking about Harry Brook at £465k, Jofra Archer at £450k at the same franchise, that's where I sneaked in my value for money, because he's virtually half the price of Archer, but he performs.

Lydia Greenway:

"I've gone for Charley Phillips again here. I think she was a bargain at £15k.

"It's brilliant to see a player like her in the form that she's been in.

"And the wickets that I've mentioned, she's got big wickets. She's got Sophie Devine, Georgia Voll has been in there, Phoebe Litchfield as well, Hollie Armitage.

"So she's just been able to go in, has got quite a slingy action and just hits the top of off-stump. So it's been a pleasure to watch."

Love to watch

Nasser Hussain:

"Adil Rashid. Because in an era when spin bowlers have to bowl it quickly, have to bowl it into the surface, I still love the fact that Adil Rashid is brave enough to toss the ball up with all the variations.

"He's right at the top of his game, in an era where spinners sometimes just bowl darts.

"Adil Rashid, love watching him."

Stuart Broad:

"Trent Boult. He's done a few quirky things on the field, celebrations. He particularly upset Jonny Bairstow at Lords, but that was his ball of the tournament for me, the inswinger into the bottom of leg stump.

"I spoke to Jonny and think it was a bit of choice language that sent him off, but that's what Trent does. He's a little bit unusual at times, but he's an incredible bowler.

Sports.title: Atherton: 'England must become Root's team - he has a unique opportunity'
Sports.content:
Fresh from exclusively speaking to Joe Root following his reappointment as England captain, Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton looks further into the move...

Sitting down with Joe Root, he seemed pretty relaxed, optimistic and excited about taking on the captaincy for a second time.

And there's a fundamental reason for that, I suppose. How many of us in life get a second chance at something?

When you're made captain or you lead an organisation, people always say: 'Make sure you do it your way and don't have any regrets at the end of it because you won't get another go at this.'

Joe Root is getting another go at it.

The key points from Joe Root's interview Root rules out curfew despite ECB guidelines and tells players to "be adults" when using alcohol

The England captain was "gutted" at the departure of former England Test head coach McCullum departure but has reasserted his excitement for a new era with incoming coach Stephen Fleming, who he admires

Root admits to "over-bowling" Jofra Archer during his first spell as captain but has vowed to protect England's "generational talent" this time around

Root has refused to rule out a return for Ben Stokes for the 2027 Ashes

How many of us would love to retrace our steps and have another go at something that we did well or not so well the first time around? He's got that opportunity now.

He's got a chance to bring all his wisdom and his knowledge and perhaps right some of the mistakes he made first time around.

I mean, he had a good time of it as England captain. Nobody has won more games in the role; equally, nobody has lost as many, so it wasn't a completely smooth ride for him.

The hope is that he can bring a lot of that knowledge and wisdom to bear the second time around.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Root gives his first interview since being reappointed England Test captain

He will want to do it a little bit differently, because you've got to think that between his first coming and his second coming as captain, there's been four years of Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum driving an England team to play in a way that probably no other England team in the history of the game has played.

Root is coming in on the back of that.

A lot of our interview is about how he wants to keep certain things of Bazball - if you want to call it that - but also tweak some things and put his own stamp on it.

This has now got to be Root's team again, not Stokes' team. So the transition to that will be a fascinating one.

'Captaincy won't affect Root like last time, nor his batting'

I asked him whether it was out of a desire to do it or a duty because there are very few other options.

You have to remember that when he gave up the captaincy the first time around, he talked about having an unhealthy relationship with it, so I put a couple of questions about that to him.

Is he certain he won't be damaged by the captaincy again? A lot of the answers revolve around the COVID years.

He had to lead England during a couple of COVID years, and he felt that had a particular negative impact on him.

Of course, it is a very different time now.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking after the New Zealand Test win in 2022, Root explained why he'd taken the decision to step-away from Test captaincy

And I'm confident the pressures of captaincy won't impact how he performs with the bat. It didn't the first time around.

Although in the interview he says he felt it impacted him initially, he actually felt that, in the last year or 18 months of his captaincy, he was batting as well as ever. The numbers suggest he did pretty well as a batting captain; I think he averaged 46 during that time.

The biggest line is about the curfew, which we put out there. And I'm very happy that he's done that.

Curfews are a crazy way to run a grown-up, professional sporting team. I'm very glad that, between him and new Test coach Stephen Fleming, they've sat down and said: 'Let's treat these players as grown-ups.'

If they step out of line and mess up, there is going to be consequences. Your expectations have to be clear to the players, but treat people like grown-ups.

Sports.title: Australia exposed by Bangladesh in stunning start to first Test
Sports.content:
Bangladesh's bowlers overshadowed Australia's Big Four getting back together on day one of the first Test as the hosts were dismissed for 198 and Hasan Mahmud took a career-best 6-55.

Bangladesh's top-order batters then combined to reach 96-1 at stumps and cut the first-innings deficit to 102.

Bangladesh lost their last Test match against Zimbabwe in June by an innings and 85 runs but in Darwin on Thursday made a dream start to their tour of Australia, where they are playing their first Test series since 2003.

Australia are beginning a schedule of at least 20 Tests over the coming 12 months, with tours of New Zealand, South Africa, India and England - where The Ashes begins at Trent Bridge from June 18. Steve Smith admitted their start against Bangladesh was "not our best"

"Still plenty of cricket to be played, obviously," Smith added.

"It would have been nice to have taken a few more [wickets]. So, hopefully we start ⁠well in the morning, pick up a few early ones and ⁠put pressure on."

Mahmud starred for the visitors with consistent line and length, striking in his sixth and seventh overs to remove openers Jake Weatherald (23) and Travis Head (22) after Australia won the toss and raced to 45 without loss on a green-tinged pitch.

Image: Bangladesh's Hasan Mahmud made the difference with the ball on day one

From there, Mahmud and fellow pacemen Taskin Ahmed (2-55) and Ebadot Hossain (2-39) dominated the first two sessions, bowling with discipline to exploit the conditions and get on top of a batting line-up that was held together primarily by Smith's defiant 71.

Smith was the next-to-last wicket to fall, advancing at Mahmud before top-edging a high catch to wicketkeeper Litton Das, bringing an innings featuring seven boundaries and a six to an end.

The day started positively for the hosts, with skipper Pat Cummins winning the toss. Playing just his second Test in 13 months, he reunited with fellow pacemen Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc and veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon in a frontline attack long known in Australia as the Big Four.

A partisan crowd was in full support of Darwin-born Weatherald but he never really settled and needlessly swiped at a ball from Mahmud. Head was out soon after, chopping on a delivery that was bowled from around the wicket as Australia slipped to 52-2.

Ebadot had Marnus Labuschagne (1) caught by Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto, and could have dismissed Smith early too, but a chance at third slip was put down.

Despite having their first-choice bowling attack back together, Australia were unable to take more than one Bangladesh wicket, with Mominul Haque (35) and Tanzid Hasan (32) going on to share an unbeaten 60-run stand.

'Opportunity here that may have been missed' - Ponting questions Australia selectors

Speaking to Australia's Channel 7, former captain Ricky Ponting said: "Look, what's the state of Australian cricket?

"This has been a very, very successful cricket team. (But) right now, there are a couple of chinks in the armour and the selectors decided to stick with what they know.

"At the end of last season, I thought the time was right now to blood a couple of youngsters into these two Test matches. I said (Campbell) Kellaway and (Ollie) Peake were the ones that I wanted to have.

"So they decided not to do that. But my worry is, when do they do that? Are you going to debut these guys in South Africa against (Kagiso) Rabada and (Marco) Jansen and co?

"I think that would be a whole lot harder. So I just feel there's an opportunity here that may have been missed."

Sports.title: Carrick rules out £100m signing for Manchester United as Rashford rejoins squad
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing this summer due to their finances, with the manager also insisting that Marcus Rashford “is our player” despite the forward and club preferring him to depart.

In the current window United have invested a total of £85m on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos but have never spent £100m on a single transfer.

This is in contrast to Manchester City, Tottenham, Liverpool, Arsenal, and Chelsea, the rest of the traditional top six, who have all spent £100m-plus on a player in recent years.

Carrick was asked how United can compete. “Money’s money. I get that,” said the manager. “It’s still about football and that’s where the competition lies. What we feel naturally as a group is to try and win games. So there’s a lot that goes into that, but certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever.”

Carrick guided United to third last season and was asked why the money from Champions League qualification cannot be invested in expensive elite players.

“To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it,” he said. “For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, push everything in every boundary that we can to be able to win again, basically.”

The 45-year-old was asked whether United can win the title without any players worth £100m or more in the squad.

Carrick said: “A little bit depends on what position that is and what you’ve got and the dynamics you need at certain points. Sometimes you do need that if it’s the right player. Again, it’s not purely on money. Obviously over time we need to be pushing to look to enhance the squad. So, yeah, 100% we need to do that.

“We’ve done really good business. So we’re delighted with that [but] we want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that, so that never stops.”

View image in fullscreen Youri Tielemans, who arrived from Aston Villa, was one of United’s big summer signings. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

Rashford joined the squad at their County Kildare training camp base on Sunday following a post-World Cup break. The 28-year-old has been on loan the past season and a half at Barcelona and Aston Villa respectively, due to a breakdown in his relationship with the club’s executive and the former United head coach Ruben Amorim.

Relations have eased and Rashford is focused on working under Carrick, though the player’s preference is to depart. The club want the same as they seek to reduce the wage bill. The forward’s final two years of his deal are worth £35m.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Carrick was asked if Rashford will stay beyond the 1 September deadline. “He’s our player and has trained really well,” said Carrick. “It’s been good to have him around the group again.”

The manager was asked if he wants Rashford to remain. “He’s a very good player, Marcus, and if you’re going to have a career over 10 or 15 years, there’s going to be times when things go in a direction and maybe a different direction. All right, that happens,” he said. “There’s ups and downs, and that doesn’t judge you as a one-off kind of [state]. It’s what happens over time, and now we’re in a positive place as a group, and Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so it’s quite exciting.”

Asked if Carrick views Rashford as not for sale, he said: “No, he’s our player and he gives something a little bit different in the group.”

Harry Maguire, Noussair Mazraoui and Tielemans have all indicated United can win the championship. “We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” said Carrick. “I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that – it’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because that’s the club we are.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 8: Crystal Palace
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 16th (NB: this is not necessarily Ed Aarons’ prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 15th

Prospects

After winning a third trophy in the space of 12 months under Oliver Glasner with the Conference League triumph at the end of May, Crystal Palace fans were brought down to earth with a bump at the start of July when the Austrian was unveiled as Nottingham Forest’s new manager. Seeing the man who led the south London club to the first major honours in their history jump ship to the team who many believe played a part in Palace’s demotion from the Europa League was a bitter pill to swallow, even if the highly rated Pierre Sage had been confirmed as Glasner’s replacement three weeks earlier.

While the fans must wait until October for him and Forest to visit Selhurst Park, the Frenchman’s task is now to try to build on Glasner’s unprecedented success while juggling the demands of a Europa League campaign. The departure of Maxence Lacroix has left Palace’s defence without a natural leader and replacing the France defender with a similar character could go a long way to determining how they fare.

Daichi Kamada’s decision to sign a new one-year contract rather than follow Glasner out of the door means that – at the time of writing – eight of the players who started in the FA Cup final victory over Manchester City last year remain at the club. The tricky bit will be holding on to the likes of Daniel Muñoz, Adam Wharton and Ismaïla Sarr until the window closes, with Muñoz attracting interest from Saudi Arabia.

Spending around £80m on Jørgen Strand Larsen and Brennan Johnson in January looks even more mistaken after agreeing a deal with Everton to swap the latter for Dwight McNeil seven months later. That has restricted Palace’s budget this summer and could come back to haunt Sage if he cannot strengthen the squad sufficiently with another marathon season ahead.

Off-field picture

To everyone’s great relief, work finally started on the new main stand at Selhurst Park this summer almost a decade after the plans were first announced. Expected to cost at least £150m and be completed by late 2028 or early 2029, it will increase the capacity of Selhurst Park to 34,000. Yet the financial strain of a much-needed project has complicated matters off the pitch, with Josh Harris, David Blitzer, and Woody Johnson reportedly keen to sell their combined 79% stakes despite Palace’s recent success. It will be up to Steve Parish, the chair who has guided Palace through their best-ever era, to convince them to stay on or find some new partners.

Owner-fan relationship

Having stepped in to help rescue Palace from administration in 2010, lifelong supporter Parish has been instrumental in establishing the club in the Premier League and will always be remembered for leading them to a first major piece of silverware. But that doesn’t mean he is exempt from criticism and there are many fans who blame the 61-year-old for failing to keep hold of Glasner after not strengthening the squad sufficiently last summer after their FA Cup success. Palace are still missing the calming influence and talent-spotting skills of Dougie Freedman, the former sporting director who surprisingly left for Saudi Arabia last March.

The manager

Sage worked wonders at Lens last season in only his second senior post as a manager, guiding them to second place in Ligue 1 before winning the Coupe de France. Having cut his teeth as a youth team coach at Lyon, the 47-year-old from eastern France who stopped playing at the age of 24 to concentrate on his coaching career seized his opportunity when he was promoted to become interim manager in November 2023. But he lasted only a year having been given the job permanently before moving to Lens six months later. Sage has still yet to manage 100 matches at professional level and his appointment looks risky. Palace are banking on him bringing stability.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Óscar Mingueza: from Barcelona to south east London via Celta Vigo. Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images

Óscar Mingueza missed out on being part of the Spain squad that won the World Cup but the former Barcelona defender who was signed on a free transfer after his contract with Celta Vigo expired looks an excellent addition. He is capable of playing on the right of a back three but prefers wing-back and was outstanding for Celta last season. Aston Villa and Newcastle were rumoured to have been interested in the 27-year-old, who’s won four caps for Spain’s senior team and came through Barça’s La Masia academy, making 66 appearances. His sister, Ariadna, also plays for Spain.

Stat attack

The biggest challenge facing the new Crystal Palace manager is making the side’s attack more productive. While just seven teams in the 2025-26 Premier League generated more expected goals in open play, only Wolves scored fewer. The gap between the figures was 0.31 per game for Palace, the second-worst mark in the big five leagues behind Pisa (0.36), who finished bottom of Serie A.

Set for a breakthrough

Joél Drakes-Thomas made his senior debut in the Conference League at the age of just 16 years and 192 days in December before becoming Palace’s youngest-ever Premier League player by more than a year two days later. The winger has been a regular for England’s Under-16s and starred for Palace’s Under-18s as they won the Premier League Cup in April, as well as playing 45 minutes for the first team in their FA Cup defeat to non-league Macclesfield. There are high hopes that Drakes-Thomas could be the next big star to emerge from Palace’s academy that was upgraded to category one status in 2020.

World Cup impact

Yéremy Pino only managed 69 minutes in two substitute appearances for Spain during the group stages before suffering a collarbone injury that ruled him out of the rest of the tournament. But the forward still picked up a winners’ medal – the first-ever Palace player to do so. Elsewhere, Sarr continued his brilliant club form with four goals for Senegal, with Kamada and Muñoz making it eight in total for the Palace contingent. Meanwhile, goalkeeper Dean Henderson became the first Palace player to feature for England in a World Cup finals match in the third place playoff against France.

Sports.title: Kieran Trippier: ‘The Championship is relentless … it’s totally different to the Premier League’
Sports.content:
When the question inevitably comes, Kieran Trippier is happy to set the record straight. Fresh from training, head to toe in Wolves kit – vest, shorts and club-branded sliders – he walks into a suite at their Compton Park base, conversation soon shifting to an episode that rocked supporters and stopped outsiders in their tracks: three days after signing, the manager Trippier cited as a significant driver behind his decision to drop into the second tier, Rob Edwards, was sacked. All the while, a deal for his replacement, César Peixoto, was being accelerated.

“I’m not going to sit here and lie, I wasn’t expecting it,” Trippier says. “But it’s the club’s decision. I had good chats with Rob, of course, but I’m here to play for Wolves. There are many surprises in football and that certainly was a surprise, I’m not going to deny that. But I just cracked on, I was with my kids on holiday, training in Mallorca and just looking forward to day one in pre-season.”

Other reports followed the bombshell news. “I’ve read it all: that I was looking to rip my contract up, and all this nonsense. I was just looking forward to reporting back to Wolves. I don’t know where it even came from to be honest, that I was looking to rip my contract up – it certainly didn’t come from me, otherwise you would have heard it from me, that’s just the player that I am.”

It is a line in keeping with Trippier’s endearing straight-talking character that has made him a big hit everywhere he has been. He left Newcastle at the end of last season after playing an instrumental part in their rise under Eddie Howe, the crowning glory the Carabao Cup win last year. He spent three seasons at Atlético Madrid under Diego Simeone, where he won La Liga, after four at Tottenham under Mauricio Pochettino, culminating in a Champions League final appearance. He represented England at four major tournaments, playing every game en route to the Euro 2024 final.

Now he is back in the second tier for the first time since promotion with Burnley 12 years ago, poised to start Wolves’ Championship opener against Blackburn on Friday. He accepts it is not a natural segue. Instead of entertaining Barcelona at St James’ Park last September, here comes Bolton at Molineux in October.

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier in a huddle with his new teammates during Wolves’ 3-0 friendly win against Racing Santander. Photograph: WWFC

“I’m not ashamed to go to the Championship because I played in it for many years,” Trippier says, recalling his first taste of the division: defending alongside Darren Moore while a teenager at Barnsley. “I had a good chat with Eddie Howe and Ross Wilson [Newcastle’s sporting director] and made my decision at the end of the season that I wanted to try something new. There were a few [interested] clubs but it was important for me that I was close to my children.”

Trippier, who calls Manchester home, knows what to expect from an unforgiving league. He recalls being part of a Burnley side that triumphed 2-1 at Wolves in the penultimate game of 2012-13, to extinguish lingering fears of relegation and all but condemn Wolves to League One. “I’ve been speaking to my teammates because the majority of them have never played in the Championship, so it’s important for myself and the lads who have to help them and try and make them understand that it’s going to be difficult.

“I’ve just said: it’s relentless, because it is … and it’s totally different to the Premier League. Going to Lincoln away is going to be a difficult game, but they’re good lads who have listened to me, Tommy [Doyle], Adam [Armstrong]. The lads will be ready.”

This is Trippier’s first external interview since joining Wolves on a two-year contract with the option of a further 12 months. He canvassed the opinions of Doyle, Conor Coady, John Ruddy and Sam Johnstone, with whom he was on holiday in Turkey before signing, to tap into “the insides of the club”. Edwards’ sudden departure – a month after André committed his future to the club and 48 hours after Raúl Jiménez returned to enhance the feelgood factor generated by Trippier’s arrival – warrants discussion, but the full-back is well placed to talk on numerous fronts, including Howe’s exit after four and a half years.

“He helped the club stay in the Premier League, twice qualified for the Champions League, won a trophy, but the most important thing he did was reconnecting the supporters with the team. I was told before the [Saudi Arabia-led] takeover that it was not a good place to be – the fans were against the owners, the board etc – but when the new owners came in, and the manager, he [Howe] connected everyone, just like Gareth Southgate did with England.”

Is Howe’s legacy deserving of a statue? “He’s won a trophy, hasn’t he?” Trippier says with a smile, “but that’s not for me to decide … the parade was incredible, the big banner of the manager showed the love the supporters had for him and still have now. When I first went there, it was a tough place [to play], especially after getting beat by Cambridge [in the FA Cup third round], but maybe that was a blessing, really, so we could just focus on [staying in] the Premier League … he will go down in history there, for sure. I’m gutted to see him go.”

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier holds the Carabao Cup trophy aloft with Alexander Isak on board the open-top bus with their teammates and manager Eddie Howe (front row, left) as they pass St James’ Park. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Then there is England’s World Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina, when their low block crumbled late on. “I’ve been in that position many, many times with Simeone – I could name 30 games when he’s done it and we’ve managed to see it out, typical Simeone for you. He’s the master of the dark arts and seeing out games. Thomas Tuchel has been in that position many, many times, won a Champions League trophy with Chelsea, did unbelievably with Bayern Munich … it just didn’t happen. We were against one of the greatest players ever who can flick a switch,” Trippier says of Lionel Messi, clicking his fingers. “I’ve played against him many times where he just walks for 60 minutes, but then he can score a hat-trick. That’s just the magic of him.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Peixoto is unknown to most but Trippier says he was aware of the Portuguese’s pedigree before the 46-year-old, who spent last season in charge of Gil Vicente, succeeded Edwards. Peixoto’s command of English has meant Trippier has not needed to dip into his Spanish to converse. “When the postman used to come in Madrid, I used to get my son to answer because he was fluent,” Trippier says, smiling.

So, what’s Peixoto like? “Really demanding. Honest. On the training field he is 100mph, nuts – in a good way – but he’s really, really demanding and I think that’s what we need as players if we want to be successful. He’s very demanding, like Pochettino and Simeone. He has his own rules: don’t break his trust, don’t be late. I wouldn’t like to be on his bad side, let’s put it that way.”

View image in fullscreen The Wolves manager, César Peixoto (second right), slows down from his 100mph on the training pitch to speak with Kieran Trippier (left), Andre (centre) and Toti Gomes at a pre-season training in Faro, Portugal. Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty Images

Trippier turns 36 in September, twice the age of Mateus Mané, an exciting talent who Trippier witnessed first-hand when marking him with Newcastle last season and one of those Wolves hope will illuminate a positive season. “I feel good, I feel probably in the best shape I’ve been in for many, many years. I’m not as fast as I used to be but I always believe I am clever and fast up here,” Trippier says, tapping his temples. “I feel like I’ve still got many years left in the tank.”

For Wolves, his signing was a coup. “It’s similar to when I went to Newcastle, when I left Atlético Madrid … There were a lot of eyebrows raised, but throughout my whole career I’ve had no regrets.”

Trippier, who is part of Peixoto’s leadership group, acknowledges he and his teammates will begin the campaign with a target on their backs. “Going into the Blackburn game, the first game of the Championship season, all eyes will be on us,” he says.

“When teams get relegated from the Premier League, everybody wants to beat them. It was a tough year for Wolves last year, but this season is a new season, like a reset. The reality is now we’re in the Championship, so you have to forget what happened and look forward, be positive. Our goal has to be to go straight back up to the Premier League.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Brian Madjo and the tendency to lump expectations on young shoulders
Sports.content:
A STAR/SUPERNOVA IS BORN

Aston Villa supporters could have been forgiven for approaching the new season with feelings of great anxiety, nagging angst and face-twitching trepidation. Youri Tielemans has gone: such an elegant player with an eye [and nose? – Football Daily Ed] for the spectacular. Morgan Rogers has also departed: so energetic and skilful, always carrying that goal threat. And goodbye to Lucas Digne. But Villa fans who have been keeping their eye trained behind the curtain may not have been quite so concerned. Earlier this month, their 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo – 6ft4in, body of iron ore – was cleared by the court of arbitration for sport to play competitive fixtures for the club. Born in London but already capped for Luxembourg, Villa and Fifa were in diagreed over whether Madjo, signed from Metz in January for £10m, qualified as a home purchase or an international transfer. If it was the latter, as a minor, he wouldn’t have been eligible until turning 18 next January. While waiting for the verdict, Madjo banged in four goals in pre-season friendlies, against Walsall, Real Sociedad and Indonesia All Stars, and upon finally being cleared for the big boys, could have scored as many again in 45 minutes against the best team in the world, Paris Saint-Germain.

Having become the youngest player ever to start in Uefa’s annual amuse-bouche, Madjo took a smidgen less than those 45 minutes against PSG to become the youngest to score in one. He’d already missed three gilt-edged chances by the time he bagged his goal, showcasing if nothing else an innate ability to turn up at the right place at the right time. When he finally converted, it was the hardest chance of all, roofing a volley from a tight angle on the left; all the while, he casually flung two-time European champion and Ecuador international Willian Pacho around like an old tattered sock. A bravura performance on debut, then, and the precursor to a tug-of-love between Luxembourg, for whom he’s only played friendlies, and England – the young man was born in Enfield but brought up in the Grand Duchy when his Cameroonian parents moved there (Cameroon have yet to throw their hat into the ring, but they’re surely tug-adjacent at the very least).

All of this comes with the usual supermassive-star-or-supernova caveats: there’s nothing to be gained from lumping expectation on young shoulders too soon. Remember how Andy Carroll appeared to have all the tools too … why aye. But there’s also no point in flat-out denying the increasing insurgence of youth in today’s game – Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal is one competent Bigger Cup campaign away from completing football, and he’s only 19 for goodness sake – so file Madjo (17) and his fellow Super Cup teammate George Hemmings (19) alongside Arsenal’s Max Dowman (16), Manchester United’s JJ Gabriel (15), Liverpool’s Rio Ngumoha (17) and Manchester City’s Ryan McAidoo (18) as some of the prospects to keep an avuncular eye on. We also hear Portugal are planning their Euro 2028 hopes around some lad at Al-Nassr; we’ll keep you updated once we’ve found out a bit more about him.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I don’t know what I’m going to do without you, I don’t know how to carry on. All I ever did was play football, and now I have a fair few doubts as to whether I’ll carry on doing it for much longer. You were by my side from the start, we were so ⁠close to the end [of my career]. Why didn’t you hang on just that little bit longer so we could finish it together?” – Lionel Messi ponders his future in football after the death of his father and agent, Jorge, at the age of 68. The Argentina superstar was persuaded to play at the World Cup by his father, whose health deteriorated in the days before the start of the tournament. On Wednesday, Messi made his first appearance for Inter Miami since Jorge’s funeral in a 3-2 defeat to Club León in the Leagues Cup.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi could not prevent Inter Miami’s defeat to Mexican side Club León on Wednesday. Photograph: Dax Tamargo/Shutterstock

“May I be the first of 1,057 tiny violin players to offer no sympathy whatsoever to Bob Cushion” – Matt Scott (and 1,056 others).

“Roberto Martínez’s managerial career. Not so much a CV as a series of passport stamps” – Kev The Poet.

“I see from Big Website’s Chelsea preview that Jordan Henderson will be contributing a lot “off the pitch”. Presumably that will be from a bit further off the pitch than the advertising hoardings?” – Phil Taverner.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day is … Phil Taverner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Chelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for Rodri
Sports.content:
Manchester City have rejected Barcelona’s second bid of around €60m (£51m) for Rodri, while Chelsea have set a 5pm (BST) Friday deadline for the club to bid £120m for the midfielder’s potential replacement, Enzo Fernández.

On Tuesday Barça improved on their initial offer of €45m but this has been turned down. City, it is thought, want between £60m and £65m for Rodri, who captained Spain to victory at the World Cup and is a former Ballon d’Or winner.

As the 30-year has expressed a preference for Barça, City accept it is all but inevitable he will head to the Camp Nou so Fernández has been identified to take his place in Enzo Maresca’s squad.

As Chelsea’s captain and a World Cup winner at Qatar 2022, Fernández would add seniority and leadership. However Chelsea’s stance is that as City and other suitors have already had two months of the transfer window to firm up interest in Fernández, if the £120m valuation is not met by an official bid for this sum by 5pm on Friday, the 25-year-old will remain their player.

To generate some of the finance required Tijjani Reijnders may be sold to Al-Qadsiah. Discussions are advanced between City and the Saudi Arabian club for a package worth around €60m for the 28-year-old Dutchman who joined last summer.

Jérémy Doku has signed a contract extension that will keep him at City until 2031. The 24-year-old winger said: “With Enzo [Maresca] here now I am really excited about the new season. His style of football is the kind we love, so that’s exciting for the players.

“The City fans are also a huge reason I have signed this new contract. I feel their love and support, and it means the world to me. I want to focus of bringing them the success they deserve.”

Sports.title: Seven players we’re excited to watch in the Championship this season
Sports.content:
The Championship, often called the most exciting league in football, is also among the least predictable competitions in Europe. It’s the perfect stage for players to show off their talent before progressing to top-flight football. We’ve picked seven players we’re excited to see in the Championship this season.

Jarrod Bowen: West Ham

Bowen is the best player in the Championship. The West Ham captain, who has seemingly committed his future to the club, will be aiming to fire them back to the top flight. Across the last three seasons, only seven players scored more Premier League goals than Bowen (38), while his 25 assists were bettered by only Bruno Fernandes (39) and Mohamed Salah (35).

Bowen has 65 goals and 49 assists in 231 top-flight games with West Ham, making him the player with the most Premier League goal involvements (114) for the club. This season will be his first outside the top tier since he was at Hull City in 2019-20.

In his final three seasons at Hull, Bowen was involved in more goals (64: 52 goals, 12 assists) than any other player in the Championship. Expect more of the same this season.

Zan Vipotnik: Swansea City

Few expected Vipotnik to finish as the top scorer in the Championship last season given he had only scored seven times in 42 league appearances for Swansea in his first campaign in the division. But he was a thorn in the side of many defences in 2025-26, scoring 23 goals even though Swansea had a fairly ordinary campaign, finishing 11th and nine points off the playoffs.

The Swans were heavily reliant on the Slovenian, who scored 40.4% of their goals (23 of 57); no one else managed more than six. The arrival of Ross Stewart from Southampton may help Vipotnik, as the Scottish forward averaged the second-most goals per 90 minutes (0.73) in the Championship last season (800+ mins played).

Vipotnik has been linked to Hull City, newly promoted to the Premier League. If he stays at Swansea, he could become the first player to score 20+ league goals in successive Championship seasons since Marlon Harewood in 2002-03 and 2003-04.

Ethan Galbraith: Stoke City

It was a surprise when Swansea allowed midfielder Galbraith to join Championship rivals for £10m this summer. True, it’s a lot of money for a player who has played just one season of Championship football, but it could be a worthwhile investment.

Galbraith joined Swansea from Leyton Orient last summer and was one of their most composed players in possession. Technically gifted, Galbraith displays a lot of calm on the ball. He completed more passes per 90 minutes than any other Swansea midfielder or forward in the Championship last season (49.6); he also regained possession from opponents more times than any of his teammates (201).

The Northern Ireland midfielder will face Swansea in his first match of the season on Saturday afternoon. He’ll be trying to get Stoke off to a promising start while reminding Swansea fans what they are missing.

Lorent Tolaj: Bristol City

This will be a fourth successive season of progression for Tolaj. He played in the National League in 2023-24 for Aldershot (scoring 19 goals), moved to League Two with Port Vale during 2024-25 (when he scored 14 goals), then jumped up to League One last season, scoring 18 goals – one for Port Vale and 17 for Plymouth. Now he’s going to test himself in the Championship after a £4m move to Bristol City.

Not only did Tolaj finish last season as the fourth top scorer in League One, he also made eight assists (a tally only beaten by six players). Only Dom Ballard (27) was involved in more goals than Tolaj (26) in the third tier; they will be teammates this season after Ballard joined Bristol City from Leyton Orient.

Being a high-volume shooter helped his goal tally, with Tolaj’s 113 shots more than any other player in League One last season. He averaged 3.7 shots per 90 minutes – a figure that only Aaron Connolly bettered.

Léo Scienza: Southampton

Scienza had a big impact at Southampton after joining the club from Heidenheim last September. With 10 assists in 39 league matches, Scienza was Southampton’s leading assister in the Championship. The Brazil-born forward also scored seven goals.

He topped the club rankings for expected assists per 90 minutes (0.28), and only Ryan Manning (2.2) averaged more chances created per 90 minutes (2.1) in the Championship for Saints.

One of the most exciting players in the division when running with the ball at his feet, Scienza was involved in 11 Championship goals after a ball carry last season – three more than any other player. Only Abdul Fatawu (78) had more of his ball carries lead to either a shot or chance created than Scienza (75).

Othmane Maamma: Watford

Watford fans are very excited to see Maamma again this season. The worry is that, with plenty of clubs across Europe interested in him, he might not be around for long. Watford signed Maamma last summer and he quickly made a name for himself at the Under-20 World Cup, winning the tournament with Morocco and picking up the player of the tournament award.

Maamma made his Watford debut in November, going on to score four goals and set up one more in the Championship. He created 30 open-play chances, the fourth most at the club from his first appearance onwards. The 20-year-old led the Championship rankings for take-ons per 90 minutes (8.9), successful take-ons per 90 (2.9) and take-ons in the opposition’s half per 90 (6.5) last season when considering all players to play at least 800 minutes.

Watford have a great track record of elevating young players and moving them on for big transfer fees – Maamma will surely be the next.

Mason Melia: Lincoln City

Eighteen-year-old Mason Melia is one to keep a close eye on this season. Lincoln fought off a handful of clubs to bring him in on loan from Tottenham for the season. Despite his youth and inexperience, he is an exciting prospect.

Before moving to Spurs, Melia made a name for himself in the League of Ireland with St Patrick’s Athletic, where he scored 21 goals at an average of one every 202 minutes – the first of those goals came against UCD in June 2023 when he was just 15 years and 281 days old.

Melia made his Premier League 2 debut for Spurs in April and made a fast impact, scoring three goals in six appearances in the competition, including his first just three minutes after coming off the bench in a 3-2 win over West Ham. It might be a few months until Melia is trusted with a place in Lincoln’s starting XI, but he has a bright future.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: We have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade – how well do we actually know him? | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
Phil Foden says he is excited about working under Enzo Maresca, his new manager at Manchester City. We should call this exactly what it is: a very obvious barefaced lie. No doubt Foden is excited about playing football again, about challenging for trophies with his boyhood club, the new Premier League season, his new contract, a fresh start, etc, etc.

But let’s be real. Holidays are something you get excited about. Birthdays. Weddings. Amazon deliveries. The new Charli xcx album. Christmas. Playing for Enzo Maresca inspires plenty of emotions, but excitement would probably feature pretty low down a list. At best, you brace for Maresca. You steel yourself. You look in the mirror every morning and ask yourself whether you’re man enough for him. But if you’re excited, then he simply isn’t doing his job.

Hours of classroom work and painstaking video analysis. Relentless discipline on the training pitch as he drills his blueprint into your nervous system. Blunt feedback. Homework assignments to complete on international duty. My favourite bit of Maresca fastidiousness is that when his teams score a goal, the captain is banned from participating in the celebration and must instead come to the touchline to receive further tactical instruction.

For all the churn and upheaval in east Manchester this summer, perhaps the most intriguing plotline of the nascent Maresca dynasty is something that hasn’t really changed at all. Under Pep Guardiola, Foden won everything there is to win in club football. He’s been earmarked as a generational talent since he was a child, played for England in three international tournaments, embedded himself in one of the greatest club teams ever seen. He’s now 26 years old. On some level, we have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade. How well do we know him?

To take one example: it’s the year 2026, and nobody really knows what his best position is. Is he a forward or an attacking midfielder? Is he at his best central, or wide, or wide coming central? Deep, on the last line, between the lines? Come to think of it, what is it he does again? Good passer, but not really a pure creator. Good feet, but not really a pure dribbler. Scores goals, but not an elite goalscorer (with the exception of 2023-24, when he inexplicably started walloping in 25-yard screamers). Arguably not top 10 in the world in any single facet of the game. Yet still incontrovertibly very good, for reasons that have long been internalised but which still feel hard to articulate. How, after 49 international caps and 225 games in the most scrutinised league in the world, is this even possible?

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola changed where and how much he used Phil Foden repeatedly over his time at Manchester City. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

In nine seasons as his manager, Guardiola provided all the answers, albeit not always in an intelligible order. “Winger suits him better,” he said in 2022, predicting he would eventually move to the centre. By 2023, he was warning Foden that he was too much of a “free instinct” to be trusted with a central role.

Two years later, he said Foden’s best position was as a No 10, “a little bit free and close to the box”. Occasionally, he was used as a false 9. Last season, he was deployed in a deeper midfield role. (“Not a player to control the game,” Guardiola would say just before he left.)

So over the years Foden would become a kind of footballing Calpol: a plug-in solution versatile enough to be deployed for pretty much any purpose. Does this explain the sharp decline? In 2024, he was the Premier League player of the year. By the 2025-26 run-in he was essentially a passenger: unused against Real Madrid, a 90th-minute pity substitute in the Carabao Cup final against Arsenal. Two days before England’s epochal game at the Azteca Stadium, Foden was at Wimbledon watching Iga Swiatek in the third round. What happened? How does he recapture the best version of himself? And – more pointedly – what if we’ve already seen it?

View image in fullscreen Phil Foden spent the early summer watching other sports after being left out of England’s World Cup squad. Photograph: Andy Hone/LAT Images/Getty Images

These are questions with implications that go well beyond City and Maresca. For English football, which has spent decades trying to unlock the secret of industrial talent development, to work out how players grow and why they flourish, Foden is Patient Zero. Take a preternatural teenage talent, hand-picked from a cast of millions. Furnish him with the best facilities, the best footballing education, that money can buy. Surround him with champion players and one of the best coaches in history, at a club where there is stability and a process and he can mature at his own gradual rate: neither thrown in too early, nor held back too long, nor pounded into the ground. If you were trying to engineer an elite football career from the ground up, Foden is how you would do it.

If it turns out he peaked at 24, what does that say about the system that created him? If your generational talent ultimately can’t beat Noni Madueke and Ivan Toney to a place in the World Cup squad, whose fault is that? Foden? The media hype machine? The coach who developed him, nurtured him, showed him the road to greatness, but also played him in about eight different positions and never quite allowed him to forge his own identity as a footballer?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Obviously it’s not really Pep’s fault. But Foden is perhaps unique among Guardiola’s prodigies in that he was there right from the very start of the journey. This actually happens a lot less than you think. Lionel Messi was already 21 when Guardiola took over at Barcelona and basically destined to be brilliant. Pretty much all his greatest players were refined and improved rather than nurtured wholesale from childhood. And so Foden is a kind of player English football has never really produced in its history: a street talent adapted over years, by painstaking degrees, into an incredibly complex but essentially bespoke player, a single solution for a single team.

Foden is 26 and still largely devoid of context. We don’t know how he’d play in a struggling team. We don’t know what would happen if he had the keys to dictate a game. We don’t know what happens when you give him responsibility. We don’t even know much about his tactical intelligence, because he’s played his entire career under a guy telling him exactly where and when to run. Perhaps this explains the wild discrepancy between City Foden (17 major trophies) and England Foden (a goal on average every 18 months).

View image in fullscreen Foden’s best season for City was in 2023-24 when he scored 27 goals in all competitions. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images

Now, under a new manager, with a new midfield, Foden faces – remarkably – a make-or-break season. Bernardo Silva has gone. Rodri may well follow. Rayan Cherki is probably ahead of him in the pecking order. In a Premier League increasingly built around lightning pace and brute physicality, where does Foden fit into the new vision? What happens if he endures a third disappointing season in succession?

But there are opportunities here too. City’s World Cup players are only just returning and there should be time for him to stake a claim. A more vertical, high-energy style may just suit him. For all his kooky control-freakery, a new manager like Maresca will never be able to exert the same stranglehold as the man he replaced. For better or worse, this may just be the season when we finally find out who Phil Foden is.

Sports.title: Celta Vigo’s La Liga opener postponed due to fungal outbreak on pitch
Sports.content:
Celta Vigo’s ⁠season-opening La Liga match against Osasuna has been postponed after ⁠a fungal outbreak ⁠affected ​the pitch at Estadio de Balaidos, the Spanish club ⁠said on Thursday.

Celta had been due to host Osasuna on Sunday, ⁠but the fixture was postponed with ​the decision ‌agreed by both ‌clubs and the Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) ‌following a technical inspection by La Liga.

The inspection found a fungal outbreak had damaged the Balaidos playing surface, while adverse weather conditions had undermined recent ‌progress in its recovery, leaving the pitch unfit for use.
