World.title: U.S. ambassador calls settler siege of Palestinian homes a 'horrific act of terror'
World.content:
U.S. ambassador calls settler siege of Palestinian homes a 'horrific act of terror'

toggle caption Nidal Eshtayeh/AP

JERUSALEM — The U.S. Ambassador to Israel condemned the actions of Jewish settlers who are besieging the home of an American Palestinian family in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the siege a "horrific act of terror."

Since Sunday, according to local officials and family members, settlers have gathered near the home in the village of Qusra and harassed those inside, defying efforts by the Israeli military to defuse the situation.

A group that has included up to dozens of men has thrown stones, attempted to bring down a stone wall nearby, and prevented the occupants from leaving despite dwindling supplies.

Speaking to The Associated Press by phone from his home in Ohio, the home's owner Lou Ridi said his 48-year-old brother and nephew, who have been holed up in the home to defend it, had been unable to leave the house and did not have access to food or water for several days.

Sponsor Message

On Thursday morning, the owner's brother Qusai Abu Rida said that he and his teenage son had been evacuated by Israel's military. It was unclear what would happen to the property and at least one other that has been targeted.

Israeli troops intervened in recent days to try to restore order. The military said that overnight Thursday its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" on the outskirts of Qusra and a nearby village, and detained one Israeli. It added that additional soldiers had surged to the area, which is about 16 kilometers (10 miles) of the Palestinian city of Nablus, to "carry out defensive missions and patrols."

Journalists on the outskirts of Qusra said roads into the village were closed. Israeli police did not immediately respond to questions about whether any Israeli civilians had been arrested.

Palestinians and the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians as clashes have surged in the last few years.

Huckabee's post on X was an unusually sharp rebuke from a U.S. official, even as he defended the Israeli military's response. Huckabee is a longtime ally of Israel's settler movement and in the past has expressed support for Israeli control over the occupied West Bank while condemning settler violence.

Sponsor Message

Home security footage from Thursday morning appeared to show a few settlers still hiding by a damaged stone wall near the house.

Ridi said that settlers have been harassing his home for months before the situation escalated in recent days, saying they had cut off the water and electricity to his house and thrown stones, causing damage to the property as well as at least one more house in the area.

"We are prisoners in our own house, hostages in our own house," he said.

Last month, a mosque in Qusra was set on fire in another apparent settler attack. That followed the killing of an Israeli settler, which triggered violence that left two Israeli soldiers and four Palestinian villagers dead.

Settlers have been building more outposts in an effort condemned by many in the international community as aimed at dismantling any remaining hopes of establishing a Palestinian state in the occupied West Bank.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 war, as part of a future state. Many settlers and their supporters say the entire area should belong to Israel for historical, religious and security reasons.

World.title: Sailors and their families have lives on pause, uncertain if they'll return to Mideast
World.content:
Sailors and their families have lives on pause, uncertain if they'll return to Mideast

toggle caption Fadhel Madhan/AFP via Getty Images

Shortly after the war with Iran started in late February, one military spouse was about to go back to Bahrain with her husband. Then they got a call from the U.S. Navy.

"A day before we were supposed to leave to be stationed at Bahrain together, we were told we need to go somewhere else for a short period of time, and then here we are five months later," she said.

NPR has agreed to withhold their names and location. The Navy spouse is concerned about the potential impact on her husband's career. The two of them are now living out of three duffel bags, in their seventh hotel room.

"We were at one location for a while and then, spur of the moment, sent to another location for what ended up being 10 weeks," she said. "So it's a lot of moving with very short notice, and you can't really unpack or own too much because you never know when you're going to be going somewhere else."

Sponsor Message

They're on what's called temporary duty status, so they aren't eligible for base housing or money for rent to pay for housing in the community.

U.S. bases in the region remain targets for Iran. Bahrain is less than 130 miles from Iran by sea, and ships have to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. After a first story ran on NPR in April, the Navy conceded that at least 1,500 troops and their families had been ordered to evacuate the Navy base in Bahrain.

Home to the Navy's 5th Fleet, the base has been the Middle East hub for the Navy and U.S. international partners. On Jan. 12, just over a month before the evacuation, the base began a $15.8 million overhaul of the barracks for junior sailors.

Some evacuees remain in what's called their "safe havens" — places that military members and their families have designated as the place they will return to if there's an emergency overseas. Others are still moving from base to base. Adm. Karl Thomas, commander of the Fleet Forces, told NPR that the Navy hasn't released an overall plan, but reopening Bahrain to families seems unlikely in the near future.

National Security As Iran war reignites, military families face the challenges of lengthy deployments As Iran war reignites, military families face the challenges of lengthy deployments Listen · 4:07 4:07

"We're really trying to take each case individually and make sure those people are taken care of and we understand what they want. But with things heating back up over there right now, it's not an option," Thomas said.

With most of their belongings still overseas, families have had to decide whether to buy a car and replace clothing, according to advocates, sailors and family members.

"We're looking at the monetary issues and challenges for some of those families that aren't where they intended to be," Thomas said.

Sponsor Message

Some sailors and families came through Norfolk, Virginia. Hundreds have arrived in Tampa, Fla., home of U.S. Central Command. Blue Star Families, which advocates for military families, is bringing food to families living in hotels. As the school year rolls around, families with children are trying to enroll in local schools in the area. They may not have all their records, said Suzy Malloy, executive director of Blue Star's Tampa chapter.

"When the kids first arrived, we gave them backpacks and school supplies because, you know, they left so quickly they didn't think to grab all of what they needed to go back to school," she said.

Inge Michiels runs Jetpet Global, which transports animals in and out of Bahrain. Her clients include military and civilian defense workers. She still lives in Bahrain and remembers when the war began six months ago.

"The early days were quite shocking, especially since Bahrain is considered safe. It's a small island with friendly people. So when I woke up, I was literally blasted off my bed," she said.

Clients weren't prepared for the cost and paperwork involved in transporting pets out of the Middle East. It can cost several thousand dollars, and prices skyrocketed during the first few months, when flights out of Bahrain were canceled. Many people had to leave their animals behind. Pets were left with neighbors or friends and still haven't left the country.

"A lot of people are in panic mode, and our team as well. We are going under that same stress where alarms go off and deprived sleep and uncertainty," Michiels said.

The country is still under periodic attack. For most clients, she said, all she can tell them is to be patient.

World.title: LeBlanc, U.S. counterpart meeting again after Canada displeased with latest tariff offer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian trade officials are meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington once again, as both sides hustle to lock down a crucial trade deal ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's pressing tariff deadline.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc's office confirmed to CBC News on Thursday morning that he and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette will meet with Greer this afternoon.

It will be the second meeting this week between the Canadian and American trade officials, and the fourth in just three weeks.

The two sides have ramped up discussions since Trump threatened to impose 50 per cent duties on hundreds of Canadian goods, on top of sectoral tariffs already in place. Those tariffs are slated to come into effect Aug. 19.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

As previously reported, sources on both sides of the border say the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see.

The Americans are also seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and which covers security and energy, the sources said.

CBC News previously reported LeBlanc and Greer are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has met several times with Canadian negotiators in recent weeks. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

However, sources also told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Those tariffs, according to the U.S. government, are due to a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

The Canadian side is willing to offer movement on some of those concerns, according to industry sources with knowledge of the situation. In addition to ending the booze bans, Canada is also considering lifting retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and making some changes on dairy.

Ford open to putting U.S. booze back on shelves

Also Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford — a frequent critic of Trump — said he'd be "more than happy" to bring U.S. booze back onto his province's shelves if a fair deal is reached that protects Ontario's steel, auto, forestry, agriculture and manufacturing sectors.

Ford also said his message to Americans is "a tariff on Canada is a tax on the American people."

"Remember when it comes to the [U.S.] midterms, you have to get that bully and send him a message," Ford said.

The Ontario premier's comments on U.S. alcohol bans echo those from Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette's office, who said in a statement last week the removal of U.S. alcohol from Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ) outlets will remain in effect "until an agreement that we deem fair has been negotiated."

"The sale of alcohol falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Quebec government. Quebec, and Quebec alone, will make that decision," the statement says.

World.title: Members of Okanagan Indian Band mourn loss of forests and irreplaceable artifacts in B.C. wildfire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of homes were destroyed in the Bradley Creek wildfire, but members of the Okanagan Indian Band say the most important things that were lost do not carry monetary value.

“I'm not worried for myself. I'm worried for the people who are going to be here long term,” said 91-year-old Okanagan Indian Band Elder Frederick Louis.

Louis lost his home, and every photograph and artifact he and his late wife had collected over their lifetimes, in the fire.

He said the land that members of the Okanagan Indian Band have foraged for generations is now ash.

He said his community will rebuild, but he worries about the environment his grandchildren will inherit.

Elder Frederick Louis lost his home and all his belongings in the Bradley Creek Wildfire. (Alexandre Vallée-Roy/Radio Canada)

Louis, who worked in forestry and as a firefighter, said he has watched over the last decade as climate change impacted his homeland.

“Our watershed is all burned off," he said.

He said it will take decades to repair the landscape.

Louis said in all his years living at the head of Okanagan Lake and working in the woods, he has never seen a fire burn as quickly, or as intensely, as the Bradley Creek fire, but he had been expecting it.

“It's been just getting drier and drier,” he said.

“We kept holding our breath for this.”

The Bradley Creek wildfire burns west of Vernon, B.C., on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

He said when the fire ignited on Aug. 1, it exploded through the forest.

“It came so fast that all of the residents on the west side there, they came out with nothing."

Louis said he lost treasured berry-picking baskets gifted to his late wife by her great-grandmother. They were more than 100 years old, and so tightly woven they could still have carried water.

“I can't really think of how valuable they were," said Louis.

He has been staying in a hotel in Vernon along with his family while next steps are being figured out.

The home and garden belonging to his sister, Dora Louis Alexis, also an elder with the Okanagan Indian Band, was untouched by the fire. She remains on evacuation order, and has been receiving updates on her property from her grandson, who is a firefighter.

He told her that animals – coming from the community and the forest – have been finding refuge in her garden.

“Right now we're not there, and it's OK for the chickens and the other animals — the wolves, the deer and everything — to come and eat because their habitat is being burnt out also,” said Alexis.

Dora Louis Alexis was worried about her rabbit that she had to leave behind. It survived the fire by burrowing underground. (Alexandre Vallée-Roy/Radio Canada)

Two of her sons lost their homes in the fire, but Alexis said she knows they will rebuild.

She said things are replaceable, lives are not.

Louis’ niece, Machell Louis, said that even though many people from her community have lost their homes, Indigenous people can never be homeless. They always have their land to return to, she said.

“My uncle may be houseless, but he is not homeless. He will always have a home. We will always have a home,” she said.

Sharmelle Paul and her family were able to return to their home at the head of Okanagan Lake on Okanagan Indian Band land. (Genevieve Lasalle/Radio Canada)

This week, members of the Okanagan Indian Band joined the Okanagan Nation Alliance at Kin Beach in Vernon to pray for water.

Sharmelle Paul, her husband and children returned to their property on Okanagan Indian Band land Tuesday. Almost immediately, they left again to join others in prayer at Kin Beach.

"We came to pray for the water and the rain and everyone, not just ourselves," said Paul.

"I've been thinking about the berries and the animals and how dry it's been."

Prayers have been held throughout the Okanagan region by the Okanagan Nation Alliance. A gathering was held at Kin Beach in Vernon on Aug. 11. (Genevieve Lasalle/Radio Canada)

Okanagan Indian Band Chief Dan Wilson asks that people remain patient and continue to support one another.

“Everything's still surreal. We're still kind of numb.”

He said many homes and historic structures are gone, but the community’s new school and powwow grounds were saved.

“Our community is totally unrecognizable,” said Wilson.

He said more information for residents will be available in the coming days, and thanked the communities and bands across Canada that have supported the Okanagan Indian Band by sending food and resources.

World.title: The U.K. sees its hottest day of the summer as western Europe suffers through another heat wave
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.K. recorded its hottest day of the year on Thursday, with the temperature reaching 38.1 C in West London, the national weather service said.

The Met Office said the temperature surpassed this year's previous high of 38 C, recorded on June 28. It remained below the U.K.'s August record of 38.5 C, set in 2003.

A dog runs over dried grass in front of Tower Bridge during the fifth heat wave of the year in London on Thursday. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/The Associated Press)

Britain, like France, is experiencing its fifth heat wave of the year.

The Met Office said earlier this week that only average conditions were needed for the rest of August to beat last year's record for the hottest year.

A boy rides a bicycle in Greenwich Park amid dried grass in London on Tuesday. (Kin Cheung/The Associated Press)

It has been particularly difficult to work in British hospitals, according to the Royal College of Nursing, and nurses have been known to collapse from heat exhaustion.

WATCH | Europe susceptible to power outages, water shortages: Rising temperatures make Europe more flammable, scientists say | Duration 2:06 Europe has been deemed the fastest warming continent, something scientists say has made the region more flammable and more susceptible to power outages and water shortages.

"When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed," said Nicola Ranger, the college's chief executive and general secretary.

This summer has shown that both Britain and France are ill-equipped to deal with these levels of heat.

Air conditioning is a rarity outside of shops and offices, for example.

A woman cools herself with a folding fan while walking under intense summer sunshine in Grenoble, France, Wednesday. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

Like many parts of Europe, Britain and France are facing widespread drought conditions that have shrivelled crops and drained rivers, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.

A sunflower field scorched by drought and heat in Guidel, France, on Wednesday. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

Britain's Southern Water, which oversees supplies in the south of England, has applied for a rare drought order that would ban businesses from non-essential water use, including cleaning cars and filling non-domestic swimming pools, saying an "exceptional" lack of rain has threatened supplies in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle will decide on the application, which would be the first such ban since May 2006.

A heron fishes at a reservoir in Sowerby Bridge, England, on Thursday. (Jon Super/The Associated Press)

With the land parched and no sign of any meaningful rain coming, authorities in Britain and France remain on high alert for wildfires.

In Britain, which is increasingly looking sandy brown rather than its traditional luscious green, firefighters have been out in force this week trying to contain a wildfire in the New Forest in southern England.

A visitor uses an umbrella to shield from the sun as she walks around Stonehenge, near Amesbury, Britain, Thursday. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council, the same as last year's record-breaking total.

Though not on the same level as those witnessed in France, Greece and Spain, they provide ample evidence of the need for the U.K. to adjust to a new reality.

British PM considers BBQ ban

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues amid the risk of further wildfires as extreme heat continues to grip parts of the U.K.

"I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear," he said. "People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time."

French firefighters were back in action, too, after a desperate summer and are threatening to go on strike to demand more staff and resources to cope with increasingly extreme weather events.

One broke out late Wednesday in the northern Pas-de-Calais region, and another in Brittany, far from the hotter, drier and more fire-prone regions in southern France. A historic fire devoured forests near Bordeaux last month and pushed a quarter of a million people from their homes.

World.title: Twitch users: Amazon could use your content for AI training. Here's what you should know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twitch users: heads-up.

Amazon, which owns Twitch, is now using content on Twitch to train artificial intelligence (AI) models — a move that has garnered fierce backlash from both streamers and users on the interactive livestreaming platform.

Users' accounts are opted in by default but you can choose to opt out and disable the default setting, the company announced on Wednesday.

Many users have decided to do that after accusing Amazon of using their creative content without their permission.

" The only thing that surprises me is that there is an opt-out toggle at all," one user wrote in a post on Reddit.

" I don't even stream and I turned it off just on principle," another user wrote.

WATCH | How AI is changing the Internet: Say goodbye to the internet as you know it | Duration 8:06 Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet. For The National, CBC’s Nora Young breaks down the future of search and what happens to information when bots do most of the reading online.

The latest controversial policy comes as tensions grow between AI companies seeking data and creators demanding more control over their own content.

It also comes on the heels of other m ajor streaming and gaming platforms, including YouTube Live, Netflix and Roblox, using AI for various purposes such as content optimization, live production assistance and recommendations.

As part of the new policy, Amazon will be able to collect streams, clips, images, chats and channel content for AI training purposes, according to Twitch.

In order to turn the default setting off , users will need to click on their Twitch profile picture and go to Settings, then to Security and Privacy. There, you can disable the switch for Training for Generative AI.

When asked why users are given the choice to opt out rather than opt in, the company's chief product officer, Mike Minton, said most users would not voluntarily agree to opt into the data collection if was not rolled out by default.

'On by default'

"If it was opt-in, nobody would opt-in ... that’s honestly the answer. So it’s going to be on by default," Minton said in a livestream on the website on Wednesday.

Minton's comments ignited further backlash from the Twitch community.

" It's an implicit understanding that they know they aren't doing something popular," one Reddit user said.

" If no one would opt in to your new "feature," the feature you are introducing is anti-consumer," another user wrote.

Users also described the setting as hard to find on the website, accusing Twitch of doing that by design.

CBC News has reached out to Twitch but did not immediately hear back.

Disabling the setting will not block AI-powered features on Twitch, according to the company, which includes auto-commenting, ad selection and chat moderation tools.

Twitch said collected data will not be resold, but users are concerned about how the content would be used.

Hundreds of users decried the new policy during Twitch's livestream, accusing the company of exploiting creators' work.

Reuters said Twitch could not confirm whether user content had already been scraped for training.

World.title: Canadian pediatricians document steep rise in severe e-scooter injuries, deaths in children, teens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As e-scooters become increasingly common across Canada, pediatricians, emergency physicians and other experts warn that injuries — often severe and involving younger people — are rising, while regulations struggle to keep pace.

Dr. Daniel Rosenfield, a pediatric emergency physician at SickKids hospital in Toronto and chair of the injury prevention committee for the Canadian Pediatric Society (CPS), says he has seen "a complete exponential rise" in every type of injury that can result from an e-scooter crash — from minor scrapes to major brain injuries and death.

Bad injuries used to be "once in a blue moon," he told CBC News. Now, "anytime we get a call from EMS that says, 'E-scooter trauma inbound,' we're prepared for severe injuries," he said.

E-scooter injury cases at SickKids rose from 26 in 2023 to 46 in 2024 and 107 in 2025, Rosenfield said.

"And this year we're likely on target for more than that."

At the Montreal Children’s Hospital, e-scooter injuries have increased by a factor of 10 since 2023, said Dr. Laurie Plotnick, who heads the hospital’s emergency trauma team.

Children, who were injured without the involvement of another motor vehicle, have suffered "severe facial injuries … broken jaws, broken bones around the eyes," she said.

"We're talking about severe brain injuries."

The experiences at those hospitals are mirrored across Canada and around the world. A CPS survey of Canadian pediatric specialists, conducted from late 2025 to early 2026 and published Thursday, documented 10 deaths, 12 ICU admissions and 26 hospitalizations lasting more than two days over the previous 12 months as a result of e-scooter crashes. Head injuries were present in about half the cases.

"The vast majority, if not all, are unhelmeted," Rosenfield said.

The most severe injuries tended to involve boys between 10 and 15 years old, he said.

The CPS survey records the experience of pediatric specialists rather than providing a rigorous quantitative analysis. But a separate study published Tuesday in the Emergency Medicine Journal provides multi-year hospital administrative data from three U.K. hospitals that closely aligns with what Canadian pediatricians are seeing.

That study found e-scooter cases at hospitals in Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield rose from fewer than 10 in 2019 to almost 150 in 2024. Head injuries were among the most severe, and fewer than two per cent of those injured were wearing helmets.

From 69 km/h to a critical care unit

That U.K. data mirrors what Canadian families are experiencing firsthand.

Just over a year ago in London, Ont., Crystal Dunkley's son Shaun was not wearing a helmet when he took a family friend's e-scooter out for a ride one evening, as he had done many times before.

That evening, Shaun, then 12, hit a raccoon as it ran across his path.

"He believes he was going 69 kilometres an hour when this happened," Crystal Dunkley recalled in a video interview Wednesday.

An ambulance rushed Shaun to the Children's Hospital in London, where he was intubated and admitted to the Pediatric Critical Care Unit with a fractured skull. He was in a coma for over a week.

"The doctors told us that with the brain bleed they determined he had, there was a possibility he would not make it, and if he did, then he would likely be very disabled," Crystal said.

Following his e-scooter crash, Shaun Dunkley was in a coma for over a week and spent more than a month in the London, Ont., children's hospital. (Crystal Dunkley)

Shaun ultimately recovered completely after 34 days in Children's Hospital and more time at a rehabilitation facility in Toronto. Crystal said he now approaches people riding e-scooters on the street and tells them to wear a helmet.

"Not a day goes by that I don't see multiple young children riding them without helmets, sometimes two or three to a scooter," Crystal said. "Some of these scooters can go … like I said, the one he was on was going 69 kilometres an hour."

'Anything but toys': Why regulation is lagging behind

Most parents are surprised by the extent of their child's injuries, Rosenfield said.

"And to be fair to the families, these devices are often marketed as toys," he said. "And as a device that can go zero to 40 kilometres an hour in a number of seconds, I will tell you they're anything but toys."

The CPS survey also notes that younger people may be less familiar with road rules, less risk-averse and at greater risk of injury because of their developmental stage.

But it also argues there are problems with rules and laws, describing them as "unclear and made up of a patchwork of regulations, varying depending on the province/territory."

Many parents simply aren’t aware of the rules in their province or city, said Plotnick, the Montreal Children’s Hospital physician. “Parents are surprised when they have children who are under 14 severely injured … to hear that actually the legal age is 14 in Quebec.”

The minimum age for riding an e-scooter varies by province, while some cities have banned the devices altogether — though those bans are often ignored. Several provinces, including B.C., Ontario and Quebec, cap e-scooter speeds at 24 or 25 kilometres per hour.

"I can tell you for sure people go faster than that," Rosenfield said.

“We need public education,” said Plotnick. “We need to educate parents. We need to lobby for manufacturers to have clear messaging on the products and we need better enforcement.”

Rosenfield is not advocating for an e-scooter ban, pointing to their utility to complement public transit and reduce automobile traffic.

"I do think they have a use in an urban environment," he said. "I just think we need to figure out what that looks like and how to make those devices safe."

World.title: With U.S. midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the U.S. heads toward the midterm elections, a gruelling primary season has further entrenched a rift between the insurgent progressive and centrist wings of the Democratic Party.

At stake is control of Congress this November and, beyond that, the presidency in 2028.

The centrists argue candidates touting moderate and pragmatic policies is the path to flipping seats from Republican control. While progressives say more uninspiring, establishment candidates will not galvanize a coalition of young people, the working class and diverse voters that could propel the party to victory.

"I don't even know how I could go about being sure which group has the most appeal," said Hans Noel, an associate professor of Government at Georgetown University and co-director of the Georgetown Democracy Initiative.

He says that while progressive candidates may alienate some voters who otherwise might have voted Democrat, they will also bring new voters to the party, including those who may not have voted at all.

There are also intangible characteristics, like personal likeability, said Noel: "How do you add that all up and make a strong prediction? It's hard."

LISTEN | What direction should the Democratic Party take?: Two Blocks from the White House 29:47 As progressives win U.S. primaries, what’s the direction of the Democratic Party?

Primary wins and losses

The primary season — where Democratic voters choose their candidates for upcoming general elections against Republicans — has given both sides wins, losses and lessons.

On Tuesday, in the key battleground state of Wisconsin progressives were dealt a blow when democratic voters narrowly chose moderate David Crowley in the primary for governor over self-described Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, who was projected to win in the polls.

Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley speaks to the media on Wednesday in Middleton, Wis., after winning the primary. Crowley will take on Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November's midterm election. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

Hong's campaign was plagued in its final days by past comments she made advocating for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and also saying it was time to "cancel Thanksgiving," calling it a celebration of colonialism. During the campaign, she backed away from all these comments, saying her views had evolved.

Hong ultimately wasn't endorsed by progressive flagbearers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Other races where moderates were able to hold progressive challengers at bay included those in Washington and Missouri .

In the swing state of Michigan earlier this month, however, progressive Addul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders, eked out a victory against centrist candidate Haley Stevens despite over $60 million being spent on her behalf, largely from super PACs.

WATCH | What Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory means for Democrats: Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory called a win for progressive Democrats | Duration 2:04 U.S. Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's narrow victory in a Michigan primary has been described as a win for progressive Democrats, but has some in the party worried that being seen as too progressive will hurt their chances to defeat Republicans in the upcoming midterms.

El-Sayed, like other progressive candidates, campaigned on issues like medicare for all, getting money out of politics, taxing billionaire wealth and calling for an end to military aid for Israel. He has also been praised for his communication skills.

In response to the U.S. President Donald Trump calling him "full of shit," El-Sayed shot back : "At least I don't let mine go all over the Oval Office."

El-Sayed's victory followed wins from progressive candidates who took on more moderate democrats in strongholds of New York and Colorado.

Notably, in Maine, another battleground state, progressive Graham Platner delivered a win before he dropped out due to sexual assault allegations.

Discontent among young voters

Bhaskar Sunkara, president of left-leaning magazine The Nation and former vice chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, says El-Sayed's win and others like it are a "huge check" on the Democratic Party.

"Voters, particularly young voters, are really discontent with the leadership of the party … and just generally feel that the Democratic Party doesn't stand for anything. It's not combative enough."

Progressive politicians U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, left, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, right, campaigned alongside Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed at July's the People V. The Powerful rally in Detroit. El-Sayed went on to win the Michigan senate primary nomination on Aug. 5, in a tight race. (Jose Juarez/The Associated Press)

Sunkara went on to say that El-Sayed is a better candidate than Hong with working-class voters.

"I think there is a way in which some candidates have been tarred with stances they had in 2019, 2020. This sort of abolish the police, the discussion of whiteness or whatever else. Abdul never had that problem."

Hong wasn't the only candidate backing off from past comments.

New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made headlines earlier this week when asked about her past support for defunding the police. "I have a local city councilman that has this saying: 'Woke 1 was crazy,' " she said before laughing.

Can progressives win key battleground states?

While some in the progressive wing re-evaluate past positions that could alienate voters this election cycle, many moderate democrats continue to warn of liabilities in swing states.

Fareed Zakaria, host of CNN's Sunday public affairs program GPS , cited Washington Post data to point out that while El-Sayed had the support of Michigan's most educated counties and college towns, his opponent did better in rural and lower-income areas.

"The left has the passion, but the middle still has the votes needed to win in general elections," Zakaria said.

Kate de Gruyter is the vice-president of communications at Third Way, a leading centrist democratic group that is spending $15 million between now and 2028 to discredit Democratic Socialism.

LISTEN | What's behind the wave of Democratic Socialist wins in the U.S.: Front Burner 36:53 Understanding the rise of ‘democratic socialism’

"Their theory of the case is that they're somehow going to be able to persuade all these voters in the middle that they absolutely need to win in November to back their candidate. We've never seen that happen over the entirety of the Trump era," she said in an interview.

De Gruyter added that El-Sayed's decision to campaign with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker as one example of "a whole universe of things that Republican ad makers are salivating at."

De Gruyter went on to suggest that the reason Democrat Kamala Harris lost the presidential election in 2024 was that she was seen as too lax on issues like immigration and plagued by stances she'd taken in the past on " transgender policy ."

In the final weeks of the campaign. Trump's team ran an ad using a five-year old clip of Harris saying that "every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access" to taxpayer-funded gender transitions.

"The idea that we should move further left makes no sense at all," she said.

The interesting thing is that while that can all be true, there are also plenty of arguments that suggest the opposite, according to Noel, the Georgetown associate professor.

U.S. Vice-President and then presidential candidate Kamala Harris takes part in a phone bank at the Democratic National Convention Headquarters on Nov. 5, 2024. Her unsuccessful campaign has been criticized by both progressives and moderate democrats. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

"And it can also be true that Harris actually lost because she was too tied to the establishment and Biden. And too close to Israel … progressives called her a cop. Either of those differences could have been enough because it was a fairly close race."

Either way, Democrats are riding favourable waves into the midterms.

Trump's polling is low . He has entered into an unpopular war in Iran . And all of this should help the Democrats, whether they're progressives or moderates in the mid-terms, said Noel, adding that if the Democrats don't do as well as expected there will be a lot of "what happened?"

"If all the progressive candidates lose and the centrist candidates win, well, that's going to be an easier story."

World.title: Unsealed documents reveal details of RCMP's response, investigation into Tumbler Ridge shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Documents unsealed through efforts by CBC News and a consortium of media outlets reveal new details of the RCMP's response and investigation into the February 2026 mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.

The documents, which include search warrants, production orders and sealing orders, provide a snapshot of a complex investigation, laying out for the first time law enforcement's account of the day shots rang out at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The newly unredacted files from the RCMP paint a picture of how front-line officers experienced the events of that day.

Significant portions of the documents remain redacted, including timestamps crucial to the chronology, such as how long it took officers to enter the school after receiving reports of shots fired.

The documents say that on Feb. 10, 2026, RCMP responded to an active shooter at the high school in Tumbler Ridge and found six deceased victims in a school littered with spent shell casings. They identify the shooter as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, who was found dead in the school with self-inflicted gunshot wounds.

Search warrants filed by the RCMP describe the evidence, physical and electronic, that police identified as they attempted to piece together what happened that day.

One sealing order filed in early March describes concern that releasing records connected to the investigation could compromise future public inquests and pose a risk to the public.

911 calls reported erratic driver, shots fired

The mass shooting, one of the worst in Canadian history, shook the small northern B.C. community, and is now the subject of a coroner's inquest investigating the role that mental health, access to weapons, and artificial intelligence played in the tragedy.

Throughout the documents, Van Rootselaar is referred to by her last name, full name, "Jesse," and "the shooter."

A production and sealing order sworn by Const. Jonathan Paquin of the RCMP North District Major Crime Unit on March 6 describes a flurry of 911 calls received the morning that chaos unfolded in Tumbler Ridge.

A memorial to the victims of the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooting is pictured in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., on Feb. 12, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

On Feb. 10, RCMP received a call about "an SUV that had been driving erratically from [redacted], which is the residence of Jesse."

The vehicle driven to the school was later identified as a green 2023 Hyundai Palisade.

A caller reported that "there were two dead bodies and shotgun shells on the floor" and they "thought that the eldest son was armed and had left, and that the mother and son were dead."

RCMP advised the caller to leave the scene untouched, close the door and return to their residence.

RCMP then received multiple calls of shots fired at the secondary school.

The documents include a minute-by-minute accounting of various officers arriving on the scene, hearing shots fired, entering the school, and locating deceased victims and the deceased shooter.

"Police were shot at by the suspect which caused them to hold while being shot at," it reads in part.

Because timestamps are redacted from the documents, it's unknown how much time elapsed between the events described over several pages.

For example, the documents do not relay how much time passed between the initial 911 call describing the erratic vehicle, and police entering the school. This week, CBC News and a consortium of other media have been in court to argue that some of the redacted information be made public.

The production order also reveals confusion over whether there was a second shooter in the school, possibly because the shooter went by the aliases Jesse Jacobs and Jesse Strain, in addition to Jesse Van Rootselaar.

One inspector identified the shooter as the "eldest child in the STRAIN/JACOBS family, and that they were obsessed with guns," the document reads.

"[The] inspector reported that a possible second shooter was Jesse VAN ROOTSELAAR," reads the document, though it's later detailed that police identified these were the same person.

Details of firearms remain sealed

A search warrant filed the day after the shooting describes evidence sought by police, including "human biological substances including but not limited to: blood, hair, fingerprints and human tissue," "firearms, ammunition, spent cartridge casings," and "computers, cell phones or tablets, that may belong to Jesse Van Rootselaar."

A production order lists physical evidence located inside Van Rootselaar's home, including a Sony Handycam, a black iPhone with a cracked screen inside a black case, a purple Aocwei laptop, a MacBook Air, an SD card and a purple digital camera.

An RCMP officer is pictured at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 11, 2026, the day after a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A search warrant filed on Feb. 11 describes the scene at Van Rootselaar's home. It says two RCMP corporals observed "a shotgun [redacted] that was unloaded as well as a pellet gun" and "insecure firearms inside the residence."

Between Feb. 13 and 20, a firearms tracing investigation with the Canadian Firearms Program attempted to trace four firearms of those seized from the secondary school and a second, redacted address. The details of the firearms are redacted, though two shotguns and a rifle are listed.

Electronic records sought

A section of the order describes a Police Records Information Management Environment — or PRIME — review of the teen.

Any individual who interacts with law enforcement in B.C., from witnesses to suspects, is entered into PRIME's centralized database, regardless of the nature of the interaction.

The order says Van Rootselaar was carded to 12 PRIME files, dating back to April 2018 when she would have been around 10 years old. The details of those incidents are redacted.

A section about Van Rootselaar's social media accounts is redacted in its entirety, with nearly seven pages of text fully blacked out.

But the file says on Feb. 15, 2026, RCMP were notified by the FBI that OpenAI had located two ChatGPT accounts believed to be used by Van Rootselaar. Details of those accounts are also redacted.

"Jesse's ChatGPT account was subject to an internal review in June 2025 after Jesse's chat conversation discussed matters that could be related to the school shooting," it said.

"OpenAI banned Jesse's ChatGPT account and did not notify police at that time."

A request to seal

One document, an application for an order to seal filed March 6 by Paquin, shows that police were concerned that unsealing the production order filed concurrently could compromise ongoing investigations, and potentially put the public at risk.

Paquin argues that disclosure would harm a newly-announced coroner's inquest, because "while this is not a criminal trial, it is a court proceeding involving a jury." He argues that while the province had not yet called a public inquiry, any potential future inquiry could be influenced by information that had been made public.

RCMP and victim services are pictured at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"This is a large and complex investigation that has garnered significant national and international attention with significant media coverage of the incident and the police investigation," it reads in part.

"For this reason, I believe that evidence outlined in this Information to Obtain if prematurely disclosed would certainly be disseminated through various news outlets that would affect and influence the current ongoing criminal investigation, the coroner's inquest, and a potential Public Inquiry."

Paquin also argues that making the contents of the document public could inspire further acts of mass violence, invoking high profile incidents in the U.S.

"I am aware that mass casualty incidents can inspire copycat attacks. For example, the Columbine High School massacre is well known to have had this effect where it inspired other shootings in the following years," he writes.

"I believe premature disclosure of this Information to Obtain without a complete criminal investigation, and the following Coroner's Inquest or Public Inquiry where all the facts are known could put the public at risk."

World.title: Carney has a ‘weak hand’ in Trump negotiations: Shuv Majumdar
World.content:
Article content

With next week’s deadline for new U.S. tariffs on Canadian imports fast approaching, the opposition Conservatives are calling on the prime minister to finally start delivering on trade — and to stop the unilateral concessions. In this interview, Rob Breakenridge speaks with Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar, the party’s shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, about the state of talks ahead of the Aug. 19 deadline and about the letter that Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre sent to Mark Carney this week. Majumdar says the Liberals have put Canada in a position of weakness heading into these talks, and that Carney has failed to utilize Canada’s strengths to build leverage with Washington. Instead, the Conservatives accuse the prime minister of making too many concessions without having secured any reciprocal gains from the Trump administration. We’ll look at where things stand heading into next week — and beyond. Watch full video directly below.
