World.title: Is the peso punching above its weight? The results of our latest MND Peso Index™
World.content:
THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Fourth edition

Welcome to the fourth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued or undervalued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

Unlike previous editions, our latest MND Peso Index™ assessment is being published in the same month as its underlying price survey, making it even more timely.

Our headline finding for August 2026 indicates that the peso was overvalued against the dollar by 2.4%, a decrease of 0.5 percentage points compared to the 2.9% overvaluation we determined in late June.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in August 2026?

In August 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, overvalued the Mexican peso by 2.4%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Aug. 6, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.64 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 17.22 pesos per dollar on Aug. 6.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 17.22 to the US dollar — was overvalued by 2.4% in early August.

In other words, the USD:MXN exchange rate — if it reflected the rate at which the peso could buy the basket’s goods and services in Mexico at the same dollar prices as in the United States — would be 17.64.

In the table below, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (ie., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the overvaluation assessment for the peso.

If the implied rate is lower than the current exchange rate, it implies that the item is less expensive in Mexico than you would expect it to be, and vice versa.

Why did the peso’s ‘overvalued’ assessment decrease between late June and August?

The MND Peso Rate — the mean implied exchange rate — changed considerably between late June and early August, declining by 37 centavos from 18.01 to 17.64.

The difference between the Banxico USD:MXN fix rate we used in late June (17.50) and that we used in early August (17.22) was 28 centavos. In an article published last Friday, we wrote about the reasons why the peso has recently appreciated.

The gap between the MND Peso Rate and Banxico’s FIX rate in early August was 42 centavos, down from 51 centavos in late June. The narrowing of the gap between the two rates is the reason why the peso’s overvaluation assessment fell from 2.9% in late June to 2.4% in early August.

But why, you might wonder, did the MND Peso Rate come down? The decline was the result of changes in the implied rates for seven of the 20 goods and services. The implied rates for the other 13 goods and services stayed the same between late June and early August.

The implied rates for four products — diapers, a hose, motor oil and eggs — declined. In the case of the diapers and the motor oil, the implied rate declined because prices in Mexico fell. In the case of the hose and the eggs, the implied rate declined because prices in Dallas increased.

The implied rates for two goods and one service — dog food, a Costco rotisserie chicken and pet grooming — increased. In the case of the dog food and the rotisserie chicken, the implied rates increased due to price increases in Mexico. In the case of the pet grooming, the implied rate increased due to a price reduction in Dallas.

Overall, the combined downward effect of the four lower implied rates outweighed the upward effect of the three higher rates. Thus the MND Peso Rate fell between late June and early August.

The cost of the Mexican and US baskets both fell in August

While the MND Peso Index™ is NOT a cost-of-living index, it is worth noting that the total costs of the Mexican and U.S. baskets of goods and services were lower in early August than in late June. However, the reduction was minimal in both cases.

The basket of goods and services in Mexico cost 5,650 pesos on Aug. 6, a reduction of 59 pesos, or 1%, compared to June 29. The slight decline in the cost of the Mexican basket in early August came at a time when inflation was easing, with Mexico’s annual headline rate falling to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June.

The basket of goods and services in Dallas cost $350.68 on Aug. 6, a reduction of $3.50, or 1%, compared to June 29. The slight decline in the cost of the Dallas basket in early August came at a time when inflation in the United States was also slowing, with the annual headline rate in the U.S. falling to 3.4% in July from 3.5% in June.

Although the cost of the Mexican basket declined in peso terms between late June and early August, its price increased when converted to dollars because the peso appreciated 1.6% in the period. The cost of the Mexican basket rose to US $328.12 on Aug. 6 from $326.21 on June 29.

The MND Peso Index™ has now found the peso to be overvalued in April, May, June and August

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June and 2.4% in early August.

The difference between the lowest overvaluation assessment — our most recent one — and the highest is just 1.6 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has appreciated 5.4% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Aug. 11 was 17.08. If the Banxico FIX rate was 17.08 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Aug. 6, the overvaluation assessment for the peso would have been 3.3%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 17.22 published on Aug. 6, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: Sheinbaum celebrates Mexico’s historic medal haul at 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 All CAC Games medals to get cash prizes: Conade chief Rommel Pacheco announced that every medal won by Mexican athletes at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — not just an athlete’s best result, as was previously the rule — will earn a cash reward.

🥇 Payouts by medal color: Individual golds are worth 50,000 pesos, silvers 35,000 pesos and bronzes 15,000 pesos, with different amounts for team events.

🇲🇽 Best-ever CAC Games performance: Mexico won a record 407 medals (167 gold, 125 silver, 115 bronze) at the Santo Domingo Games, held July 24–Aug. 8.

⚽ Pacheco touts 2031 Women’s World Cup bid: Mexico, the U.S., Costa Rica and Jamaica are the only bidders for the 2031 tournament, and Pacheco said Mexico would be a “great host,” as it was for the recent men’s World Cup.

🇨🇴 Mexican aid en route to earthquake-hit Colombia: Two Air Force planes carrying 19.5 tonnes of humanitarian aid left for the city of Pereira on Wednesday morning, with Army troops also deploying to help.

📦 58.5 tonnes of aid by Friday: Sheinbaum said additional shipments will go out Thursday and Friday, bringing food, water and medicine to Colombia, where Monday’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake has killed at least 254 people.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The most significant information from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference was that:

Each and every medal won by Mexican athletes at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games will be rewarded with a cash prize. Mexican humanitarian aid is on its way to Colombia, where a major earthquake on Monday caused widespread damage and significant loss of life.

Mexico’s performance at the recent Olympics-style sporting event in the Dominican Republic and its response to the temblor in Colombia underscore its position as a regional power.

Mexico — the Western Hemisphere’s third most populous country and fourth largest economy — invariably lends a hand when disaster strikes in the region. It went to Venezuela’s assistance when a powerful earthquake struck that country on June 24, while this month it sent more than 300 firefighters to British Columbia, Canada, as intense forest fires raged in the province.

All medals won by Mexicans in Dominican Republic will be rewarded with cash prizes

At the start of her press conference, Sheinbaum noted that medalists from the recently concluded Central American and Caribbean Games were in attendance.

“We’re very proud of you, of the role you played at the Central American Games, a medal record,” she said.

Medallero final de los XXV Juegos Centroamericanos y del Caribe #SantoDomingo2026 🥇🥈🥉 Felicidades a cada una de las delegaciones por una cosecha llena de esfuerzo y orgullo. ¡Nos vemos en los próximos Juegos! 💙 Final medal standings of the XXV Central American and Caribbean… pic.twitter.com/7JtZ7jjcUW — Santo Domingo 2026 (@SDQ2026) August 8, 2026

Mexico won a total of 407 medals at the 16-day event held from July 24 to Aug. 8 in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic. Mexican competitors took home 167 gold medals, 125 silver medals and 115 bronze medals.

Rommel Pacheco, director of the National Commission for Physical Culture and Sport (Conade), told reporters that Mexico’s medal haul amounted to its best ever performance at the Central American and Caribbean Games, a multi-sport event contested by more than 30 countries every four years.

“Behind every one of these medals, there were months [and] years of training,” Pacheco said.

Later in his presentation, the Conade chief announced that all medalists from the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games would receive a cash prize from the government for each and every medal they won.

“As you know, when [Mexican] athletes win medals at the Central American Games, the Pan American Games, the Olympics or World Championships, they get a scholarship and also an economic stimulus,” Pacheco said.

“… Normally, only the best medal [an athlete wins] is rewarded. But the president said to me: ‘I think we should reward all the medals.’ So the surprise is that for both athletes and trainers, all the medals will be rewarded,” he said.

Pacheco later noted that an individual gold medal is rewarded with 50,000 pesos (US $2,930), while silver and bronze medals are rewarded with 35,000 and 15,000 pesos, respectively.

“For teams it varies a little bit,” he said.

“… What’s going to happen is that all medals are going to be rewarded. For example, we have a swimmer who, on her own, won 11 medals,” Pacheco said, referring to 23-year-old Guanajuato native Celia Pulido.

Pacheco: Mexico will be a ‘great host’ of 2031 women’s World Cup

Pacheco noted that Mexico is vying to be a host of the 2031 FIFA women’s World Cup.

Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica submitted a joint bid to host the quadrennial tournament. No other bids have been submitted, meaning that it’s all but certain that the four Western Hemisphere countries will host the 2031 event.

Pacheco said that if Mexico is confirmed as a co-host of the 2031 women’s World Cup — the next edition of which will be played in Brazil next year — Mexicans will be “happy.”

Hosting a World Cup “grows the spirit of the sport,” he said.

“We will be a great host as we were with the [men’s] World Cup,” Pacheco said.

Sheinbaum: Mexican aid heading to Colombia today

Sheinbaum told reporters that the Mexican government received a specific aid request from the government of Colombia, where a 7.4 magnitude earthquake on Monday toppled buildings in various towns and cities and claimed at least 254 lives, according to a Reuters report on Wednesday morning.

She said that two Mexican Air Force planes carrying 19.5 tonnes of humanitarian aid departed the Felipe Ángeles International Airport on Wednesday morning to fly to Pereira, Colombia.

“Mexican Army troops are also obviously going to help in all the [rescue and recovery] work,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that Mexico will send more humanitarian aid to Colombia on Thursday and Friday. A total of 58.5 tonnes of Mexican aid, including food and other essential goods, will be sent to the South American country between Wednesday and Friday, Sheinbaum said.

“Water is being sent, medicine is being sent as well,” she said.

“We’re going to be in contact [with the Colombian government] … in order to provide all the support Colombia needs,” Sheinbaum said.

World.title: Argentina Dollar Reserves: Caputo’s US$10bn Cushion
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Deputy economy minister José Luis Daza said Argentina’s central bank will buy about US$10 billion more in dollar reserves before the October 2027 elections.

He announced it on 12 August 2026 at the Experiencia IDEA business summit in Rosario.

The central bank (BCRA) has already bought roughly US$13.5 billion so far in 2026, beating its US$10 billion target for the year.

Gross reserves reached about US$49.56 billion on 11 August 2026 — the highest level in nearly seven years.

The official wholesale peso closed near ARS 1,490 per dollar; figures here use US$1 = ARS 1,493.

Economy Minister Luis Caputo rejects the “atraso cambiario” warning that the peso is overvalued.

Argentina is quietly stockpiling dollars before the 2027 vote. Here is why Luis Caputo is betting on a firm peso — and what could still go wrong.

Argentina is building a bigger stash of Argentina dollar reserves before the next big election, and the government is not being shy about it. On 12 August 2026, a senior official said the central bank plans to buy about US$10 billion more in dollars before voters go to the polls in October 2027.

Argentina plans to buy US$10 billion more in reserves. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Argentina dollar reserves: what Caputo is building

“Reserves” are simply the pile of dollars (and gold) the central bank keeps in the vault. Countries use them to pay foreign debts, cover imports, and steady their currency when markets get nervous.

José Luis Daza, the deputy economy minister who runs economic policy, laid out the plan at a business event in Rosario. His message was blunt: the bank agreed to buy US$10 billion this year, is already near US$14 billion, and will buy roughly US$10 billion more between now and the vote.

The numbers back him up so far. The bank has bought about US$13.5 billion in 2026, and gross reserves hit around US$49.56 billion on 11 August — the most in nearly seven years.

Is the peso overvalued? The “atraso cambiario” fight

A currency is “overvalued” when it buys more abroad than the local economy really justifies. In plain terms, an expensive peso makes imported goods and foreign holidays feel cheap, but it makes Argentine exports pricey and hard to sell.

In Argentina this worry has a name: “atraso cambiario,” or exchange-rate lag. Critics say Caputo is keeping the peso artificially strong, which could force a painful devaluation later.

Caputo waves the argument away. “If they are going to accuse you of exchange-rate lag at 1,400, they cannot sell you worry at 1,500,” he said in July, arguing that competitiveness comes from lower taxes and costs, not a weaker peso.

His broader pitch is a call for patience: hold the line until the recovery finally reaches ordinary wallets on the street. Whether people feel that improvement before they vote is the open question.

Which election? The 2027 vote, not the midterms

To be clear, this is not about the 2025 legislative midterms — those already happened last October. The “elections” here are the October 2027 general elections, when President Javier Milei will seek re-election alongside a fresh round of congressional seats.

That timing matters. A government with plenty of dollars in reserve can defend its currency and avoid a messy pre-vote crash, which is exactly the kind of drama that has sunk Argentine incumbents before.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

If you earn dollars and spend pesos in Argentina, a firm peso is a mixed blessing. Your rent, restaurant bills, and flights in pesos convert into more dollars than they did a year ago, so Buenos Aires feels less of a bargain — a ARS 1,493,000 monthly rent now costs about US$1,000.

For investors, a fatter reserve cushion lowers the odds of a sudden devaluation that would wipe out peso gains overnight. It is one reason Argentine bonds and stocks have drawn fresh interest, though the same strong peso can squeeze local exporters you might be backing.

The risk in defending a strong peso

Here is the catch. Defending a currency is expensive, and the very dollars the bank is buying can be the ones it has to sell if confidence cracks.

Argentina has been here before, spending reserves to prop up the peso only to devalue anyway. If exports stall or inflation refuses to fall fast enough, the “cushion” could deflate quicker than the government hopes.

For now the strategy is holding, and the reserve numbers are real. The test is whether Caputo can keep buying dollars, hold the peso steady, and let voters feel the recovery — all before October 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will Argentina’s central bank buy in reserves? Deputy economy minister José Luis Daza said the BCRA will buy about US$10 billion more in dollar reserves before the October 2027 elections, on top of roughly US$13.5 billion already bought in 2026. What does “atraso cambiario” mean? It is Spanish for exchange-rate lag — the idea that the peso is being kept too strong (overvalued), which some economists warn could force a painful devaluation later. Caputo rejects the claim. Which election is this about? The October 2027 general elections, when President Javier Milei seeks re-election. It is not the 2025 legislative midterms, which already took place. How big are Argentina’s reserves now? Gross international reserves reached about US$49.56 billion on 11 August 2026, the highest level in nearly seven years, with the official peso trading near ARS 1,490 per dollar.

Sources: Infobae; El Economista; Buenos Aires Herald; Ámbito; El Litoral; Headtopics/Infobae (Caputo, July 2026); BCRA data, 11 August 2026.

World.title: Bolivia Dollar Withdrawals Reach US$5,000 From Friday 14 August
World.content:
Bolivia · Expats

Key Facts — What opens 14 August Balances of US$3,001 to US$5,000 can be withdrawn in cash.

— The band Stage two covers dollar savings between US$3,001 and US$5,000.

— How the stages work Each phase unlocks a higher balance band, smallest savers first.

— The timeline Nine stages run from July 2026 to July 2027 by balance size.

— Any conditions Payment is in cash at your own bank, all at once or in parts.

For anyone who watched dollar savings freeze inside a Bolivian bank, the queue is finally moving. Each stage unlocks a larger slice of trapped money.

A former Banco Central de Bolivia building and a nearby bank branch on a Bolivian street corner. From Friday, 14 August 2026, savers holding US$3,001 to US$5,000 can withdraw their dollars in cash. Photo: Gomez Romero Briza Margoth via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Bolivia dollar withdrawals take a bigger step from Friday, 14 August 2026. Savers holding US$3,001 to US$5,000 can now collect that money in cash.

What Changes on Friday 14 August

From Friday, 14 August 2026, a new group of savers can withdraw dollars held in Bolivian banks. This is stage two of the central bank’s plan to return dollars it had held back.

Stage two covers accounts holding between US$3,001 and US$5,000. Anyone whose dollar balance falls in that band can now go to their bank and ask for the cash.

The central bank is the Banco Central de Bolivia, known as the BCB. It set the nine-stage schedule and is providing the cash that funds the payouts.

How Bolivia Dollar Withdrawals Work

Bolivia dollar withdrawals are being released in stages, sorted by how much each account holds. The very smallest balances, of US$1,000 or less, were freed first, earlier in 2026.

Stage one opened on 15 July 2026 for balances of US$1,001 to US$3,000. Stage two then follows on Friday, 14 August 2026.

Each later stage lifts the ceiling to a higher band of dollar savings than the one before. Bigger balances wait their turn in the months that follow.

Why the Dollars Were Trapped

For about two years, many people in Bolivia could not pull dollars out of their own bank accounts. The country had simply run short of the hard currency needed to pay for imports.

Bolivia earns fewer dollars than before, mainly because natural gas exports have fallen. Foreign reserves dropped sharply, and banks slowly stopped handing dollars back to account holders.

So dollars sat frozen inside accounts, visible on paper but out of reach. The staged return plan is the government’s way of slowly giving that money back to savers.

The Nine-Stage Timeline to 2027

The schedule runs in nine steps, from July 2026 through July 2027. Each month of the schedule roughly opens the next balance band up the ladder.

After the US$3,001 to US$5,000 band in August, the US$5,001 to US$8,000 group opens in September 2026. Higher bands then open month by month.

Balances of US$30,001 to US$50,000 are due to open in February 2027. Sums above US$50,000 are set to be completed by July 2027.

Who Gets Paid, and How

You collect the money from the same bank where your dollar account already sits today. There is no separate office or special window to visit.

The central bank sends cash to those banks so they can pay savers. In the first stage it released US$48 million in cash.

Payment is made in US dollars, in cash, over the counter at the branch. Bring whatever identity documents your own bank asks for when you go to collect.

What This Means for Foreigners

Many foreigners living in Bolivia keep savings in dollars, not local currency. Some found those dollars locked away for months, just like the savings of local residents.

If you are an expat or nomad with a Bolivian dollar account, check your balance band. Your turn to withdraw depends only on how much money you hold in that account.

Smaller savers can already withdraw their dollars, while larger balances unlock later in the yearly cycle. The rules are the same whatever your nationality.

How Much You Can Take Out

In stage two, the band is US$3,001 to US$5,000 of dollar savings. Your place in the withdrawal queue is set entirely by your account balance.

Once your stage opens, reports say you can take all, part, or none of it. You are not forced to empty the account at once.

Officials describe the plan as permanent, not a one-day window that quickly slams shut. That gives savers room to plan around their own needs.

What Savers Should Do Now

First, find out which band your dollar balance falls into. That single fact tells you which month of the schedule your money becomes available.

Then ask your own bank exactly which documents to bring and on what day to come. Branch procedures can differ, so confirm the details in advance.

If your balance band has already opened, there is genuinely no rush to act on the very first day. The money stays yours whether you take it now or later.

The Bigger Picture for Bolivia

The return plan is funded partly by a change to the banks’ legal reserve rules, called the encaje legal. That change took effect in late January 2026.

It is meant to rebuild trust after years of dollar shortages. Confidence in the banks had worn thin during the long squeeze on cash.

The wider dollar shortage has not vanished, and imports and subsidies still strain the country’s reserves. The scheme returns savings without ending the underlying problem.

What to Watch Next

The next balance bands are scheduled to open one after another in the months after August. As of 13 August 2026, no delay to the plan had been announced.

Watch for official notices from the BCB and your own bank. Those notices confirm the exact dates, the documents required, and any change to the published schedule.

Larger balances unlock only later, stretching into 2027, so patience is built into the plan. For now, the smallest savers are the first to be made whole.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can withdraw now?

Savers whose dollar balance falls in an already-open band can withdraw. As of 14 August 2026, that means balances up to US$5,000.

How much can I take out?

Stage two covers dollar savings of US$3,001 to US$5,000. Reports say you may take all, part, or none of it.

When do larger balances unlock?

Bigger bands open through late 2026 and into 2027 by size. Balances of US$30,001 to US$50,000 are due in February 2027.

Is there a catch?

The money is genuinely returned, in cash, at your own bank. But the wider dollar shortage behind the freeze has not gone away.

Sources: Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB) notices and schedule, with ABI, Infobae, elpost.com.bo and Unitel reporting on the phased dollar-deposit return, July 2026 to July 2027. Balances in US dollars.

World.title: Brazil Decrees Unlock Hydrogen, CCS and SAF
World.content:
Brazil · Energy

What happened: On 12 August 2026, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed decrees regulating low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and storage (CCS), and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

On 12 August 2026, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed decrees regulating low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and storage (CCS), and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Hydrogen: Decree No. 13,096 puts flesh on Brazil’s 2024 low-carbon hydrogen law (Lei 14.948/2024), with roughly R$18.3 billion (~US$3.55 billion) in tax credits earmarked for 2030–2034.

Decree No. 13,096 puts flesh on Brazil’s 2024 low-carbon hydrogen law (Lei 14.948/2024), with roughly R$18.3 billion (~US$3.55 billion) in tax credits earmarked for 2030–2034. SAF: Airlines must cut 1% of flight emissions using cleaner fuel from 2027, rising to 10% by 2037, under the “Fuel of the Future” law (Lei 14.993/2024).

Airlines must cut 1% of flight emissions using cleaner fuel from 2027, rising to 10% by 2037, under the “Fuel of the Future” law (Lei 14.993/2024). CCS: Oil regulator ANP will license projects that pump carbon dioxide underground, in two stages — research, then operation.

Oil regulator ANP will license projects that pump carbon dioxide underground, in two stages — research, then operation. Local content: Hydrogen projects using electrolysis must source at least 15% locally; other routes must hit 40%.

Hydrogen projects using electrolysis must source at least 15% locally; other routes must hit 40%. Next step: Regulators ANP and ANAC have 240 days to write the fine print; a first hydrogen auction is expected in 2027.

Brasília has spent nearly two years sitting on the rulebooks. Now the paperwork that unlocks billions in clean-energy spending is finally signed.

Brazil’s new energy transition decrees are meant to turn two-year-old laws into real projects, real auctions and real money. On 12 August 2026, President Lula signed a package of rules covering low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, and sustainable aviation fuel, alongside a separate move to open the retail power market.

Lula signed decrees regulating hydrogen, CCS and SAF. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Brazil’s energy transition decrees actually do

Think of a law as the skeleton and a decree as the muscle. Brazil passed the laws in 2024, but companies could not act until the government spelled out the details.

These decrees do that. They tell investors who qualifies for tax breaks, how projects get certified, and how much of the kit must be made in Brazil.

Energy Minister Alexandre Silveira framed the package as a way to draw private capital into industries that barely exist here yet. The goal is simple: give companies enough certainty to write big cheques.

Low-carbon hydrogen: a R$18.3 billion bet

Low-carbon hydrogen is a clean fuel made by splitting water with renewable electricity, or from other sources that emit little carbon. It can replace fossil fuels in heavy industry such as steel, cement and fertiliser.

Decree No. 13,096 regulates the 2024 hydrogen law and its two support schemes. One, called PHBC, offers tax credits worth about R$18.3 billion (~US$3.55 billion) between 2030 and 2034.

The other, Rehidro, suspends federal PIS and Cofins taxes on machinery and materials for approved projects. Those taxes can drop to zero once a plant is running and meets its sustainability targets.

There is a catch for local jobs. Projects using electrolysis must buy at least 15% of their equipment in Brazil, and other technology routes must reach 40%. A new certification system, SBCH2, will grade each batch by how much carbon it emits.

Carbon capture and sustainable aviation fuel

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, means trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the air and pumping it deep underground into rock. The decree lets the oil regulator ANP license these projects in two phases — first research and evaluation, then operation — with long-term monitoring built in.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is jet fuel made from plants, waste or other renewable sources instead of crude oil. It is the main way airlines can cut emissions without new aircraft.

From 2027, airlines flying in Brazil must reduce their emissions by 1% using SAF, climbing to 10% by 2037. The government projects SAF output of 2.1 billion litres by 2030 and 3.6 billion litres by 2035, avoiding more than 8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide over a decade.

A new certificate scheme, CS-SAF, lets airlines trade the “green” value of the fuel even when they cannot pump it at their own airport. Regulators ANP and ANAC have 240 days to publish the detailed rules.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

Brazil has cheap, clean electricity and vast farmland, which makes it a natural home for green fuels. If you invest in the region, these decrees are the starting gun for a wave of projects in the Northeast and beyond.

For residents, the promise is jobs and new industrial hubs, plus cleaner air over time. The local-content rules mean some of that spending should stay in Brazilian factories rather than flowing straight abroad.

There is reason for caution too. The first hydrogen auction has slipped to 2027, and much depends on regulators finishing the fine print on schedule. For now, Brazil has the backbone in place; the test is whether the money follows.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Lula sign on 12 August 2026? He signed decrees regulating low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, and sustainable aviation fuel, plus a separate rule opening the retail electricity market to smaller consumers. What is low-carbon hydrogen and why does Brazil want it? It is a clean fuel made by splitting water with renewable power or from other low-emission sources. Brazil has abundant cheap renewable electricity, so it hopes to produce and export the fuel to heavy industry. How much money is involved? The hydrogen program alone earmarks about R$18.3 billion (~US$3.55 billion) in tax credits between 2030 and 2034, on top of tax suspensions for equipment. When do the aviation fuel rules start? Airlines must cut 1% of their emissions with sustainable aviation fuel from 2027, rising gradually to 10% by 2037, once regulators finish the detailed rules.

Sources: Ministério de Minas e Energia; Decreto nº 13.096/2026; Lei 14.948/2024 (low-carbon hydrogen); Lei 14.993/2024 (Combustível do Futuro); eixos; Metrópoles; O Tempo; Poder360.

World.title: Paraguay Residency, the Cheap South American Route, Just Changed Its Rules
World.content:
Paraguay · Expats

Key Facts — The rule Resolución DNM 407/2026 governs residency files submitted from 6 July 2026.

— One test A single economic-solvency standard now runs across the residency categories.

— Who it covers Retirees, remote workers and property owners use the same solvency route.

— The 90-day rule Permanent residency must be filed before a temporary card expires, from roughly 90 days ahead.

— The fee MERCOSUR temporary residency costs Gs. 2,230,040, about US$374, below one month’s minimum wage.

For years the standard advice for a low-cost second residency, Paraguay has quietly rewritten the terms. Anyone mid-process now has to prove where their money comes from.

Apartment and office towers rise above the tree line in Asunción, Paraguay’s capital. Since 6 July 2026, Resolución DNM 407/2026 applies one economic-solvency test to residency files, with the MERCOSUR temporary fee at Gs. 2,230,040 (about US$374). Paraguay residency, long the cheapest legal foothold in South America, now runs on a single economic-solvency test for nearly every applicant. Resolución DNM 407/2026 has applied to every residency file submitted since 6 July 2026, catching some applicants mid-process.

The new rule, in force since July

Paraguay has long topped nearly every list of cheap, low-friction places for a foreigner to gain legal residency. That reputation now comes with heavier paperwork.

Resolución DNM 407/2026 governs how the Dirección Nacional de Migraciones now weighs residency files. Its tighter rules apply to any application submitted from 6 July 2026 onward.

The change landed squarely on people who were already partway through the older process. Some had planned their finances around the looser requirements that came before.

One solvency test for every applicant

The headline shift is the move to a single economic-solvency standard for residency. It now sits at the centre of most applications, whatever the applicant’s profile.

Before the reform, different categories of applicant followed slightly different documentary paths. The new resolution folds those threads into one common financial yardstick.

Residency guides report that the resolution defines twelve documentation categories of solvency. The full official category list, however, has not been published in a verifiable form.

What Paraguay residency now demands

Paraguay residency today turns on convincingly showing that you can support yourself. Applicants must document both their income and enough financial solvency to live.

The bar is meant to prove real, ongoing means rather than a one-off token balance. Officials increasingly want evidence that the money is genuinely and lawfully yours.

That marks a clear shift from the lighter, more forgiving checks of earlier years. The route stays open to newcomers, but the file each one submits is now thicker.

Proving where your money comes from

The clearest new demand is documenting the origin of the income you rely on. A healthy bank balance, on its own, no longer settles the question for officials.

Applicants are now expected to show the actual activity that generates their funds. Pay slips, pension statements or business records can all help build that picture.

This origin-of-income requirement is the part quietly catching many applicants off guard. It rewards those who keep clean, traceable and well-labelled financial records.

Who the categories cover

The unified solvency route is what the great majority of foreign applicants now use. In practice it spans remote workers, investors, retirees and property owners alike.

Paraguay handles these varied profiles through one residency framework, not a spread of separate visas. The exact proof each person files still differs in the detail.

What every applicant now shares is the same core economic-solvency test. The paperwork simply bends to fit the particular source of a person’s income.

Remote workers and the missing nomad visa

Paraguay is genuinely popular with remote workers, yet it offers no dedicated digital-nomad visa. Digital nomads instead travel the same ordinary residency route as everyone else.

In practice that means proving foreign income and its source, exactly like any other applicant. The absence of a special nomad track still surprises many newcomers.

For location-independent earners, tidy and consistent documentation is the real practical hurdle. Long-running contracts and clear payment histories help make a convincing case.

Retirees and the pension route

Retirees remain one of the core audiences for Paraguayan residency. They typically satisfy the test by showing a pension or another steady retirement income.

The same solvency logic now applies squarely to their residency files. The key is documenting clearly where the pension money actually comes from.

For many retirees the headline cost stays modest by regional standards. The extra effort now falls mostly on the paperwork, not on the price.

The 90-day permanent-residency window

Temporary residency in Paraguay is not meant to be the end of the road. Holders are generally expected to convert it into permanent status over time.

Guides describe a filing window that opens before the temporary card expires. Some say it begins around the 21st month of a standard 24-month term.

Practically, applicants should aim to file within roughly the 90 days before expiry. Missing that narrow window risks an unwelcome lapse in legal status.

What the fees actually cost

The MERCOSUR temporary residency fee is set at Gs. 2,230,040 when paid in cash. That is about US$374 at roughly Gs. 5,965 to the dollar in August 2026.

Paid by card, the very same permit costs a little more, at Gs. 2,291,366. That works out to roughly US$384 on the same exchange rate.

Permanent residency runs higher, at Gs. 2,787,550 in cash under the same schedule. In dollar terms that is roughly US$467 at current rates.

The fee against a local wage

Those guaraní figures can look steep until you weigh them against local earnings. The DNM itself lists Paraguay’s minimum wage at Gs. 2,899,048 a month.

So a MERCOSUR temporary permit actually costs less than a single month’s minimum wage. Few residency programmes anywhere in the region come noticeably cheaper.

Even the permanent fee, near US$467, still sits below that same monthly wage. Cost, not paperwork, remains Paraguay’s real selling point for would-be residents.

What mid-process applicants should do

Anyone already partway through should assume the new file standard now applies to them. The safest move is to gather income and origin-of-funds documents early.

Those nearing a temporary card’s expiry should watch the 90-day permanent-residency window closely. Filing late can, in the worst case, force an unwelcome fresh start.

None of this closes the door on Paraguay as a low-cost destination. It simply rewards applicants who arrive organised and can clearly show their money’s source.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who qualifies for Paraguay residency now?

Most foreign applicants qualify through a single solvency route. Retirees, remote workers, investors and property owners all use it, with proof scaled to their income.

What is the new income test?

It is a single economic-solvency standard requiring documented income. Applicants must also show the origin of their funds and the activity behind them.

What changed for people mid-process?

Applications filed from 6 July 2026 fall under the tougher solvency rules. People who started earlier may now face heavier documentation than they expected.

How much does Paraguay residency cost?

The MERCOSUR temporary fee is Gs. 2,230,040, about US$374 in cash. Permanent residency costs Gs. 2,787,550, roughly US$467, both below Paraguay’s monthly minimum wage.

Sources: Paraguay’s Dirección Nacional de Migraciones (Resolución DNM 407/2026 and official aranceles migratorios), ABC Color and RSM Paraguay, plus residency guides. Guaraní values converted at about Gs. 5,965 to US$1 (August 2026).

World.title: MST Paints US Embassy in Brasília: ‘They Profit From Death’
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

What happened: Activists spray-painted the wall of the United States embassy in Brasília early on Thursday, 13 August 2026.

Activists spray-painted the wall of the United States embassy in Brasília early on Thursday, 13 August 2026. The message: “Os EUA fazem guerra e lucram com a morte” — “The USA makes war and profits from death.”

“Os EUA fazem guerra e lucram com a morte” — “The USA makes war and profits from death.” Who claimed it: Brazil’s Landless Workers’ Movement (MST), alongside youth group Levante Popular da Juventude.

Brazil’s Landless Workers’ Movement (MST), alongside youth group Levante Popular da Juventude. US reaction: The embassy called the act “unacceptable” and said it is working with local police.

The embassy called the act “unacceptable” and said it is working with local police. Motive: Protest against the US arms industry and what the MST calls “imperialist” policy, including weapons sales linked to Gaza.

Protest against the US arms industry and what the MST calls “imperialist” policy, including weapons sales linked to Gaza. Backdrop: A months-long US–Brazil clash over tariffs, sanctions and Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution.

A wall of paint in Brasília has turned a diplomatic cold spell into a very public shove — and both governments are watching how the other reacts.

The US embassy Brasília graffiti landed on a raw nerve. On Thursday morning, 13 August 2026, activists from Brazil’s Landless Workers’ Movement painted a blunt accusation across the embassy wall: the United States “makes war and profits from death.” Washington called it unacceptable. Brazil’s police opened a case.

Activists painted the US embassy wall in Brasília. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the US embassy Brasília graffiti actually said

The main line was in Portuguese. “Os EUA fazem guerra e lucram com a morte” translates as “The USA makes war and profits from death.”

The same message appeared in English on the wall. A nearby banner read, in Portuguese, “US war industry = deaths, hunger and the destruction of nature.” Headlines across Brazil quickly shortened it all to three words: “Lucram com a morte” — “They profit from death.”

Who did it, and why

The Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, better known as the MST, claimed responsibility. So did the Levante Popular da Juventude, a left-wing youth movement that often works alongside it.

In a statement, the MST described the action as “collective and peaceful.” It said young members were protesting against the US arms industry and what it called Washington’s “imperialist” foreign policy.

The movement tied its anger to Gaza. It said the United States is one of the largest suppliers of weapons to Israel, and it blamed US policy for war, hunger and “criminal blockades and sanctions” against nations across Latin America and the wider world. The protest coincided with a national gathering of landless youth being held this week.

How Washington responded

The embassy did not brush it off. It said it was aware of the vandalism and that “such acts are unacceptable.”

The full statement went further. “Such acts are unacceptable, and we are working with local authorities,” it said. “The USA remains committed to dialogue with the Brazilian people and ensuring the security of our personnel and facilities.”

Brazil’s Federal District Civil Police opened an investigation through its Asa Sul precinct. Officers said they would pull security-camera footage to identify who was involved.

A relationship already under strain

This did not happen in a vacuum. US–Brazil relations have been tense for more than a year.

The friction started with trade. In 2025, President Donald Trump imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian goods — reaching 50% at their peak — and openly linked them to the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro, whom he called the victim of a “witch hunt.” Some farm products were later exempted, and the exact effective rate has shifted over time, so treat any single figure with care.

The dispute widened from there. Washington placed Magnitsky sanctions on Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes and revoked visas for several Brazilian officials. In early August 2026, reports said the United States pulled the visa of Brazil’s ambassador, a step Brazil called a “hostile escalation.” The graffiti, then, is street-level anger layered on top of a state-level standoff.

Why this matters if you live or invest in Latin America

You may not care who paints a wall. You should care about what it signals.

When a large, organized movement targets the US embassy and openly claims it, that is a sign the diplomatic chill has spread into public mood. That mood can shape trade talks, tariff decisions and the tone of Brazil’s 2026 election — all of which touch prices, contracts and the currency you convert your money into. If you run a business, hold Brazilian assets, or simply plan to stay a while, a strained US–Brazil relationship is not background noise. It is part of your risk map.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the graffiti on the US embassy in Brasília say? The main phrase was “Os EUA fazem guerra e lucram com a morte,” meaning “The USA makes war and profits from death.” The same line appeared in English, and Brazilian media shortened it to “Lucram com a morte” — “They profit from death.” Who was behind it? Brazil’s Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) claimed responsibility, together with the youth group Levante Popular da Juventude. The MST said the action was collective and peaceful. How did the United States respond? The embassy called the vandalism “unacceptable,” said it was working with local authorities, and stressed it remains committed to dialogue with the Brazilian people and to protecting its staff and buildings. What is the wider context? US–Brazil relations have been strained by US tariffs tied to Bolsonaro’s prosecution, sanctions on a Supreme Court justice, and visa disputes, including the reported revocation of the Brazilian ambassador’s visa in early August 2026.

Sources: Metrópoles; Gazeta do Povo; Jornal de Brasília; O Tempo; Jovem Pan; BBC News; CNN; Al Jazeera; Wikipedia (2025–2026 Brazil–United States diplomatic dispute).

World.title: What a SAT Invoice Really Needs, and Why Clients Can’t Demand Your Constancia
World.content:
Mexico · Expats

Key Facts — What’s required to issue a CFDI, a client needs only your RFC, name, postal code and tax regime.

— Not required SAT says the full Constancia de Situación Fiscal is not needed to bill you.

— The penalty demanding it is an infraction, with fines of MXN 21,000 to 120,000 (about US$1,230 to US$7,030).

— Who it protects freelancers, remote workers and tenants asked to hand over their whole tax file.

— How to report SAT takes complaints through MarcaSAT and its online denuncia portal.

Across Mexico, businesses routinely demand your entire tax file before billing you. But the law says four small details are all they can ask for.

A laptop, an open notebook and a calculator on a home-office desk. To issue a SAT invoice in Mexico, a client needs only your RFC, name, postal code and tax regime — not your full Constancia de Situación Fiscal. (Photo: Unknown author, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.)

To issue a SAT invoice, a client legally needs only your RFC, name, postal code and tax regime. Under Mexican tax law, the full Constancia de Situación Fiscal is not required, and demanding it can be fined.

What a SAT Invoice Actually Requires

In Mexico, every formal payment should come with a CFDI, the electronic invoice known as a factura. Freelancers, landlords and remote workers deal with them almost every time money changes hands.

To generate that invoice, the person billing you needs a short, specific set of data. In practice it is far less information than many clients routinely ask you to send.

The required fields are your RFC, your name or business name, your postal code and your tax regime. Nothing more than that is legally needed to produce a valid factura.

The Data You Must Share

Your RFC is your taxpayer ID, the backbone of any invoice. Without it, the system simply cannot link the factura to you.

Your postal code and tax regime tell SAT where you are registered and how you are taxed. Both come straight from your own registration and rarely change from one client to the next.

Your name or razón social completes the set. These four items together are all a client needs to bill you correctly.

Why the Constancia de Situación Fiscal Is Not Required

The Constancia de Situación Fiscal is a full snapshot of your tax file. It lists your address, regime, obligations and status in one document.

Many businesses have grown used to demanding it before issuing an invoice. SAT has now made clear that this practice has no legal basis.

Everything a valid invoice needs already sits inside SAT’s systems. The recipient’s data is verified there at the moment of issuance.

What SAT Actually Said

SAT set out its position in an official statement early in 2026. It confirmed that the Constancia should not be required to invoice.

The data on an invoice, the agency stressed, is checked against its own registries. Asking for the full document adds nothing but friction.

The message was aimed at businesses, but it protects the people they bill. That includes freelancers, contractors and tenants across the country.

The Penalty for Demanding It

Refusing to invoice unless you hand over the Constancia is not just rude. Under the Código Fiscal de la Federación, it is an infraction.

The tax code defines the conduct as a breach in its Article 83. The matching fine sits in Article 84 of the same code.

Those fines run from MXN 21,000 to MXN 120,000 per case. That is roughly US$1,230 to US$7,030 at current exchange rates.

Who This Protects

For a freelancer or contractor, your tax file is deeply sensitive. It reveals your home address, your income bracket and your full fiscal history.

Handing the whole Constancia to every client and landlord spreads that data widely. The new clarity from SAT means you no longer have to do so.

Remote workers billing Mexican companies stand to gain the most. They can share a handful of fields and keep the rest of their file entirely private.

How to Push Back Politely

If a client asks for your Constancia, you can decline with confidence. Offer the required fields instead and cite SAT’s guidance.

Most requests come from habit rather than bad faith. A short, factual reply often settles the matter without conflict.

Keep your core data points ready to send in a note. It turns an awkward exchange into a quick, routine reply.

How to Report an Abuse

If a business still refuses to invoice you, SAT wants to hear about it. The agency has opened channels for exactly this complaint.

You can report through MarcaSAT, the tax authority’s phone line, or its online denuncia portal. Keep records of the refusal to support your case.

A complaint is not only about your own invoice. It flags a pattern that SAT can act on across the market.

What It Means for Your Privacy

Data privacy is a growing concern for anyone working across borders. Your fiscal profile is among the most revealing documents you hold.

Limiting what leaves your hands is a simple, effective safeguard. Sharing a handful of fields instead of a full file is a real gain.

The rule aligns everyday billing with basic data hygiene. Less exposure now means far less risk later if a client’s records are ever breached.

A Quick Checklist Before You Bill

Before your next job, save your four billing details somewhere easy to reach. A note on your phone or a pinned message to yourself works well.

Confirm that your tax regime matches your current activity in SAT’s portal. An out-of-date regime is a common reason an otherwise valid invoice fails.

Then treat any request for more as optional rather than mandatory. You alone decide whether the full Constancia ever leaves your hands.

The Bottom Line for Freelancers

The takeaway is short and practical. To be invoiced, share only your RFC, name, postal code and tax regime.

You are not obliged to surrender your Constancia de Situación Fiscal. A client who insists is on the wrong side of the tax code.

If the pressure still continues, the reporting channels are open. The penalty behind the rule gives your refusal real, enforceable weight.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do I need to give to be invoiced?

You only need to share your RFC, name, postal code and tax regime. Those fields let any client issue a valid CFDI.

Can a client demand my Constancia?

No, they cannot. SAT has confirmed the Constancia de Situación Fiscal is not required to issue an invoice.

What’s the fine?

Demanding the Constancia is an infraction under Mexico’s federal tax code. Fines range from MXN 21,000 to 120,000, about US$1,230 to US$7,030.

How do I report it?

You can report a refusal to invoice through MarcaSAT or SAT’s online denuncia portal. Keep evidence of the request to support your complaint.

Sources: El Informador; SAT (Servicio de Administración Tributaria); Código Fiscal de la Federación.

World.title: Chile Tax Reform Clears Congress With a VAT Break for New-Home Buyers
World.content:
Chile · Expats

Key Facts — Corporate tax the company rate falls in steps from 27%, reaching 23% from the 2029 tax year.

— New homes a qualifying new-build home gets a temporary break from Chile’s 19% value-added tax.

— The window the relief is reported to run for a 12-month period, tied to a signed purchase promise made in that time.

— Where it stands the Senate approved the final vetoes on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, and the bill now awaits the president’s signature.

— Who gains a buyer of a new-build home stands to save the most, since the VAT is close to a fifth of the price.

The part most buyers will feel is not the company rate at all. But a rare one-year window to buy a new-build home without the value-added tax.

The Gran Torre Santiago tower, lit green during construction, rises over the capital’s financial district at night. Chile’s new tax law opens a one-year window in which a qualifying new-build home is freed from the 19% value-added tax. (Photo: Jorge Barrios Riquelme, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.)

The Chile tax reform, the sweeping overhaul known locally as the megarreforma, has cleared Congress and now awaits the president’s signature. Its headline measures cut the company tax rate toward 23% and offer new-home buyers a one-year break from the 19% value-added tax.

What the Chile Tax Reform Changes

The package does two big things. It lowers the tax that companies pay on their profits.

And it gives new-home buyers a temporary escape from a large sales tax. For a business, the general company rate starts at 27% and falls in stages.

For a home buyer, the prize is a one-year window with no value-added tax on a qualifying new build. Chile’s value-added tax, known locally as the IVA, is set at 19%.

Removing it from the price of a new home is the single biggest saving in the law for a foreign buyer.

The VAT Break on New Homes, Explained

In Chile, buying a brand-new home from a developer normally means paying the 19% value-added tax on top of the price. That tax is baked into what the seller charges.

The reform sets up a temporary exemption for new-build homes. During the window, a qualifying first sale of a new dwelling is freed from that 19% charge.

The exact rules are set by the tax authority rather than by a headline. So the precise list of which homes qualify, and how, will be spelled out in the fine print.

How Big the Saving Is for a Foreign Buyer

The math is simple, and it is why this clause matters. If a new home would normally carry the 19% value-added tax, the exemption takes that whole slice off the price.

Put plainly, the tax is close to a fifth of what you would otherwise pay. On a mid-range new apartment, that is a substantial sum kept in your pocket.

No other part of the reform touches a foreign buyer so directly. The company rate cut helps investors and firms, but the VAT break helps anyone signing for a new home.

What a Signed Purchase Agreement Means

The relief is tied to a document Chileans call a promesa de compraventa. It is a signed promise-to-buy contract, agreed before the final deed is done.

In practice, the buyer and seller commit in writing to complete the sale on set terms. Coverage indicates the promise must be signed within the 12-month window to count.

That timing is the part to watch. If the window matters, then when you sign the promise.

Not just when you move in, is what decides whether the break applies.

The Corporate Tax Cut, Phased to 2029

The company rate does not drop to 23% overnight. It steps down over several years, which is easy to misread if you only see the start and end numbers.

The reported path is 27% now, then 25.5% in 2027 and 24% in 2028. The rate reaches 23% from the 2029 tax year.

Smaller firms have their own track under the Pro Pyme regime. That regime is reported at 12.5% through 2027, rising to 15% in 2028.

Where the Reform Stands in Congress

The bill has moved through its final legislative steps. The Chamber of Deputies backed the presidential vetoes on Monday, 10 August 2026.

The Senate then approved the same vetoes on Wednesday, 12 August 2026. With both chambers done, the text is one step from becoming law.

The remaining act is promulgation, the president’s formal signing and publication. Until that happens, the measures are approved but not yet in force.

The Constitutional Court Still Has a Say

Approval by Congress is not always the last word in Chile. The reform faced challenges lodged with the Constitutional Court, the body that reviews whether laws fit the constitution.

Reporting points to three challenges filed against parts of the text. A ruling was awaited around 13 August 2026.

As of publication, no final court decision had been confirmed in the sources reviewed. The outcome could shape the timing of the law taking effect.

Confirmed Versus Still Pending

It helps to separate what is settled from what is not. The corporate rate cut and the new-home VAT break are in the approved text, with strong support in tax briefings.

What is still moving is the final paperwork. Promulgation had not been confirmed as complete, and the Constitutional Court review was still open.

The precise mechanics of the housing exemption are the softest part. The 12-month window and the promise-of-sale trigger are reported, but the fine print governs the detail.

Who Stands to Benefit

Two groups gain the most. Companies see a lower profit tax over time, and buyers of new homes get a rare tax-free window.

For a foreigner planning a move, the home clause is the headline. A newcomer buying a new apartment in Santiago could avoid a large one-off tax.

Existing homes bought from a private owner are a different case. The value-added tax generally applies to new builds sold by developers, not to ordinary resales.

What a Buyer Should Do Now

The sensible move is to confirm the details before acting. Check whether the law has been promulgated and whether your target home qualifies.

Ask the developer and a local tax adviser to put the exemption in writing. Timing around the signed promise is where the saving is won or lost.

The reform is a real opportunity, not a guarantee. Treat the VAT break as confirmed in principle, but verify the effective dates before you sign anything.

Frequently Asked Questions

What changes for a homebuyer?

A qualifying new-build home can be bought without Chile’s 19% value-added tax during a temporary window. The relief is tied to a signed purchase promise made within that period.

How big is the VAT saving?

Chile’s value-added tax is 19%, so the exemption removes close to a fifth of a new home’s price. On a mid-range new apartment, that is a substantial one-off saving.

When does it take effect?

The bill cleared Congress on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, but it must still be promulgated by the president. The measures are approved and not yet in force until that signing.

Is it final yet?

Not entirely, as of publication. Promulgation was pending and the Constitutional Court was still reviewing challenges to parts of the text.

Sources: Infobae América, KPMG and Cuatrecasas tax briefings, Chilean government (Ministerio de Hacienda), EFE.

World.title: Moraes Impeachment Request Filed Over Source Breach
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Who and when: On 12 August 2026, opposition leader in the Chamber of Deputies Cabo Gilberto Silva (PL-PB) filed an impeachment request against Supreme Federal Court (STF) Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

On 12 August 2026, opposition leader in the Chamber of Deputies Cabo Gilberto Silva (PL-PB) filed an impeachment request against Supreme Federal Court (STF) Justice Alexandre de Moraes. The grounds: The request claims Moraes broke the constitutional protection of journalists’ sources when he approved a police search tied to a reporter’s coverage.

The request claims Moraes broke the constitutional protection of journalists’ sources when he approved a police search tied to a reporter’s coverage. The trigger: On 11 August, Moraes authorized a search and seizure against Raimundo Cutrim, a former Maranhão state official whom federal police named as the source for journalist Luís Pablo.

On 11 August, Moraes authorized a search and seizure against Raimundo Cutrim, a former Maranhão state official whom federal police named as the source for journalist Luís Pablo. The backstory: Pablo had reported in late 2025 on STF Justice Flávio Dino’s family use of an official vehicle; police say data seized from Pablo in March 2026 led them to the source.

Pablo had reported in late 2025 on STF Justice Flávio Dino’s family use of an official vehicle; police say data seized from Pablo in March 2026 led them to the source. Press reaction: Globo, Folha de S.Paulo and Estadão all criticized the STF, calling the move a threat to press freedom.

Globo, Folha de S.Paulo and Estadão all criticized the STF, calling the move a threat to press freedom. Where it goes: Impeaching an STF justice is decided by the Senate, and no such case has ever succeeded in Brazil.

A police search aimed at a journalist’s confidential source has handed Brazil’s opposition its latest opening against Justice Alexandre de Moraes — and pulled the country’s biggest newspapers into the fight.

A fresh Moraes impeachment request landed in Brazil’s Senate this week, and this time the argument is about press freedom. The opposition says the Supreme Federal Court justice crossed a constitutional line by helping police track down a reporter’s confidential source.

The opposition filed an impeachment request against Justice Moraes. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What the Moraes impeachment request actually says

The request was filed on 12 August 2026 by Cabo Gilberto Silva, a federal deputy for the PL party and the opposition’s leader in the Chamber of Deputies. He delivered it to the Senate, which is the only body that can put a Supreme Court justice on trial.

His core claim is that Moraes violated Article 220 and Article 5 of Brazil’s Constitution, which protect freedom of the press and a journalist’s right to keep sources secret. In plain terms, the opposition argues that once the court helped police unmask a source, that legal protection stopped meaning anything in practice.

The search that started it

Here is the chain of events, as reported by Brazilian outlets. On 11 August 2026, Moraes authorized a search and seizure operation against Raimundo Cutrim, a former senior official in Maranhão state whom the federal police identified as a source for journalist Luís Pablo.

Pablo had published reports in late 2025 questioning the use of an official court vehicle by relatives of STF Justice Flávio Dino. Moraes had already approved a search of Pablo himself back in March 2026, and police say data pulled from the reporter’s seized phones and devices is what led them to Cutrim.

The federal police requested the new search, and the Prosecutor-General’s Office (PGR) signed off on it. Dino’s office has denied any wrongdoing over the vehicle, saying it was an armored car provided under a security agreement, and complained that the minister and his family were the ones being improperly watched.

Why the big newspapers pushed back

The reaction from Brazil’s largest news organizations was unusually blunt. Folha de S.Paulo said the decision “violates press freedom” and questioned why the case sat at the Supreme Court at all.

Estadão called it an “attack” on the free press and described the long-running “fake news” inquiry that Moraes oversees as an “instrument of intimidation.” O Globo went further still, calling the breach of source confidentiality “unconstitutional” and warning that it sets a “dangerous precedent.” All three pointed to the same constitutional guarantee that reporters can protect their sources.

An adviser leaves the court

Around the same time, one of Moraes’s advisers stepped down. Marina de Cerqueira Sant’Anna Rezende left her post in the justice’s office after about a year, with the dismissal made at her own request.

The exoneration took effect on 8 August 2026 and was published in the official gazette on 13 August, signed by STF President Edson Fachin. The court has not linked her departure to the source controversy, and no public evidence ties the two events together — so treat any connection as unconfirmed.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy, and investors watch the relationship between its courts, Congress and press as a gauge of how stable the rules are. When the country’s biggest newspapers and its top court clash openly in an election year, it feeds the sense of institutional friction that can rattle markets and unsettle long-term planning.

For a foreign resident or investor, the practical takeaway is narrower but real. A weaker shield for journalists’ sources can mean less independent scrutiny of the officials and agencies whose decisions touch your visa, your taxes and your business — which is exactly why press-freedom fights are worth following, not just political theater.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the STF, and what does impeachment of a justice involve? The STF is Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, the highest court in the country. To remove one of its justices, the Senate must accept the case and then convict by a two-thirds vote — 54 of 81 senators — something that has never happened in Brazilian history. Who filed this Moraes impeachment request and on what grounds? Opposition leader Cabo Gilberto Silva (PL-PB) filed it on 12 August 2026. He argues Moraes breached the constitutional protection of journalistic sources by approving a police search that helped identify a reporter’s confidant. Was the journalist himself the target? The 11 August search targeted Raimundo Cutrim, the former state official named as the source, not the reporter directly. However, police say the lead came from data seized during an earlier search of journalist Luís Pablo in March 2026. What has Moraes or the court said? The search was requested by federal police and approved by the Prosecutor-General’s Office as part of an existing investigation. As of publication, Moraes had not issued a public defense of this specific decision, and the STF has not commented on the impeachment request.

Sources: Poder360; CNN Brasil; Gazeta do Povo; editorials from Folha de S.Paulo, O Estado de S.Paulo and O Globo. Reporting verified as of 13 August 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Seals Security Contracts as “Operation Pegasus” Remark Goes Unexplained
World.content:
A decree set since August 10 has sealed a wide range of Costa Rican security information from public view, including records of which companies win government security contracts. The dispute over it sharpened Wednesday when a governing-party lawmaker referred to an “Operation Pegasus” during floor debate in the Legislative Assembly, then declined to say what she meant.

President Laura Fernández Delgado and Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde signed Executive Decree 45870-MSP on July 27. It was published in Alcance No. 104 to the official gazette La Gaceta on August 10 and took effect immediately, without prior public consultation, because the text classifies itself as confidential and restricted. The government declared the records a state secret covering its principal intelligence and security bodies.

The declaration reaches the National Public Security Council, the National Intelligence and Security Directorate known as the DIS, and a high-level working group called Fuerza Élite, along with any other security and defense coordination directed by the presidency. It covers documents, files, budgets, operational plans and meeting recordings.

Fuerza Élite brings Fernández together on Mondays with the ministers of security and justice, DIS leadership and police chiefs to coordinate the response to organized crime. It is the same group at whose first session she ordered polygraph examinations for senior police and government officials.

The reach that has drawn the sharpest objections is financial. The decree seals command structures, technological resources, reliability-vetting protocols and their results, budget line items and spending categories. It also covers public procurement files, supplier identities, technical requirements, bids, contract awards, financing arrangements and records of how those contracts are carried out.

The government justified the measure on grounds of public interest and national security, citing the threat posed by criminal structures tied to drug trafficking, contract killing and money laundering. Disclosure, the text argues, would expose institutional vulnerabilities and endanger officials and their families.

That rationale follows a period of sustained concern about criminal penetration of the security forces themselves, including a confidential police intelligence report that flagged 116 officers along the southern border over alleged links to trafficking networks. The decree invokes articles 27, 30, 130 and 140 of the Constitution, several provisions of the General Police Law and the General Public Administration Law, along with Constitutional Chamber rulings and opinions from the Attorney General’s Office.

Wednesday’s exchange began when Frente Amplio deputy Sigrid Segura Artavia challenged the scope of the decree and asked what the government was concealing, raising the possibility that authorities might be acquiring or using technology to monitor citizens who oppose them.

She named Pegasus, the surveillance program developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group, as the cautionary example. The software can extract messages, emails, photographs and location data from a compromised phone, and can switch on its microphone and camera. NSO Group has said it sells the tool only to governments and state agencies for use against serious crime and terrorism.

Pueblo Soberano deputy Kattia Calvo Cruz replied by referring to “the Pegasus operation” and denying it had anything to do with surveillance. “The Pegasus operation is not that. It has absolutely nothing to do with that,” she said, adding that Costa Rica faces a critical security situation and that classifying sensitive security information is a power the executive branch holds and is exercising.

Calvo did not say what the phrase referred to. Segura pressed her on whether the mention amounted to confirmation that the government uses the technology, and said such a program would be worse than the presidential data-analysis unit that triggered a privacy scandal under an earlier administration.

Asked afterward by reporters to explain what she had meant, Calvo declined to give a direct answer, saying she would respond if the question were put to her in the plenary chamber. She later referred the matter to her press officer. No evidence has been presented publicly that Costa Rica has acquired or deployed Pegasus, and Calvo explicitly rejected that reading of her own words. What remains unresolved is what operation she was describing.

Legal opinion on the decree has divided sharply. Of five attorneys who reviewed the text, four concluded it is plainly unconstitutional. Constitutional scholar Rubén Hernández estimated that slightly more than 90 percent of it would fail a constitutional review, and said only the portion concerning the DIS might survive, though not as currently drafted because it is written too broadly.

David Delgado argued that a state secret cannot be created by decree at all and requires a law passed by the Assembly, pointing to Constitutional Chamber rulings 13236-2003 and 00320-2005, which held that limiting access to administrative information through state secrecy is a matter reserved to legislation. Manrique Jiménez said a regulation cannot impose such a restriction on its own, and that any secret must be defined precisely and narrowly rather than leaving broad discretion to the executive.

Marvin Carvajal accepted that a declaration could in principle come by executive decree but said this one contravenes constitutional law, arguing the executive cannot declare state secrets wholesale. Fabián Volio was the lone defender, holding that the decree satisfies constitutional requirements because it governs a matter tied to national security, and that the reserve may properly cover documents, analyses, statistics and evidence gathered by such bodies.

The University of Costa Rica’s Freedom of Expression and Right to Information Program issued its own objection late Wednesday, saying a restriction of that breadth runs against the principles of publicity, transparency, maximum disclosure and accountability. It acknowledged that article 30 of the Constitution recognizes state secrets as a limit on access to information of public interest, but argued the provision grants no unlimited power to decide what citizens may know.

Information held by public administrations is presumed public, the program said, and may be withheld only where there is sufficient justification and express legal authorization. It noted that Costa Rica has no comprehensive law regulating state secrecy. The Inter American Press Association warned separately from Miami on August 11 that a measure of such breadth could obstruct journalism and restrict access to information of public interest, and recommended that journalists and citizens ask the Constitutional Chamber to rule on whether the decree conforms to the Constitution.

There is precedent for that route. Roughly three decades ago, a state secrecy decree covering arms purchases was challenged before the Constitutional Chamber, which never ruled because the government repealed the measure itself 78 days later. In the repealing decree, the executive of the day wrote that alongside protecting national defense it considered it equally essential to guarantee public confidence in institutions and full transparency in administrative contracting.

Opposition lawmakers have signaled they intend to test the current decree. Claudia Dobles of Coalición Agenda Ciudadana questioned why the declaration reaches contracting and the handling of public funds. Álvaro Ramírez, who leads the Liberación Nacional bench, said his party will examine the measure’s legality, singling out the confidentiality applied to DIS purchases.

The decree remains in force while those objections gather. Any challenge alleging violation of a fundamental right, such as access to public information, would go to the Constitutional Chamber, a body already at odds with the president over her claims about criminal infiltration of the judiciary. A claim that the decree conflicts with existing legislation could instead be brought in administrative court.

World.title: Lionel Messi Says He May Not Play Much Longer After Father’s Death
World.content:
Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi said Wednesday that he has “a lot of doubts” about whether he will continue playing football “for much longer,” in an emotional farewell letter to his father and agent, Jorge Messi, who died Friday at the age of 68. In his first public reaction since his father’s death, the 39-year-old star reflected on the final months of his father’s life, which were marked by the worsening cancer that ultimately killed him, according to media reports.



Jorge Messi’s declining health, after playing a central role throughout his son’s brilliant career, coincided with the 2026 World Cup in North America. Argentina lost the final 1-0 to Spain on July 19 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. “I don’t know what I’m going to do without you, I don’t know how to go on. All I ever did was play football, and now I have a lot of doubts about whether I’ll keep doing it for much longer,” Messi wrote in a letter posted on Instagram alongside photographs of himself with his father.

“You kept asking me to play in one last World Cup, and just days before it started was when you got much worse. It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament,” the Argentina captain added. “I kept telling you we were going to reach the final so you could travel.”

I Never Managed to Feel Right

The former FC Barcelona forward, whose contract with Inter Miami runs through 2028, said he wanted to win the World Cup so he could take the trophy to his father. But he acknowledged that he was unable to do so because his body failed him in the title match against a Spain side that overwhelmed Argentina.

“A huge hug to you and your family during these difficult moments, Leo. Stay strong,” Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi’s longtime rival in the debate over the world’s best player, replied to Wednesday’s post. Jorge Messi’s poor health, which became public during the World Cup, ended with his burial Sunday near Rosario.

In Argentina’s opening match against Algeria, Messi cried after scoring one of his three goals in a 3-0 victory. Afterward, he acknowledged that the unusual display of emotion was connected to his father’s condition. “Every time a match ended, I waited for and missed your message. That was when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn’t stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and so you could see one of the matches,” Messi wrote.

“We reached the final and you couldn’t be there. I wanted to win it so I could take it to you and show you another one. I couldn’t. My legs had nothing left.
