World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Saving China’s Vanishing Fields of Knowledge
World.content:
Every summer, millions of Chinese high school students who have just completed the national college entrance examination, or gaokao, face a pivotal decision: which university and major to choose. At the same time, media outlets and social platforms fill with debate over which fields of study offer the best employment prospects and financial returns. Driven by pragmatism, students tend to favor majors that lead to well-paid or stable careers, such as computer science, software engineering, medicine, and accounting.

At the other end of the spectrum are disciplines that appear to have little practical value and remain unfamiliar to most people, including Western Xia studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, silk manuscript studies, and Dunhuang studies. In recent years, these fields have come to be grouped under the poetic term “lengmen juexue,” often translated as “niche and endangered disciplines.”

The phrase combines two concepts. Lengmen, or “niche disciplines,” refers to traditional humanities fields with small research communities that attract limited scholarly attention and produce results slowly. Juexue, or “endangered disciplines,” refers to fields of exceptional cultural significance that require highly specialized expertise and risk disappearing as senior scholars retire. In other words, lengmen describes their circumstances, while juexue reflects their value. A true niche and endangered discipline must satisfy both conditions: it has only a small community of researchers while preserving an irreplaceable body of cultural knowledge at risk of being lost.

Many of these disciplines have a long history. Fields such as philology, Confucian classics, epigraphy, bibliography, ancient musicology, and calendrical studies were once central to Chinese scholarship but gradually became marginalized following the introduction of Western academic disciplines in the modern era. The term juexue itself dates back more than a thousand years. During the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the philosopher Zhang Zai (1020–1077) wrote in his “Hengqu Yulu” of the need “to ordain conscience for Heaven and Earth, to secure life for the people, to continue the lost teachings of past sages, and to establish peace for all future generations.”

Today, however, “niche and endangered disciplines” is more than a descriptive label. It has become an institutional framework within Chinese academia. In 2016, President Xi Jinping called for greater attention to marginal disciplines with high cultural value and significance for Chinese heritage during a speech at the Seminar on Philosophy and Social Sciences in Beijing. Quoting an old Chinese saying, he argued that resources maintained over the long term prove their worth when they are eventually needed.

That vision took institutional form in 2018, when the National Social Science Fund of China established a dedicated funding program for niche and endangered disciplines. Since then, the Ministry of Education, the Chinese Academy of History, and other institutions have launched related initiatives. One flagship funding program provides around 350,000 yuan ($52,000) for individual research projects and about 800,000 yuan for collaborative projects, placing these disciplines on a similar footing to other major National Social Science Fund initiatives.

These disciplines contribute little to GDP growth and seem far removed from everyday life. So why do the state and the academic community devote such significant resources to supporting them?

The answer lies in their role in helping Chinese civilization understand itself and sustain its continuity. Civilizations do not endure by chance. Their longevity depends not only on creating new knowledge but also on preserving and interpreting their past.

These disciplines address fundamental questions about China’s history. Why were oracle bone inscriptions written the way they were? How was the millennia-old “Book of Documents” passed down through the centuries? How did ancient Chinese societies observe the skies and develop calendars? What does the Library Cave at the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang reveal about cultural exchange? Such questions may seem remote, but they form the foundation of a civilization’s understanding of its own history.

These disciplines also safeguard cultural continuity. The longevity of the Chinese civilization has depended on generations of scholars who continuously compiled classical texts, interpreted ancient scripts, and preserved knowledge. Without this work, vast collections of cultural heritage might survive physically while becoming increasingly difficult, or even impossible, to understand.

These disciplines also shape China’s cultural narrative. Research into frontier history, ethnic writing systems, and Chinese texts preserved overseas extends beyond academic inquiry. It informs historical interpretation, cultural identity, and international exchange.

In short, niche and endangered disciplines preserve the historical memory of Chinese civilization. Once sustained by only a handful of scholars, they have become an important part of China’s broader cultural strategy.

So what qualifies as a niche and endangered discipline? There is no definitive list. Instead, the category has steadily expanded. It initially included fields such as oracle bone studies, Dunhuang studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, and ancient script studies. More recently, it has broadened to encompass the history of ancient Chinese science and technology, ancient astronomy and calendrical studies, ethnic scripts, Chinese texts preserved overseas, frontier history and geography, and research on exchanges between China and other civilizations. Today, these disciplines are generally grouped into four broad categories: ancient scripts and extinct languages; traditional classics and endangered classical studies; ancient specialized histories and niche skills; and research on China’s frontiers and its exchanges with other ancient civilizations.

Why has the category expanded? Not because more disciplines have become obscure but because there is growing recognition that many specialized fields are indispensable to understanding Chinese civilization.

Take ancient astronomy and calendrical studies. Without them, it would be difficult to understand how ancient China developed its calendar, organized agricultural production, and structured political authority. Likewise, without research into historical ethnic writing systems, countless documents produced by frontier peoples would become unreadable. Moreover, dedicated funding programs provide specialized institutions and researchers with the long-term support needed to sustain this work.

State support has already produced significant results. The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, for example, has published major works including “Heroic Epic and Oral Tradition” and “Translations of Sanskrit Literature.” These works preserve and interpret historical texts, making them accessible to modern scholars and readers. Meanwhile, digital technologies are increasingly being used to collate ancient texts, digitize documents, and recognize historical scripts, greatly improving research efficiency. Even so, significant challenges remain.

The greatest challenge is not funding but time. One scholar may spend three decades studying just a few dozen oracle bones. Another may devote an entire career to deciphering a script that disappeared more than a thousand years ago. A third may spend decades reconstructing an ancient calendar.

Mastering a niche and endangered discipline often requires decades of training, yet an entire field can disappear within a single generation. Early Chinese astronomy, for example, demands expertise in ancient astronomy and calendrical systems, the ability to decipher ancient scripts, and a deep understanding of history. The barriers to entry are therefore exceptionally high. Since the deaths of leading scholars such as Bo Shuren (1934–1997), Xi Zezong (1927–2008), and Chen Meidong (1942–2008), the field has weakened significantly, with few young researchers able to replace them. Sustained institutional support is therefore essential.

These disciplines also sit uneasily within a modern research system that rewards speed and measurable output. Their work progresses slowly, while public awareness remains limited and relatively few young people are willing to commit to careers that require decades of patient study.

Protecting niche and endangered disciplines therefore requires training and evaluation systems tailored to their unique characteristics. Only then can more students be encouraged to enter these fields, allowing scholars to devote themselves to the long-term work of preserving and expanding humanity’s understanding of China’s past.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from International Dunhuang Programme and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.title: China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.content:
China’s central Henan province issued a notice last week urging companies to ensure employees take their full paid annual leave and encouraging employer flexibility around workers leaving early on Fridays, domestic media reported Wednesday. The move was designed to encourage travel and spending on holidays and weekend getaways.

However, on Friday, local authorities said that the notice contained “inaccurate wording” and had “not undergone proper approval procedures,” and in response to public concerns, would be revised and reissued.

The original notice required employers to simplify leave approval procedures and called on company leaders to “lead by example” by taking time off themselves. It also clarified that all employees are entitled to the same paid annual leave regardless of whether they are permanent, temporary, dispatched, or contracted workers.

In addition, it encouraged employees to maximize their breaks by combining leave with weekends and public holidays, and said those with school-age children should receive priority when applying for leave during school breaks.

Henan is among several provincial-level regions that have introduced measures this year to better enforce paid annual leave, in line with China’s latest and first specific five-year plan on boosting consumption, approved by the State Council in July.

The Henan notice sparked heated discussion on social media, jumping to the trending topics list on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users voiced support and called for a nationwide rollout of the policy. Others took the opportunity to criticize a long-standing workplace culture in the country that promotes skipping leave to demonstrate dedication.

“I no longer have to lose pay to travel,” an employee who has worked at a state-owned enterprise in the Henan city of Luoyang for 10 years told Sixth Tone. “We were so excited when we saw the news that afternoon, and everyone cheered when our company issued (its own) notice the next day.”

She said taking time off previously meant losing a significant portion of her salary. “Now, (the notice) makes me feel more motivated to work,” she said. “People will complete their tasks more thoroughly before going on leave.” The employee added that she is already planning to combine her annual leave with the weeklong National Day holiday, at the beginning of October, for a longer break.

Two private-sector employees in Henan, however, told Sixth Tone that they had yet to receive any notice of a change in annual leave from their companies.

Similar notices have also been issued this year in the northern port city of Tianjin, the eastern provinces of Zhejiang and Anhui, the northwestern province of Shaanxi, and the southwestern province of Guizhou.

Many notices state they aim to change “unhealthy workplace norms,” while attempting to allay workers’ concerns that taking leave could affect their pay, performance evaluations, or chances for promotion.

In 2025, Lü Guoquan, a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and then an official with the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, said only around 57% of China’s workers entitled to paid annual leave actually take it.

Under national regulations implemented in 2008, employees with one to 10 years of cumulative work experience are entitled to five days of paid annual leave; those with 10 to 20 years receive 10 days; and those with more than 20 years receive 15 days.

“To fundamentally change the situation, China also needs routine labor inspections, accessible channels for workers to defend their rights, and better job rotation systems to reduce operational pressure on employers,” Song Xiangqing, vice president of the Commerce Economy Association of China, told domestic business outlet Caijing.

In January, China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security also announced that it would revise national regulations to promote better enforcement of the paid leave system.

“Paid leave is no longer simply about work-life balance or employee welfare,” state-run Guangming Daily wrote in a commentary published Thursday. “It has become part of the country’s strategy to boost consumption and expand domestic demand. Only with sufficient, uninterrupted, and predictable time off will people have both the time and willingness to spend.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Horstgerlach/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.title: Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.content:
China’s industry associations are revoking hundreds of honorary designations that have increasingly been used as marketing tools.

In late July, the China Cuisine Association announced that all previously awarded titles — including “Chinese Culinary Master” and “Chinese Catering Service Master” — along with related certificates and uniforms, were now invalid. The association also revoked all honorary designations awarded to cities — such as the “capital of” and “hometown of” certain dishes. Local governments are now officially barred from using them in any form of publicity.

The revocation of the titles triggered renewed interest among social media users. This week, they questioned the reliability of the “National Stir-Fried Meat King” title awarded to restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, after discovering it was conferred following an online public vote on photos and videos submitted by contestants.

The title has not yet been revoked, though, in response, the China Cuisine Association said they will “communicate after reviewing relevant materials,” domestic media reported.

Originally intended to recognize exceptional craftsmanship, “master” titles were once rare state honors. But in the early 2000s, industry associations across the tea, ceramics, and jewelry sectors, and many others, began creating their own titles, allowing businesses to charge a premium by creating the perception of higher-quality products and services. However, numerous shadowy practices also emerged around the honors, including honorary title certificates being openly sold on e-commerce platforms.

Since the beginning of this year, at least a dozen national and local industry associations covering sectors ranging from cosmetic surgery to jade carving and wedding services have revoked or abolished previously-conferred honorary titles containing words like “master.”

An increasing number of industry associations began nullifying their own honorary titles after the Social Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Civil Affairs jointly released new guidelines on governing social organizations’ awards and commendations in mid-July.

The guidelines, which took effect on Aug. 1, imposed stricter eligibility requirements on organizations seeking to present awards. It also prohibits organizations from charging fees for recognition programs or partnering with, or outsourcing such activities to, for-profit entities.

China has gradually tightened oversight of awards and commendations organized by social organizations over the past decade, with its first regulations governing the practice taking effect in 2012.

Restrictions were tightened further in 2018, when award programs using national designations such as “China,” “Chinese,” and “national” became subject to stricter controls. In 2022, authorities required organizations seeking to launch honorary recognition programs to hold at least a 4A rating, the second highest on the country’s social organization rating scale.

Lu Zhen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing-based Hylands Law Firm, told local media that rather than eliminating professional evaluations altogether, the regulations are intended to draw a clearer distinction between professional qualifications and commercialized honorary awards.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An  for restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, at a shopping mall in Beijing, May 23, 2024. VCG)

World.title: ‘Laid-off’ workers turn to side jobs to survive
World.content:
Workers say they were dismissed by SMILSI after they were barred from reporting for work. Now, some struggle to make ends meet as they turn to side jobs while fighting for reinstatement.

LAGUNA, Philippines – From 6 am to 6 pm, six days a week, Dante Cantos, 55, has worked at San Miguel Integrated Logistics Services Inc. (SMILSI) as a forklift operator for about a year and a half. Before working at SMILSI, he worked for another company that closed down.

He was among the hundreds of workers who were recently put on “floating status” by SMILSI.

DANTE CANTOS. His job as a forklift operator at SMILSI involved physically demanding tasks of loading and unloading products from large trucks. Photo by Lance Ariel Bustos/Rappler

Julius Sarsuela, 39, had also been with the company for nearly three years as a reach truck operator, often working the same hours and days as Cantos. He was required to work off-shifts, particularly during inventory periods when operators like him were needed.

Like Cantos, Sarsuela was among the workers affected by the move.

Both of them are among the SMILSI workers who have joined the picket line in front of San Miguel Corporation’s (SMC) Sta. Rosa Industrial Complex in Santa Rosa, Laguna after some workers said they were dismissed, or “tinanggal,” without prior notice.

The dispute came just a few months after workers under the Unyon ng mga Manggagawa sa San Miguel Logistics-Independent (USMILSI-IND) earned collective bargaining rights.

About 800 SMILSI workers were prevented from reporting to their posts starting July 6, after the company placed them under floating status without certainty over their wages, benefits, or arrangements for returning to work. The company defended the move, after it lost a bidding process for its warehouse, transport, and bundling operations, as previously reported by Bulatlat.

SMILSI is a subsidiary of San Miguel Corporation, created to “provide effective and efficient logistics and warehousing solutions to the San Miguel group of companies.”

We reached out to SMC’s Media Affairs and Communications teams via text and through multiple email channels, including its legal, customer care, shareholder services and assistance, and whistleblower offices, on August 5, 10, and 12. We have not received any official statement as of writing. We will update this story once the company responds.

Workers set up a temporary shelter in front of the industrial complex, where multiple organizations and individuals have shown their support in person for the affected laborers. While further discussions between strike leaders and company management are being awaited, some workers are trying to find ways to earn a living.

Support

To survive during the strike, Cantos helps his wife with her small business selling personal collection items, such as soaps and bathroom supplies.

Sarsuela, a father of three with one child in high school and two in elementary school, rents a tricycle for P200 a day and works as a tricycle driver. He said he takes home about P300 to P400 a day after paying the daily rental fee.

JULIUS SARSUELA. His role as a reach truck operator involved lowering items from high racks for pickers to collect. Photo by Lance Ariel Bustos/Rappler



Their earnings, however, fall short of covering water, electricity, and internet expenses. “We only earn a few pesos at a time, just enough to get by — and honestly, even that isn’t enough,” Cantos said in Filipino.

He continued, “It’s not just food that you have to think about every day…You also have to think about paying for electricity, water, and internet.”

Cantos has one child who recently graduated from college and is preparing for the board exams. With no income, Cantos now struggles to cover the expenses associated with his child’s preparation for the board exams.

“We all know how expensive the board exams are, that’s a major expense. The problem will be covering day-to-day expenses,” Cantos said in Filipino. He continued, “Since I don’t have a job, the problem is, where are we going to get the money now?”

Cantos admitted to feeling stressed and pained as well by the lack of work. “Sometimes when you don’t have work, you get stressed thinking…Your head hurts.” He added, “My wife even told me, ‘Find any kind of work so you won’t get stressed.’”

For his part, Sarsuela said his wife recently applied for a job at another company as they anticipated the job loss. But her salary alone is insufficient to sustain a family of five — from food to rent.

“She had just started working too when we were laid off…because she knew I would lose my job,” he said in Filipino. He continued, “What my wife earns isn’t really enough. Just for my three children alone, we already spend so much, and then there’s food and the house.”

He maintains his support for the strike by visiting the temporary shelter, as he also hopes to return to his job at SMILSI. “I go [to the shelter] just to support what we are fighting for, for us to return to our jobs — so that I can support my family’s needs,” Sarsuela said in Filipino.

Latest developments

Strike leaders and SMILSI management are scheduled to meet again on Friday, August 14. Some workers are hoping the discussions will lead to a resolution. They will remain in place until at least August 15, as they await the outcome of the talks.

Legislators from the Makabayan bloc, meanwhile, filed a resolution on July 28 to direct the House’s committee on labor and employment to conduct an investigation into the “dismissal of SMILSI workers,” citing “alleged unfair labor practice, union busting, violation of workers’ right to security of tenure, and the impending mass layoff of 800 regular workers” at SMILSI. – Rappler.com

Lance Ariel Bustos is a campus journalist from Santa Rosa City, Laguna, studying Political Science and Philippine Media Studies at De La Salle University Manila. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is also the intermedia editor of The LaSallian.

World.title: Manila confirms arrest of over 100 Filipinos in China
World.content:
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier said over 100 Filipino nationals were 'taken in accordance with the law' over alleged migration law violations

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines on Thursday, August 13, reminded China of a 2013 agreement to notify consular posts within days of the arrest of its nationals as it “noted” the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA)’s statement on the arrest of over 100 Filipino nationals.

“The Department is in close coordination with our Embassy in Beijing and our Consulates-General to verify the circumstances of the arrests, ascertain the exact number and status of those apprehended, ensure that due process is observed, and extend consular assistance as needed,” said the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) in a late Thursday statement.

No other details about the arrests were made available as of Thursday evening.

On August 10, responding to a question from state-run Global Times, MFA spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that “actions have been taken in accordance with the law against over 100 Philippine nationals for illegally working or living in China.”

“We call on Chinese authorities to safeguard the welfare of the arrested Filipinos and to promptly notify our Foreign Service Posts of their arrest and detention, consistent with the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations and the 2013 Philippines-China Consular Agreement,” added the DFA.

The 2013 agreement states that the host country must notify the other country’s consulate post within four days “of the fact and reasons for which the national has been detained, arrested, or deprived of freedom by any means,” whether or not the arrested person makes that request.

That means that if a Filipino national is arrested or detained in China, Chinese authorities ought to inform either the Philippine embassy in Beijing or any of its various consulates of the nature of that arrest or detention. Filipino authorities are expected to do the same if a Chinese national is arrested in the Philippines.

“The Philippines respects China’s sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws, as it does the right of every state to enforce its own laws on foreign nationals within its jurisdiction, in accordance with due process and established legal procedure,” added the DFA.

Ties between the two Asian countries have been generally tense in the last three years under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., especially over clashes and disagreements in the West Philippine Sea, a part of the South China Sea that includes the Philippine exclusive economic zone.

Those tensions have only grown in recent months following the arrest of Chinese nationals suspected to be spying in the Philippines, Beijing’s decision to sanction Marcos’ defense chief Gilberto Teodoro Jr., a racist video on Filipinos released by a state-run publication, and strong rhetoric from China’s embassy in the Philippines, to name a few. Those are on top of clashes and confrontations in the South China Sea.

The Global Times, in asking Guo for confirmation of the arrests, framed their question by asking if it was “China’s response to the Philippines’ frequent detention of Chinese nationals.”

Guo did not answer the latter part of the Global Times‘ question, but said, “immigration staff acted in a standard and civil manner and ensured the protection of the rights and interests of the foreign nationals concerned.”

In a separate statement, Teodoro condemned the arrest of the Filipinos, labeling it as “plain and simple extortion and blackmail.” He also defended an earlier Philippine operation that resulted in the arrest of Chinese nationals.

“The law enforcement efforts against the Chinese nationals that are referred to in a recent report were done on the basis of search warrants issued by the proper courts. The individuals arrested by the authorities were the principals of these illegal enterprises. Chinese authorities stress the issue of the work visas and passports of these individuals while refusing to address the illegal activities that they perpetuated. This is an admission by them that indeed the acts of these individuals were illegal under Philippine law,” he said.

The Filipino defense chief, who is barred from entering China, Hong Kong, and Macau, rejected the idea that Chinese nationals were targeted based merely on their citizenship.

“Filipinos in China have neither the intent nor the capacity to commit violations of Chinese law, much less [on] the scale perpetuated by Chinese nationals here. The fact that the Chinese government is actively covering up for these individuals is the best evidence of their complicity in the nefarious acts of these people,” added Teodoro. – Rappler.com

World.title: Credible missile threat led to secret aircraft switch for Trump, source says
World.content:
AIR FORCE ONE. A catering truck is parked next to Air Force One, before US President Donald Trump's departure from Ankara en route to Washington after his participation in the NATO leaders' summit, at Ankara Esenboga Airport in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video.

The source declines to say where the intelligence came from but says officials had little time to prepare and had to devise the plans at the last minute

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – A threat that Air Force One could be targeted by a shoulder-fired missile prompted the Secret Service to secretly move President Donald Trump onto a smaller government jet during a trip to Turkey last month, a person briefed on the matter said on Wednesday, August 12.

The threat emerged on the final day of Trump’s visit to Ankara for the NATO summit amid heightened tensions with Iran, the source said. The Secret Service deemed the threat to be credible and imminent, prompting an extraordinary operation to conceal the US President’s movements.

The source declined to say where the intelligence came from but said officials had little time to prepare and had to devise the plans at the last minute.

A second source briefed on the matter said there was not a clear plan by those hostile to Trump for executing the threat, but only an intent, which is why the planes were allowed to fly.

Trump and a small group of aides used a catering truck to surreptitiously switch from the big blue-and-white presidential aircraft to a smaller, nondescript C-32A jet for the flight out of Turkey on July 8, while Air Force One departed separately carrying senior administration officials, White House staff and the traveling press corps, according to the first source.

Trump told reporters on Tuesday, August 11, that he made the switch at the direction of the Secret Service, which is charged with presidential security. He flew from Ankara to a refueling stop in Britain without incident.

“I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump told reporters, without providing evidence. “I think it was at ​greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for.”

The threat may have been a new type of heat-seeking missile that homes in on hot aircraft engines and has become an increasing concern for military planners, said Douglas Birkey, executive director of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. They are harder to detect than traditional radar-guided threats and “can kind of come out of nowhere” because they don’t send out detectable radio waves.

One version, the Iranian SA-67, has a simple rail launcher and is believed to use heat-seeking as well as laser guidance systems, Birkey said. A shoulder-mounted heat-seeking weapon, the 9K333 Verba, is made in Russia, he said.

Secret travel

US presidents, including Trump, have occasionally traveled under secrecy when visiting war zones or high-risk regions in order to maintain security. But those trips typically involved advance notice for journalists traveling with the president.

Some members of the press got a heads-up ahead of a Thanksgiving 2003 trip by President George W. Bush to Baghdad. Other members of the press corps covering Bush’s Thanksgiving holiday in Crawford, Texas, were misled, however. Told that Bush was spending the feast day with family, they were shocked when the president abruptly surfaced in Iraq.

The first source on Wednesday said the Secret Service did not have the luxury of time in Turkey.

“They were scrambling to head off what they thought was a credible, imminent threat,” the source said.

The Washington Post first reported details of the operation this week, more than a month after it was carried out.

The New York Times reported that US officials were alarmed to discover that Iranians knew where Trump was staying in Ankara, including the exact floor of his hotel.

On board the Air Force One jet now seen as a decoy were US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who the first source said was briefed on the maneuver; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; White House communications director Steven Cheung; and a number of other aides plus the typical 13-person press pool that included a Reuters correspondent and photographer.

White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, executive assistant Natalie Harp and director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta made the move in the catering truck with Trump, the source said.

Some media commentators ⁠and lawmakers have questioned whether the operation left Trump’s aides and journalists traveling with him at risk aboard the plane presumed to be carrying the ​President.

The first source said it was determined that it was in Trump’s best interests to keep the ruse secret as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Turkey.

Turkish officials did not immediately comment on the threat. – Rappler.com

World.title: UAE Coal Deal Highlights Why Foreign Investors Are Betting on Kazakh Coal Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – A United Arab Emirates company has secured a 25-year license to develop the Kenderlyk coal deposit in eastern Kazakhstan, expanding foreign investment in the country’s mining sector.

According to documents released ahead of public hearings in early August, MQ Emirates Group Ltd will develop Coal-Shale Field No. 1 of the Kenderlyk deposit using open-pit mining methods.

Coal production is scheduled to begin in 2028, following geological exploration and preparatory work planned for 2026 and 2027. Initial output is projected at 10,000 metric tons, increasing to the mine’s planned annual capacity of 50,000 metric tons by 2034. Recoverable reserves are estimated at 940,000 metric tons.

The Kenderlyk deposit is located around 70 kilometers from the town of Zaisan in the East Kazakhstan Region. It has been known since the late 19th century, when coal and oil shale were extracted through small surface mines. During the Soviet era, the area underwent extensive geological exploration for coal, shale, and hydrocarbons.

Several years ago, the Kazakh Industry Ministry offered parts of the Kenderlyk deposit for auction. According to the National Geological Service, the broader deposit contains 11.3 million metric tons of coal reserves across three coal-bearing formations. Coal at Field No. 1 has a relatively high ash content of 35% to 40%.

Coal remains key to energy security

Although many countries are accelerating the shift toward renewable energy, coal remains one of the world’s primary sources of electricity. It generates roughly one-third of global power. Demand continues to be driven largely by China and India. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan ranks 10th globally in proven coal reserves, with an estimated 33.6 billion metric tons, enough to sustain current production levels for more than three centuries.

The country’s largest coal-producing regions include the Karagandy and Turgai coal basins in central Kazakhstan and the Ekibastuz, Maikuben and Karazhyra deposits in the northeast. Kazakhstan exports coal primarily to Russia, Poland, Uzbekistan, Türkiye, India and Malaysia.

To support future growth, the Energy Ministry plans to auction 10 additional coal exploration blocks by the end of the year. The government has also approved the Coal Power Development national project, which includes investment projects with a combined installed capacity of around 7.8 gigawatts.

Investment in the sector continues to rise. Mining companies invested 305 billion tenge (US$654 million) in 2025, while investment is projected to increase to 553 billion tenge (US$1.2 billion) this year.

Kazakhstan is also expanding investment in its broader mining sector. The government plans to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits, among the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten reserves, into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation.

Highly concentrated market

While Kazakhstan is expanding coal production, a new report from the Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition (APDC) found that the country’s primary wholesale coal market remains highly concentrated.

The agency’s review of the 2024-25 market concluded that the sector continues to be dominated by a small number of producers operating in an essentially unchanged oligopolistic market. For coal supplied to households and municipal utilities, the ERG Group and Karazhyra company controlled a combined market share of 74.8% in 2024 and 67.9% in 2025.

In the power generation segment, Bogatyr Komir and Kazakhmys Coal accounted for 84.1% of the market in 2024 and 81.6% in 2025. For industrial coal, the ERG Group held a market share of 62.3% in 2024, increasing to 69.1% in 2025. The agency said Kazakhstan’s oligopolistic market structure has contributed to sustained price increases.

According to APDC, wholesale prices for coal supplied to households increased 30% to 35% between 2022 and 2025, while thermal coal prices rose approximately 45% over the same period.

To improve competition, the agency proposed introducing price regulation for household and thermal coal, increasing the share of coal sold through commodity exchanges to 52%, and moving off-exchange transactions to digital trading platforms.

The report also identified several structural barriers to competition, including differences in mining contract terms and limited transparency in granting exclusive coal export rights. It further highlighted concerns over the allocation of rail capacity by the national railway operator, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy.

APDC recommended establishing transparent criteria for coal export permits, ensuring equal treatment for producers and improving disclosure of available railway capacity.

The agency also identified companies that qualify as holders of key capacity in the coal market, including Shubarkol Komir, Karazhyra, Bogatyr Komir, Kazakhmys Coal and the Eurasian Energy Corporation. Once these companies are formally recognized as holders of key capacity, they will be required to sell coal under Kazakhstan’s Rules on Equal Access to Key Capacity, which are intended to promote fair competition and equal market access.

World.title: Tokayev’s G20 Invitation Reflects Broader U.S.-Kazakhstan Strategic Momentum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan confirmed that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit in the United States (US) in December, following a meeting on Aug. 12 between Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur to discuss expanding bilateral cooperation.

Although Kazakhstan is not a member of the G20, it is among the countries invited by the US to participate in this year’s summit.

The two officials discussed preparations for the summit. They expressed readiness to coordinate on its agenda, while reviewing broader prospects for strengthening the expanded strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and the US.

Kosherbayev briefed Kapur on Kazakhstan’s ongoing political and socioeconomic reforms, describing the country as entering a new stage of development. He said the Aug. 23 Kurultai elections will represent an important milestone in implementing the country’s new constitutional model.

Kapur reaffirmed its interest in expanding practical cooperation in energy, critical minerals, advanced technologies, digitalization, transportation and investment.

Growing strategic importance

According to Assylan Smagulov, Master of Political Science and director of the Voice of Youth Public Foundation, the timing of the meeting reflects Washington’s continued strategic interest in Central Asia.

“August is traditionally a period of diplomatic coordination before a busy fall schedule of international summits. When the US holds high-level meetings with the Central Asian countries during this period, it signals that the region remains an important strategic partner. That creates additional opportunities for attracting investment and advancing national interests,” Smagulov told The Astana Times.

Smagulov noted that Kapur’s participation was particularly significant because of his expertise on South and Central Asia.

“The US sent a senior official who specializes in this region and understands both its challenges and opportunities. That demonstrates Washington views Kazakhstan as an important partner,” he said.

He added that the country’s growing geopolitical importance stems from its strategic location, transportation links and abundant natural resources, including critical minerals. These factors have become increasingly important as prolonged geopolitical tensions reshape global supply chains.

“Participation in international platforms such as the G20 creates a window of opportunities for Kazakhstan to strengthen dialogue not only with the US but also with other major powers. The broader Kazakhstan’s international engagement becomes, the greater its diplomatic flexibility and its opportunities to expand economic cooperation,” Smagulov said.

Water cooperation moves from policy to practice

Water security has also become a growing pillar of U.S.-Kazakhstan cooperation. The officials reviewed Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization as a specialized United Nations agency. The initiative aims to create a platform for coordinating international efforts on water governance, facilitating data and technology exchange and developing joint solutions to global water challenges.

The proposal entered formal international consultations during the Regional Ecological Summit held in Astana in April. A summary report from those consultations is expected to guide further negotiations among UN member states ahead of the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi later this year.

On Aug. 10, representatives of Kazakhstan’s National Hydrogeological Service (Kazgidrogeology), U.S.-based IBL Elements, and Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector met in Astana to discuss technologies for treating and reusing industrial and produced water generated during oil and gas production.

The talks focused on wastewater treatment, water reuse and the recovery of valuable and critical minerals contained in produced water. Following the meeting, Kazgidrogeology, IBL Elements and Kazakhoil Aktobe signed a trilateral memorandum of cooperation establishing a framework for pilot projects in the country’s oil and gas industry.

Rather than viewing produced water solely as industrial waste, the initiative aims to assess its potential as both a water resource and a source of strategically important minerals.

“This meeting marks an important practical step in developing cooperation between the Kazakh and American sides. The signed memorandum creates the foundation for implementing a joint pilot project and scaling successful technologies to other oil and gas facilities across Kazakhstan,” said Bolat Bekniyaz, chairman of the board of Kazgidrogeology.

Expanding economic and technology partnership

Economic ties between the two countries continue to grow. Bilateral trade exceeded $1 billion during the first half of the year, an increase of about 10% compared with the same period last year. Cumulative U.S. investment in Kazakhstan has surpassed $60 billion.

Several high-level engagements this summer underscored the growing partnership.

In June, Astana hosted the C5+1 Critical Minerals Dialogue, where senior officials from the five Central Asian countries and the United States discussed cooperation on critical mineral supply chains, investment and technology. At the event, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor described Central Asia as an increasingly important component of U.S. foreign and economic policy.

Later that month, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative and the AI Opportunity Partnership, expanding cooperation in AI, advanced technologies and high-tech manufacturing. During the Pax Silica Summit, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev signed the declaration on Kazakhstan’s accession to the initiative.

On June 30, government officials and business leaders from both countries also reaffirmed their commitment to expanding trade, investment and technological cooperation during the Kazakhstan-U.S. Business Roundtable. During the event, the two countries’ business associations signed a memorandum aimed at strengthening long-term institutional cooperation.

World.title: Two Giant Tungsten Deposits Could Test Kazakhstan’s Push Beyond Raw-Material Exports
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to turn two of the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten deposits into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation, requiring ore to be processed domestically rather than exported as raw material as Astana seeks to capture more value from its critical mineral reserves.

The Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits are being developed by a venture between U.S.-based Cove Capital, which holds a 70% stake, and Kazakhstan’s state mining company Tau-Ken Samruk, with 30%. Cove Capital is expected to provide at least $1.1 billion in financing as well as processing technology and access to international markets.

The agreement was signed in November 2025 during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Washington D.C. The partners formalized the investment in February, signing a package of transaction documents, including a sale and purchase agreement and a shareholders’ agreement, for the critical minerals project.

The mines are located in the Shet district of the Karagandy Region, close to transport and transport and energy communications. Karagandy, the region’s administrative center, is around 130 kilometers from the deposits.

“The Northern Katpar project involves establishing a full production cycle in Kazakhstan, from ore mining and beneficiation to metallurgical processing, based on the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits. This is the first project of its kind to be implemented in Kazakhstan,” Tau-Ken Samruk told The Astana Times.

Its planned output includes ammonium paratungstate, or APT, a key processed product in the tungsten supply chain. The agreement envisages processing all extracted ore domestically and producing higher-value tungsten products in Kazakhstan.

The timeline

The project is currently in the Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) phase, meaning its final production capacity, economics and launch date have yet to be determined.

“This work will confirm and optimize the existing feasibility studies, and refine the project’s economic and technical indicators, as well as its mineral resources and reserves. As part of the project’s implementation, preparatory and technical work is scheduled to begin on-site, including topographic surveying, the construction of temporary access roads and fencing, the preparation of drilling sites, the opening of a field office, and other related activities,” said Tau-Ken.

The definitive feasibility study, which began in July, is expected to be completed before the end of 2027, Cove Kaz Capital told The Astana Times.

“The principal objective of this stage is to finalize the overall mine plan, define the parameters of the processing facilities and prepare the project for a Final Investment Decision, as well as for detailed due diligence by prospective financing partners,” the company’s CEO Dominic Heaton told The Astana Times.

The company said physical activity has commenced at the site in July, including surveying, access road and drill pad preparation, and establishment of field facilities.

Untapped potential

The two deposits are considered among the world’s biggest undeveloped tungsten deposits. Together, the deposits contain an estimated 410,000 metric tons of tungsten trioxide reserves under JORC standards, while total resources are estimated at 1.4 million tons, according to previous studies cited by Tau-Ken.

Cove Capital said a key distinction is between mineral resources and mineral reserves.

“The current figure represents JORC-compliant [JORC refers to an internationally recognized reporting standard used to classify and publicly report mineral exploration results, mineral resources and ore reserves] mineral resources, while the ongoing DFS [Definitive Feasibility Study] will further update the geological and technical data and optimize the development plan for the deposits,” said Heaton.

“Based on existing studies, Northern Katpar has the potential to support production of approximately 5,000 metric tons per annum, while Upper Kairakty has the potential to contribute approximately 7,000 metric tons per annum. Combined production of approximately 12,000 tons per year would be equivalent to roughly 15% of current global tungsten mine production,” Heaton explained. The company is also developing the Akbulak rare earth project in the Kostanai Region with Qazgeology national geological exploration company.

The financing

Under the agreement, the U.S. partner is expected to provide at least $1.1 billion in financing, introduce modern processing and beneficiation technologies, build a complex of production facilities and develop international sales channels for the output.

“The approximately $1.1 billion figure represents the current estimate of the total investment required to develop Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty, including the associated mining and processing infrastructure. It does not mean that the full amount has already been financed, committed or deployed,” said Heaton.

At this stage, Cove Kaz Capital Group has financed the acquisition of its 70% controlling stake in Northern Katpar, along with site preparation, drilling and work related to the definitive feasibility study.

“An important component of the prospective financing structure is the interest expressed by U.S. government-backed financial institutions. The Export-Import Bank of the United States has issued a Letter of Interest for financing of up to $900 million, while the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation has issued a Letter of Interest for up to $700 million, including project financing and development support,” Heaton explained.

Potential financing could reach $1.6 billion, but the figure remains indicative rather than committed, Heaton added. The amounts represent expressions of interest from prospective lenders, with the final financing package still contingent on completion of the definitive feasibility study, lender due diligence and a final investment decision.

Why it matters

What this project illustrates is that Kazakhstan is betting on higher-value domestic processing rather than remaining primarily a supplier of raw tungsten ore or concentrate. Cove Capital said it seeks to create an integrated domestic value chain in Kazakhstan, spanning mining, beneficiation and downstream chemical processing.

“The principal benchmark product currently planned for the Kazakhstan refinery is ammonium paratungstate, or APT, a high-purity intermediate product that is the internationally recognized benchmark product of the tungsten industry. The project may also have the potential to produce other tungsten compounds depending on the final technical configuration,” Heaton explained.

Deeper processing would allow Kazakhstan to retain more of the value generated from its tungsten resources rather than exporting mainly ore or concentrate.

“APT is subsequently used to produce tungsten oxides and powders, tungsten carbide, hard metals and other specialized materials used across advanced manufacturing, high-technology and defense-related industries,” said Heaton.

Global tungsten dynamics

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, tungsten is a strategically important metal used primarily in tungsten carbide for mining, construction and metalworking, as well as in electronics, aerospace, high-performance alloys and defense applications. Its combination of hardness, heat resistance and high density makes it difficult to substitute in many industrial uses.

Tungsten is relatively scarce in the Earth’s crust, ranking 57th among chemical elements by abundance. Its wide industrial use stems from a combination of distinctive properties. No other known metal matches tungsten in heat resistance, and its boiling point is close to the temperature at the Sun’s surface.

China has remained the world’s leading producer, importer and consumer of tungsten concentrates.

The project is advancing at a time when tungsten is taking an increasingly greater geopolitical importance as the U.S. and other economies seek to diversify critical mineral supply chains away from China. Beijing tightened controls on exports of selected tungsten products and related technologies in February 2025, adding pressure to already concentrated global supply chains.

The restrictions, alongside growing demand and trade tensions, helped push tungsten prices sharply higher in 2025. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, throughout 2025, prices went up from $266 to $551 per metric ton unit for 65% concentrate and from $331 to $675 per metric ton unit for APT.

“At the same time, the strategic importance of secure and diversified critical mineral supply chains is growing rapidly. The United States, the G7 and other advanced economies are actively seeking to reduce reliance on highly concentrated sources of supply and support the development of alternative supply chains. Tungsten is one of the critical minerals receiving particular attention in this context,” said Heaton.

Kazakhstan is emerging as a potential alternative supplier. Production began at the Boguty tungsten deposit in the Almaty Region in 2024, operated by Aral Kegen, a subsidiary of China’s Jiaxin International Resources Investment.

The project with Cove Capital is also emerging as part of a broader build-out of Kazakhstan’s tungsten industry, with additional deposits moving toward development. The country’s total tungsten trioxide reserves are estimated at more than two million metric tons. Esil-Mining, owned by Britain’s Resources Enterprise Limited, plans to begin developing the Aksoran deposit in northern Kazakhstan in 2027, with production targeted for 2028.

The planned development of Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty would take the country further downstream by combining extraction with domestic processing rather than exporting raw material.

“More broadly, our strategy is to build a portfolio of critical mineral assets in Kazakhstan and Central Asia supported by domestic processing and refining capacity,” said Heaton.

He emphasized this ambition is supported by the country’s substantial mineral resource base, a mature mining sector, extensive geological data and established industrial infrastructure.

“Just as importantly, Kazakhstan is increasingly focused on moving beyond the extraction and export of raw materials toward higher-value processing and manufacturing,” he added.

The project illustrates Kazakhstan’s broader effort to extract more economic value from its mineral wealth by pairing foreign capital with domestic processing. But major questions, including production capacity, final economics and the start of commercial output, remain unresolved while the venture completes its definitive feasibility study.

World.title: Investment Outlook for Kazakhstan Equities: Strategic Allocation to Eurasia’s Hidden Blue-Chip Market
World.content:
In life and on the investment journey, it is often said that it is the journey that counts, or it is the “journey” that is the reward.

Kazakhstan became the first country of the former Soviet Union to receive an international investment credit rating in September 2002.

According to Bloomberg data, tenge is the sixth best performing currency in the world so far this year, and the Kazakhstan equity market has outperformed global equities.

Next year, the IMF expects Kazakhstan’s economy to expand by 4.4% in 2027, while forecasting global GDP growth of 3.4%. This implies the nation would grow approximately 1.0 percentage point faster than the world economy, continuing to outperform the global average. Global investors should take notice.

Yet Kazakhstan remains one of the most attractive yet under-owned equity markets in the emerging and frontier investment universe. Despite its abundant natural resources, improving corporate governance and strategic location between Europe and China, it continues to receive only a modest allocation in most global strategic asset allocation portfolios. For long-term private clients and family offices willing to diversify beyond traditional developed and emerging markets, Kazakhstan deserves serious consideration.

While oil made Kazakhstan rich, today’s investment story extends well beyond oil. Kazakhstan is the global leader in uranium production, a significant producer of copper, zinc and ferroalloys, and is investing heavily in logistics, manufacturing and financial services. Government reforms are aimed at diversifying the economy, encouraging foreign investment and strengthening domestic capital markets.

Valuation remains one of the market’s greatest attractions. Leading local companies have often traded at attractive earnings multiples while generating robust cash flows and paying generous dividends. For value-oriented investors, this combination of reasonable valuations and strong profitability provides an attractive long-term entry point.

The financial sector is one of the strongest investment opportunities. Halyk Bank, Kaspi.kz and Bank CenterCredit have demonstrated strong profitability, healthy capital ratios and growing digital capabilities. Kaspi.kz has built one of the world’s most successful digital financial ecosystems, while Halyk Bank continues to combine market leadership with attractive shareholder returns.

The nation also occupies a unique position in the global energy transition. As the world’s largest uranium producer, the country is strategically positioned to benefit from growing investment in nuclear energy driven by electrification, artificial intelligence and expanding data-centre demand. At the same time, the Middle Corridor linking China and Europe continues to enhance the country’s role as a logistics and transport hub.

For international investors, tenge remains influenced by commodity prices, particularly oil, together with global risk sentiment and developments in neighbouring Russia. However, substantial foreign-exchange reserves and the National Fund of Kazakhstan provide an important cushion against external shocks.

Risks include commodity-price volatility, geopolitical uncertainty, lower market liquidity and evolving governance standards. Nevertheless, these risks are balanced by attractive long-term growth prospects and improving institutional quality.

For global investors and family offices, Kazakhstan remains one of the faster-growing upper-middle-income emerging markets. However, GDP growth alone is not sufficient for investment success. Investors should also assess:

Corporate earnings growth. Valuation of listed companies, Dividend yields, Corporate governance standards, Currency outlook for tenge (KZT), Liquidity on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange.

Given expected GDP growth of around 4–4.5%, Kazakhstan should continue to grow faster than the global economy, supporting a constructive long-term investment case—particularly in banking, energy, uranium, infrastructure, and selected consumer sectors.

Kazakhstan should not be viewed as a replacement for developed-market equities or large emerging markets. Instead, it can serve as a strategic satellite allocation providing exposure to return drivers that are often poorly represented in conventional global benchmarks.

For patient investors, this is precisely where the opportunity may lie. Markets that are under-researched, under-owned and occasionally misunderstood can offer attractive long-term opportunities when economic fundamentals and corporate performance continue to improve.

We therefore maintain a BUY recommendation on Kazakhstan equities as a strategic long-term allocation for globally diversified investment portfolios. Attractive valuations, world-class resource companies, strong financial institutions and ongoing economic reforms provide a compelling investment case for patient money and smart money investors and private clients alike.

The author is Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner & Portfolio Strategist at Das Family Office in Singapore.
