Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: 'I'll remember the people': Sidebottom among retiring AFL premiership duo
World.content:
Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has officially told Magpies teammates he will be retiring at season's end.

The dual Magpies premiership hero's announcement on Thursday comes just hours after Richmond midfielder Dion Prestia also called it quits.

Debuting in 2009, Sidebottom has played 373 AFL games — the second most in Collingwood's storied history, only behind Scott Pendlebury.

A member of the Magpies' 2010 premiership side as a 19-year-old, Sidebottom then kicked a famous goal late in the 2023 grand final to help seal the club's next flag 13 years later.

Sidebottom (left) and Scott Pendlebury (right) have played the most matches together as teammates in VFL/AFL history. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

With Collingwood guaranteed to be in the wildcard round of the finals, at least, Sidebottom will be hoping for a fairytale farewell.

The versatile midfielder won Collingwood's Copeland Trophy in 2017 and 2018, also earning All-Australian honours once.

"As a young kid from 'Tally' [Tallygaroopna], I could never imagine I'd finish my AFL career with over 370 games, two premierships and 18 years of memories," Sidebottom said.

"When I look back on my time at Collingwood, I'll remember the people.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"So many teammates, coaches, staff and volunteers have invested their time and energy into helping me along the way."

Sidebottom might not be the only senior Collingwood player to retire this year, with Pendlebury also weighing up his future after breaking the VFL/AFL games record in May.

The Magpies have the oldest list in the AFL and are attempting to stay in premiership contention with a group in transition.

At Richmond, Prestia has joined premiership teammate Nathan Broad in ending his career.

After starting his career with Gold Coast, Prestia enjoyed instant success after making the switch to the Tigers in 2017.

Prestia won three premierships in his first four seasons with Richmond after joining at the end of 2016. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

The midfielder played in three premierships (2017, 2019, 2020) in his first four seasons at Richmond.

Despite being riddled by injury in 2020 and restricted to just five games during the pandemic season, Prestia returned to play an important role in all four of the Tigers' finals.

"I felt like a Richmond man from the very beginning," Prestia said.

"My decision to come to Richmond was not to prove what I could do, but to be a part of a club that I saw potential for greatness, and didn't we prove that right?"

Prestia and Broad will be given a farewell in front of the Richmond army this Saturday when the Tigers host St Kilda at the MCG.

AAP

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

WALLABIES (1-15): Angus Bell, Josh Nasser, Taniela Tupou, Lachlan Shaw, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Carlo Tizzano, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Carter Gordon, Harry Potter, Hunter Paisami, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright.

BENCH (16-23): Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Jeremy Williams, Fraser McReight, Tate McDermott, Ben Donaldson, Filipo Daugunu

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm (AEST).

AAP

World.title: Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt
World.content:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

Tech.title: 2K launches new studio to build its ‘next blockbuster sports franchise’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

2K is launching a new AAA game development studio, Small Axe Studios, with an ambitious goal: to build the company’s “next blockbuster sports franchise,” according to a LinkedIn post.

The post doesn’t explicitly say what sport this new game will focus on. But an image included in the post features what appears to be a mockup soccer badge, indicating that Small Axe might be making a soccer game that goes head-to-head with EA Sports FC. The Small Axe website also lists senior staffers with experience working on EA’s FIFA series (the former name of EA Sports FC), including studio head Aaron McHardy, who once led that franchise.

Small Axe was born from 2K Sports Lab, a project 2K announced in 2023. Whatever this new game is, it will add to 2K’s existing roster of games covering sports such as basketball (NBA 2K), wrestling (WWE 2K), and golf (PGA Tour 2K).

Tech.title: Ford’s $28,000 Fathom EV nears production after $2 billion factory overhaul
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ford said today that its next-generation electric vehicle — recently dubbed Fathom — will go into production at the automaker’s recently overhauled Louisville Assembly Plant in the first quarter of 2027.

The first Fathoms will be prototypes, with Ford’s team in Louisville already in the production-level pre-tooling phase at the recently converted facility. Factory workers are working alongside team’s at Ford’s New Model Product Development Center in Dearborn, Michigan, hand-building the Fathom prototypes — and the same operators who helped design the high-stakes EV will also be involved in its production.

The factory is over 70 years old, so Ford had a lot of equipment to get rid of before it could begin the process of converting into an EV plant. Over several weeks, crews physically unbolted and hauled out heavy machinery, dragging thousands of tons of steel out the door. By February, only an empty shell remained.

The Fathom, a $28,000 electric pickup truck, will be the first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, an innovative new system designed to maximize aerodynamic range while also reducing production costs so Ford can make a profitable vehicle. For over a year, the company has been hyping it as its “Model T moment” that will revolutionize nearly everything at the 123-year-old company.

Previous Next















1 / 9

Ford said it converted the plant from one that makes gas cars, like the Escape and the Lincoln Corsair, to an EV only plant in just under a year. In total, Ford is spending $5 billion to create 4,000 new jobs at both the Louisville factory and its BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan.

Even the production process will be totally different. Rather than one long conveyor, Ford is using a new assembly tree process that splits the vehicle into three sections — front clip, rear clip, and battery deck — which enables better access so more operators can work on the vehicle at the same time. Ford will use large unicasting to create the front and rear sections, replacing dozens of stamped and welded parts as it currently uses. Ford says it can speed up the production process by up to 15 percent by using the assembly tree.

To illustrate how much more efficient this new process will be, Ford cites this example:

One example of that efficiency in action is the software module flash station, a first for a Ford assembly plant, which ensures vehicles have the latest software prior to module installation. Previously, this software flash happened after the vehicle was built, and if issues were detected, updates took 10 minutes per vehicle. With private 5G in the plant, operators can perform quality tests like these as a vehicle rolls down the assembly tree

Ford is banking on this new streamlined process, as well as its core competency of building a high-volume of vehicles, will make the Fathom’s retail price a reality. To be sure, Ford hasn’t had the best of luck when it comes to EVs. The company lost over $5 billion on EVs and software in 2024, and another $4.8 billion in 2025. The company was forced to cancel the F-150 Lightning, a truck once heralded as the most important EV ever made.

Photography by Ford

Tech.title: Meta adds AI screening to detect WhatsApp scams
Tech.content: If the model identifies a message as a likely scam attempt, the user sees a warning in the chat, which is not visible to the other person. From there, the user can decide what to do: block, report, or continue the conversation. If they decide that a warning is incorrectly flagged, the user can mark the chat as trusted, in which case the warning is removed and Scam Alert will not flag that chat again. If a user marks that they trust a chat, they can also opt in to share the last 5 messages received with WhatsApp to help improve the feature’s accuracy.

Tech.title: The Corvette Grand Sport X delivers Porsche 911 performance for a fraction of the price
Tech.content:
My drive of the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X began under oily black clouds, a torrential weather front releasing its grip on Manhattan — an inauspicious start for any mega-powered sports car. Rain pelted the waterlogged pavement, as I set course for the mountain-man roads of the Catskills, then on to Long Island and New England over three days. Fortunately, this Grand Sport, a name synonymous with value among Corvette fans, was the first of its kind: A 721-horsepower super-hybrid with a brainy, confidence-boosting AWD system. I popped the Corvette into Sport mode, Wet mode be damned. Finding tire grip galore on the Palisades Parkway, I realized the “X” badge on those wide flanks had changed the forecast to “fun.”

As a track-centric mid-engine sports car, the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X is hardly representative of mass-market transportation. But the GSX still has something hopeful to say — or shout, with every seismic blast of its new LS6 V-8 engine — about the world’s renewed love affair with hybrids.

People have always made a statement about who they are, or the person they want to be, through the car they drive or the one they dream of owning. Beetle or BMW, Porsche or pickup, Stingray or Subaru. These choices are more fraught than ever as a zero-sum game emerges between EVs and internal combustion engine cars.

You can watch that standoff unfold on YouTube, with drag races between Teslas and seemingly every ICE car since the Model T. When I came of age in Detroit, true sports-car fans scoffed at such reductive straight-line contests, the equivalent of an arm-wrestling match to determine the most gifted athlete.

On a broader level, it doesn’t have to be this way. Electrified cars like the Grand Sport X can help change the conversation and build common ground on today’s scorched earth.

Previous Next







1 / 5 Image: GM

The Corvette’s sophisticated algorithms bring two often-warring tribes together. There’s electric business in the front, and a gasoline party in the back, with no physical connection between the electrified front axle and petroleum-powered rear wheels. Finely coordinated teamwork and integration makes the GSX the latest all-wheel-drive hybrid sports car that feels like an unfair fight against purely gasoline models.

GM could use some teamwork on the hybrid front. The company currently has just two gas-electric models. Both are Corvettes. Both use electricity strictly to boost performance, like a hybrid F1 racer, with fuel economy not part of the brief.

In America, only hybrids have gained powertrain market share in 2026, with both EVs and pure ICE losing ground. With a record 15.4 percent of the market through June, hybrids are outselling EVs by nearly three to one. Even in China, hybrid sales are growing faster than those of EVs.

The Corvette’s sophisticated algorithms bring two often-warring tribes together

Three companies, Toyota, Hyundai and Honda, now control 90 percent of this booming US hybrid market. Toyota and Lexus alone sold 600,000 hybrids through June. The windfall has seen Hyundai and Kia post their best overall sales in history, including a 115-percent jump for Kia’s growing hybrid lineup. Caught flatfooted after having gone all-in on EVs, GM is racing to bring fuel-saving plug-in hybrids back to its showrooms, supposedly beginning next year.

The GSX itself replaces the Corvette E-Ray, Chevrolet’s first hybrid sports car. But it’s an entirely different animal. The 650-horsepower E-Ray was a versatile grand tourer: fast and fluid, but a bit of a mellow yacht rocker. The GSX was expressly designed as a track assassin, with heightened power, roadholding, braking, and agility.

What GM engineers call the “baby ZR1X” adopts its electrified front axle directly from the 1,250-horsepower, 233-mph record setter that I tested at Sonoma Raceway. Most every internal part number is identical. But in keeping with the Grand Sport’s reputation as a sweet spot in the Corvette lineup, the GSX coupe’s $112,195 base price is less than half that of a ZR1X at $227,395. For 2027, a non-hybrid, 535-horsepower Grand Sport asks $88,495. That rear-wheel-drive Grand Sport will be more than enough for many buyers.

Previous Next







1 / 5 Image: GM

Some want more. So the GSX’s 721 horsepower represents a 186-hp bump over a Grand Sport or 2027 Stingray. Add a monumental 655 pound-feet of torque, and the GSX easily tops the 690 horses and 531 pound-feet of a McLaren Artura, a hybrid that starts from around $260,000.

As in the ZR1X, the internal bearings in the electric motor were beefed up to handle a higher output of 186 horsepower and 145 pound-feet of torque. Push the GSX’s start button, and the engine crackles to life, before settling into a menacing basso idle. Floor the accelerator, and the cabin fills with enough pummeling, martial sound to backdrop a Christopher Nolan epic.

The electric motor plays its own whirring part, including a metallic overlay of selected frequencies amplified through the audio system. EV backers may believe silence is golden (sometimes it is) and scoff over ICE fans’ unwillingness to give up their thrashing cylinders. What they forget is that an engine’s sound offers not just drama and engagement, but critical somatic cues as to how fast you’re going, and a car’s gear or limits at a given moment. Yes, an EV can digitally imitate those cues. But for now, as with certain music, analog still beats digital among the performance cognoscenti.

Yes, an EV can digitally imitate those cues. But for now, as with certain music, analog still beats digital among the performance cognoscenti

An optional performance exhaust for $1,995 is a worthy upgrade. Corvette engineers lavished attention on the center-mounted exhaust and its four trumpeting outlets to coax out its most-pleasing harmonic frequencies. Another $2,995 for a front-end lift system is another practical spend, to avoid scraping the low-slung front splitter on every steep driveway.

Displacing 409 cubic inches, the stroked V-8 coincidentally harkens to a bygone age of muscle, when Brian Wilson ticked off the Chevrolet Impala SS’s technical virtues in the Beach Boys’ hit “409.” (Hey, it was the ’60s).

Here in 2026, the LS6 makes that old 409 seem primeval, in tech, power, or efficiency. Pricey forged cylinders can deactivate to save fuel. A lofty 13:1 compression ratio is the stuff of race cars and also contributes to cleaner fuel burn. The engine reduces emissions by 28 percent versus its less-powerful predecessor.

Previous Next





1 / 4 Image: GM

The engine’s 520 pound-feet of torque sets a high for any naturally aspirated V-8 in production-car history. This overachiever also becomes the standard power plant in a 2027 Stingray, making this “basic” Corvette even more of a sports-car bargain at $73,495. The engine manages a 25-mpg highway rating, impressive for a Stingray that can nip 200 mph.

As noted, neither the GSX nor the ZR1X gives a hoot about fuel economy. Their adrenalized performance encourages its pilots to feel the same. The GSX topped out at 22 mpg during my drives. It settled in around 15 mpg, and dipped as low as 11 or 12 mpg during barnstorming runs through the Catskills. Whichever automaker can bring a two-seat, truly mass-produced electric sports car to market — whether Porsche or someone else — energy savings will be an easy win for Team Electric.

The Corvette’s electric machine is fed by a tiny 1.9-kilowatt-hour battery mounted in the chassis’ spine, between driver and passenger. Again, that battery isn’t about efficiency or solo electric propulsion. Instead, its cells are designed to absorb regenerative energy like a fast-acting sponge, and spit it back out in rapid bursts. The motor fills any gaps in the engine’s output with an unbroken wave of torque, including during paddled upshifts from the eight-speed, dual-clutch automated gearbox.

Chevy cites a launch-controlled run to 60 mph in a sparkling 2.4 seconds, and a quarter-mile in 10.4 seconds at 131 mph. I manage 2.6 seconds to 60 mph, even on lumpy backroads in upstate New York. Those official measures are 0.1-seconds quicker than an E-Ray on both counts, and 0.2 seconds quicker than another track-centric Corvette: the mighty Z06 and its Ferrari-esque, flat-crankshaft V-8. As you’d expect, launch starts are less dramatic than in rear-drive Corvettes, all four tires hooking up with a yawn before you’re hammered into body-hugging bucket seats.

Familiar hardware, including a limited-slip rear differential with selectable Performance Traction Management settings, is retuned for this application. A superlative MagneRide suspension reads the road 1,000 times per second to adjust the viscosity of its magnetic-fluid dampers, and stiffen or soften shocks at individual wheels. The ride is firm but not spine-crunching, especially in Touring mode. Algorithms help dial in electric power for any situation, striving for handling balance and linear power delivery. In familiar tuning disagreements between passionate engineers, every GSX tiebreaker went to the track.

As compared to the E-Ray, “we’re keeping the edgier scenarios where the car feels more ready to pounce, versus a more-docile character,” says Keith Badgley, lead development engineer.

The author’s gray tester. Image: Lawrence Ulrich

Stated simply, electrified front wheels take a major burden off of rear tires, here shod with Michelin Pilot Sport all-season tires in a fat 345/25/ZR21 size. Powerful carbon-ceramic brakes are standard, helping to explain a somewhat eye-opening $23,700 price jump from a standard Grand Sport.

Like its ZR1X daddy, the GSX lets me brake deep into corners and jump back on throttle earlier, with fewer worries about the back end getting loose. In the rolling twisties of the Catskills, the GSX felt thrillingly athletic and on-its-toes. Hard-working front wheels palpably yank the ’Vette out of fast corners. Common sense is the only thing that will stop you.

The GSX also adopts the ZR1X’s specialized performance strategies. Hitting a “Charge +” button summons an Endurance mode, ensuring electrified wheels can deliver a consistent AWD jolt over a full tank of fuel, even during track sessions. A Qualifying mode preps the car for the fastest possible lap. Push-to-pass mode offers the full monty of gasoline and electric power on demand. To keep peace with neighbors, a Stealth mode lets the Corvette roll on electric power alone at speeds up to 50 mph.

The energy strategies make it virtually impossible to run the battery below 40 or 50 percent on public roads, no matter how hard you try. Selecting Charge + will also refill the battery over five miles or less of driving, using the gasoline engine and kinetic energy to generate electricity via the motor.

Did I mention this Grand Sport makes a great first impression? Rolling into fabled Woodstock, the GSX underscored how the eighth-generation Corvette is (finally) widening its appeal beyond a traditional Boomer, rock n roll audience. I can still quibble with aspects of the C8 design, especially that bluff back end. But the Grand Sports’ 3.6-inch-wider chassis, cavernous side air inlets, and forged aluminum wheels add to its exotic supercar vibe. Everywhere I rolled up in the glowering gray GSX, someone would stop in their tracks to offer questions or compliments. And not just car fans, but people who didn’t always realize this was a Corvette, but were visibly impressed when they found out. Serious fans will recognize a Grand Sport’s traditional hash marks on rear fenders, rendered in classic Admiral Blue on my test car.

The Corvette’s reworked interior will also win friends. A new auxiliary screen sits just left of the steering wheel, for easier access to launch control and PTM settings. There’s an intuitive Google-based infotainment system, graphical performance readouts, and the ingenious camera-based Performance Data Recorder to record and analyze track laps using telemetry software. A removable hardtop remains a signature coupe feature, and a GSX convertible starts from $119,195.

My GSX coupe started from $122,845 at its richest 3LT trim level. A schmear of options lifted that to $140,080. By old measures, that’s a lot of money for a Corvette. But a Porsche 911 Carrera 4 GTS hybrid, with 189 fewer horsepower, starts from $191,650, and soars past $220,000 with a modest sprinkling of options. And again, the GSX costs roughly half the price of a ZR1X.

From the chip-on-shoulder Corvette to Porsche, Ferrari, Lamborghini and McLaren, buyers who might be ambivalent about EVs are warming to this new breed of hybrid sports cars. Their advantages are becoming harder to resist.

For any type of car or SUV, I’ll argue that the hybrid love affair, rather than being seen as a rejection of EVs, is exactly the opposite. It’s a sign that Americans are already willing to meet electrification halfway. The next step becomes that much easier.

Tech.title: Suno is trying to look more like a real music production tool
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Suno is releasing Studio 2.0 with significant upgrades that push it closer to an actual digital audio workstation (DAW), rather than a bare-bones audio editor with generative AI features. The biggest addition is undoubtedly MIDI support. Suno says that MIDI was its most requested feature, and it’s basically a prerequisite for any modern DAW. Unfortunately, Suno Studio doesn’t appear to support third-party plugins or VSTs yet, so you’re stuck using its proprietary built-in synth. That synth appears to be a basic two-oscillator wavetable plugin with three envelopes and four envelopes.

The point is less about using your favorite Arturia vintage synth emulation, though, and more about using that MIDI data as a prompt. You can play in some chords, then ask Suno to turn that MIDI into audio, extend a melody, or write a B-part based on what you played. Another standard DAW feature being added in Studio 2.0 is automation. So now you can pan or change the volume of individual tracks across the arrangement.

Suno is also adding a chatbot to the Studio interface so you can prompt it for lyrics or a new guitar line. This isn’t an isolated generator either, it is tied into the current session and pulls in the musical context of your current project. So you can tell it things like “make this vocal track sound better,” and it will add reverb, compression, and EQ. Oh, and yes, Suno Studio now has a suite of simple built-in effects, including distortion, delay, reverb, compression, and EQ.

The most interesting feature of the chat interface, however, is the ability to create custom effects plugins. These can be unique reverbs, brickwalled compression, or chorus effects, similar to Polyend’s Endless AI guitar pedal. These effects are saved to your account as well, so they can be reused at a later date.

Suno Studio 2.0 is a lot more feature-packed than version one, but the beta version of the chat leaves even less to do for the users. In the demo above, Suno’s Henry Phipps can be seen cleaning up some flubbed notes and quantizing MIDI, before saying he should be asking the chatbot to do all this for him. He also leaves deciding on a vocal chain up to the AI rather than selecting effects himself.

Suno Studio is starting to look more like an actual DAW. Image: Suno

Tech.title: I looked inside an AI generated movie, and the best parts were all human
Tech.content:
Imagine a trio of bumbling, English lads who fantasize about becoming megastars while knocking back a few pints in a grimy pub somewhere in London. Picture the guys chortling and trying to one-up each other’s idealized visions of the future with a series of increasingly glitzy fantasies in which their fame leads to access to groupies and lavish parties on luxurious boats. Imagine these men are actually characters in a film — one filled with hyperkinetic smash cuts to action sequences in which they’re fighting or running from armed goons. This movie might be the sort of feature you’d expect from directors like Edgar Wright or Guy Ritchie. But all of this actually comes from Cully Hill Boys, the latest project from the AI filmmaking platform Higgsfield.

Cully Hill Boys is one of the few AI movies out this year that comes anywhere near close to looking and feeling like a traditionally produced feature. A large part of the movie’s strength is almost certainly rooted in how much Wright and Ritchie’s style has been baked into it, and it’s not just visual inspiration. In addition to posting Cully Hill Boys online, Higgsfield published many of the prompts that were used to make it. Several of those prompts mention Wright and Ritchie by name, which, along with a script written by a real screenwriter, underlines how the best parts of these films are undeniably taken from actual human artists.

Cully Hill Boys tells the story of three struggling rappers from East London whose lives are turned upside down when they accidentally steal a crime lord’s money. The project is codirected by Adilet Abish and Aitore Zholdaskali — who also helmed Higgsfield’s Hell Grind feature — and is based on a script that was initially written by Tim Planagan before it landed on the Black List screenplay submission service for unproduced projects. After acquiring the script’s AI production rights, Higgsfield tapped streamer Mikyle “N3on” Rafiq, basketball content creator Matt Kiatipis, and UFC fighter Israel Adesanya to “star” as its leads. Though none of Cully Hill Boys’ actors shot any scenes on set, each of them signed licensing agreements with Higgsfield for their likenesses to be used in the project. And while Planagan gave Higgsfield the ability to adapt this story using generative AI, he still retains the rights necessary for it to be produced traditionally.

Rather than trying to release Cully Hill Boys in theaters, Higgsfield — another service that sells access to various AI models — uploaded the film and most of its constituent prompts online in order to showcase what’s possible with its Cinema Studio suite of AI filmmaking tools. The film also functions as a gigantic ad for Higgsfield’s newly added Seedance 2.5 functionality, and to highlight new ways that studios can collaborate with digital creators.

What’s most striking about Cully Hill Boys as you begin to watch it is the way its story moves much in the same way most direct-to-video action / comedies usually do. We’re introduced to Cal (Kiatipis), Horace (Rafiq), and Oli (Adesanya) as a trio of longtime friends who just can’t figure out how to realize their dreams of becoming well-known musicians. After establishing the boys’ interpersonal dynamics, the film zooms out to show us more about who they are individually. Oli’s mom insists that he gets a real job, Cal’s ex doesn’t believe he can be a good father to their daughter, and Horace doesn’t have a lot going on outside of being the group’s designated driver. Cully Hill Boys establishes all of these details in its first few minutes with a series of scenes that flow together with a tonal and visual smoothness that you seldom see from AI films regardless of their length.

Cully Hill Boys’ story was crafted by a human with an understanding of proper pacing.

Some of that likely boils down to the way that Seedance 2.5 is capable of churning out much longer (about 30 seconds) clips than other video generation models. With films created with AI video models that only generate a few seconds of footage at a time, you can usually see and hear exactly when clips have been stitched together as a way to work around the technology’s limitations. There’s still some of that in Cully Hill Boys, but many of the project’s scenes unfold at a pace that feels much more organic and closer to what you might expect from a traditionally made feature.

Watching the movie, I got the sense its plot’s general cohesion was a reflection of Zholdaskali and Abish — who led a team of nine other directors, according to Higgsfield — closely following the beats of Planagan’s script. Planagan has said that he doesn’t use AI tools in his writing process, and it definitely feels like Cully Hill Boys is a stronger film than Hell Grind because its core narrative was crafted by an experienced, human storyteller with an understanding of proper pacing. There’s a clear logic to characters’ dialog, and the avatars have a passable emotiveness that speaks to how Higgsfield created them using photos and audio clips provided by real people. But when you pay close attention to things like incomprehensible text in books and the way that characters often have a distracting lack of chemistry, it’s easy to clock that most of the movie was made by feeding prompts into various generative models.

Image: Higgsfield AI

Scrolling through Higgsfield’s official Cully Hill Boys page, it’s actually fascinating to see how many different iterations of individual shots the film’s creative team generated using text prompts. Anthropic’s Claude was used to come up with prompts, which were sent to Seedance 2.5 to create video and speech, while ByteDance’s Seedream and Google’s Nano Banana were used for image and video editing. Per the website, Cully Hill Boys’ creative leads had to split their workflow across different models “because the rules of one job poison the other.” That meant, for example, one instance of Claude had to be focused solely on churning out prompts with wording specifically designed to generate workable images while another was dedicated to doing the same for prompts that would eventually become videos clips.

Similar to how Cully Hill Boys as a whole feels like an ad for Higgsfield as one of the many AI filmmaking platforms out there, the company’s transparency about how the film was made comes across as a way to highlight all of the models it gives its users access to. Reading the text prompts — most of which were in English, while some were in Simplified Chinese — you can see how detailed their descriptions are. But when you compare specific prompts to their corresponding scenes in the full movie, it becomes clear that these models aren’t just whipping up impressive shots and camera movements out of thin air. It’s evident there’s an extra bit of human work guiding this project.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Image: Higgsfield AI

More than a few of the prompts related to Cully Hill Boys’ zippier, more action-packed scenes reference elements of Wright and Ritchie’s styles of filmmaking. The prompts didn’t contain explicit directions to mimic any specific one of Wright or Ritchie films, but they did include asks for “GUY RITCHIE COVERAGE” and “DYNAMIC clip-style (Edgar Wright snap.)” It’s not unusual for traditional directors to pay homage by replicating one another’s signature filmmaking techniques. But Cully Hill Boys’ is a different sort of beast because its production process seemingly hinges on its underlying AI models having first been trained on Wright and Ritchie’s IP in order to understand when they’re being asked to generate similar footage.

As impressive as Cully Hill Boys is compared to other AI movies, it feels more like a (mostly) polished proof of concept than a project that’s ready for the mainstream spotlight. Rafiq, Kiatipis, and Adesanya’s fans might get a kick out of seeing their faves in a feature-length production, but this probably isn’t something that most moviegoers would be keen to watch. Higgsfield likely understands that reality. Cully Hill Boys’ real value is in its potential to further normalize the idea of AI movies in people’s minds.

Tech.title: This is Instagram’s new logo
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Instagram has unveiled a new wordmark, moving away from the recognizable cursive typeface it’s used over the last decade. The updated wordmark is a strange mix of half-cursive half-print that’s somehow less legible than its predecessor. Like, that totally says “Instagzam,” right?

“The wordmark at the top of the app hasn’t changed in 10 years, so it was time for a refresh,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced on his account. “Cleaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that’s always made it Instagram.”

Mosseri is seemingly aware that this will be a controversial change, because he also posted it to his Threads account to “see what the hot takes might be.” Plenty of Instagram and Threads commenters have already flagged that the updated version looks like it says “Instagzam,” but the general consensus otherwise is difficult to parse. Some users are mourning the loss of the now iconic cursive wordmark, while other responses — many of which look suspiciously written by bots — are a jumble of positive affirmations and emoji-vomit.

Why does “cleaner and more modern” always just mean “we made it look boring and more like everyone else’s branding.” Image: Meta / The Verge

I don’t personally think it has the same charm, but i’ll leave the rest of you to be the judge of that.

Tech.title: Wolverine on the PS5 made me care about Marvel’s mutant for the first time
Tech.content:
Going into my demo of Marvel’s Wolverine, I mainly wanted to try out the game’s very bloody combat. And it is delightfully bloody. But after two-ish hours of slashing and stabbing (and parrying!) enemies with Wolverine’s claws, I left surprised — despite no previous attachment to the character, I was deeply endeared to Logan himself.

The demo, which was held at Insomniac Games’ office in Burbank, California, started at the beginning of the game. In this story, Wolverine is rejoining the mutant task force Team X after a few years away in order to fight for his fellow mutants. He’s a reluctant hero with rocky relationships and little memory of his past — all good ways to onboard a newcomer without having to do a straight-up Wolverine origin story.

As Logan relearned how to be Wolverine, I was learning how to be him for the first time. Combat started out a little clunky for me as a result. It’s all about chaining attacks and kills to build the Rage meter, which gives you access to stronger and more devastating attacks to end combos with, all while dodging ranged attacks and parrying melee ones. It was a lot to keep track of amid showers of blood from eviscerated enemies. I found myself repeatedly trying to dodge melee attacks rather than parry them, which led to more than a few deaths as I learned the ropes.

So maybe it’s on me and the difficulty of learning new game mechanics under time pressure, but Wolverine felt far more vulnerable than I expected. This is a character whose nature revolves around being able to take punches. Building up the Rage meter unlocks Last Stand, which lets you get back up from a downed state and go a little berserk for a bit, and that does make him feel feral and dangerous. As do the gruesome finishing moves, most of which involve shredding or impaling enemies in delightfully over-the-top ways. But despite his super-fast healing and adamantium skeleton, Wolverine can die. He’s an apex predator in many ways, but he’s also a wounded animal lashing out in fear.

That’s underscored by the original story Insomniac wrote for the game and its characterization of Logan outside of combat. After the bloody opening act, the demo skipped ahead to a quieter sequence in which Logan had to go around Princess Bar and talk to his friends. His relationships here are marked by bitterness, regret, and concern about the barriers Logan has built between himself and the people he cares about. He especially felt like a sad puppy in these conversations, an outcast among outcasts.

It was in Princess Bar that I really fell for the character. My last real exposure to Wolverine was 2017’s Logan, and while I liked the movie, I didn’t have any particular affinity for him one way or another. But after fighting as Wolverine and seeing his lethality, paired with his vulnerabilities in and out of combat, I understood the character in a way I hadn’t before. I felt a surge of affection for the man who wants to care and be cared for but is afraid of his capacity to hurt everyone around him.

If you’re a Wolverine fan, you probably already knew this. But coming off of Insomniac’s Spider-Man games, the near-immediate connection I felt after just two-ish hours with this version of him is an important piece of Wolverine’s pitch. Everyone knows Spider-Man, the ever-present hero with hit after hit in theaters pretty much every few years. The Spider-Man games didn’t need to sell anyone on being Spider-Man; they needed to sell the fantasy of what it would be like to be him, the one most of us had in our minds already, and Insomniac succeeded on that front.

Lots of people know Wolverine, of course, but far fewer people know what the character is truly about compared to a cultural behemoth like Spider-Man. It’s a testament to Insomniac’s characterization out of the gate — and its scrappy, deadly, but still vulnerable combat — that I came into the demo expecting just some fun, gory mayhem and came out of it wanting to protect Wolverine at all costs.

Marvel’s Wolverine launches on the PS5 on September 15th.

Tech.title: Ford on track to complete $2B factory overhaul for Fathom EV truck
Tech.content:
Ford made a $2 billion bet two years ago when it closed its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky and scrapped the assembly line system it had used for more than a century. Its goal was to transform the factory into one capable of making a new generation of affordable EVs.

The auto giant provided an update on Thursday, stating that its factory overhaul is on track and in 2027 will be ready to start producing the Fathom, an all-electric midsize truck that costs less than $30,000 and the first EV built on its new universal platform.

Ford said it expects to begin prototype builds of the Fathom in the first quarter of 2027, with customer vehicles to follow later in the year. The U.S. automaker is already testing production-level tooling ahead of the prototypes.

The stakes for Ford are high. The company’s previous EV efforts were a drag on its profitability, while Chinese competitors and Tesla leapt ahead with vehicles that sell at volume and with a profit margin.

To catch up, Ford ditched the moving assembly line system that its founder Henry Ford launched and turned to a system developed by its skunkworks team led by former Tesla executive Alan Clarke.

This “universal production system,” as Ford calls it, uses a three-branched assembly tree. Ford will use large single-piece aluminum unicastings that use far fewer parts — a technique that Tesla has popularized — and that will allow the front and rear of the vehicle to be assembled separately on two of the branches. The third branch is where the structural battery will be assembled with seats, consoles, and carpeting. The three components will come together at the end of the line to form the vehicle.

As part of the factory rebuild, Ford has also nearly tripled the Wi-Fi coverage density in the factory to 1,080 access points to the kind of high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity required for software quality checks.

Ford said it will be able assemble the Fathom a net 15% faster than the former vehicles that were built at the Louisville plant.

The company said some employees have already spent months training on the new system at its New Models Program Development Center in Allen Park, Michigan.

Tech.title: X open sources its ranking algorithm, letting users see if they’ve been ‘shadowbanned’
Tech.content:
X is significantly expanding its open source codebase, which includes the app’s “For You” algorithm and its core ranking engine, and adding a feature that will let users see if their account or posts have been impacted by any of its ranking systems, the social network said on Thursday.

The company is making the source code for the “For You” timeline, the default feed you see when you open the app, available on GitHub under the Apache v2 license. It’s also expanding its previous efforts to open source parts of its codebase to add more detail, including the model configuration, filter, and core ranking system details. That means it includes the parameters used to weight different signals — key to understanding which posts are actually displayed. This also makes the codebase roughly 10 to 15 times larger than it was before.

“You’ll get the core ranking code that pulls posts and ranks them for any given user and assembles the feed,” X’s VP of Product Keith Coleman told TechCrunch in an interview ahead of the announcement. “You can see the systems that filter out potentially problematic, rule-violating content…And some of those systems, like the ranker and the score, you can even run yourself outside the company.”

“This is the kind of thing that I think people will be fairly shocked that we are releasing,” he added.

In addition to the repository, X is providing tools that will let users see for themselves if and how X’s ranking systems have impacted their account or posts. A new transparency tool is rolling out to an “Under the Hood” page in the app’s settings, which will let users who have posted 10 or more times over the past month download their aggregate stats as a JSON file. The file will show if any labels have been applied to their account or posts over the past calendar month.

Non-technical users can take advantage of this information by dropping it into an LLM of their choice, pointing the AI at X’s GitHub repo, and asking for an interpretation.

The company notes this tool will initially be available to a test group of accounts at least a year old as a pilot, before rolling out more broadly.

Image Credits:X screenshot

Ahead of launch, the company previewed its open source codebase to external researchers familiar with recommendation systems, who were able to get the “score,” or the numerical value calculated for every post, up and running outside of X. That was a major milestone for X’s transparency efforts, Coleman says.

From the GitHub repository, developers will be able to submit updates, known as pull requests, which X engineers will consider incorporating into its algorithm. While not all additions will make the cut, Coleman is enthusiastic about the idea.

“That would be amazing to have people submitting code that improves the algorithm…I mean, how cool would it be for the X algorithm to be not just visible to the public, but also, like, by the public?,” he said.

However, a few systems are not included in this release, like those that use Grok to predict whether a post could be violating a rule. This is meant to protect X from bad actors who could use this information to work around the company’s rules to flood the network with spam.

The changes are meant to address continuing concerns about how X’s algorithm influences politics, elections, the spread of misinformation, and more.

The platform has been home to political figures and high-profile individuals for years, and is now owned by a trillionaire who helped President Trump get elected. But Twitter had been under attack over its lack of transparency before it was bought by Musk, too. In earlier years, Republicans in Congress alleged that the California-headquartered social network leaned too far left, and claimed the network had “shadowbanned” their posts — meaning their posts were made invisible or undiscoverable without their knowledge. Twitter consistently denied this was the case.

“Our dream is that anyone in the public can be able to assess how posts are distributed on the platform, vet that it’s a level playing field, and, if they think it’s not, critique it so we can keep improving it and addressing it,” Coleman said.

“That’s the whole goal of this: [the code] can be audited; it can be critiqued. We’re going to listen, and we want to make the system one that people like and trust, and feel is fair,” he said.

Though X may be pushing itself to be more transparent around its code and other features, like its crowdsourced fact-checking system, Community Notes, it has arguably become less transparent overall under Musk, after becoming a private company again. No longer required to report to the SEC, X isn’t as forthcoming in other areas, like its user metrics, growth, revenue, or government takedown requests, which are now less frequently reported.

Tech.title: Instagram introduces a redesigned wordmark
Tech.content:
Instagram on Thursday introduced a new wordmark, which is the text-only logo that spells out the company’s name. The social media giant’s logic was that the older version of its logo felt dated after a decade in use.

The change was announced by Instagram head Adam Mosseri on both Instagram and Threads, where he described the new logo as “sharper and more modern” while still referencing the original and maintaining simplicity.

Although people can often be averse to change, particularly when it comes to brands and the logos they’ve long been familiar with, Instagram’s refreshed design is seeing some compliments among the complaints, noting the fresher look or praising the font choice.

Screenshot Image Credits:Threads

While there are certainly plenty of people joking that the logo now looks like it reads “Instagzam” because of the shape of the font used for the “r,” it’s fair to say that the name “Instagram” is such a recognizable brand that most people will immediately know what this says, despite the artistic flourishes.

The wordmark’s font recalls cursive writing as it adds old-fashioned curves to the “s,” “r,” and “g,” too. This is something of an interesting choice, given that the younger generations are no longer learning to write in cursive for the most part, so may not immediately understand why the shape that looks like the sail on a little boat is actually an “s.”

The last time Instagram updated its design was 2016, when the company moved away from the classic brown camera with the rainbow stripe to the colorful pink gradient that remains the icon today.

Meta hasn’t yet responded to a request for further comment about the redesign, or whether or not we should expect other design changes to come to Instagram in time, like a new app icon.

Tech.title: Microsoft kills off unsuccessful AI features while merging its separate Copilot apps
Tech.content:
Two years ago, Microsoft described AI as a “generational shift” in technology that it wanted to lead. Today, the company is merging its Copilot-branded consumer and business apps, and ditching a number of unsuccessful AI features.

As initially reported by GeekWire and detailed in Microsoft’s support documentation, the tech giant will combine the functionality of its consumer-facing Copilot app and the more business-oriented Microsoft 365 Copilot app.

The move is both an acknowledgement that personal and professional uses of AI often overlap, and that Microsoft’s prior strategy was too complicated to make Copilot a viable competitor to the likes of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

It also follows a broader consolidation in the AI app space that has seen Claude merging Cowork into Chat; OpenAI merging its agentic feature Operator into ChatGPT; and Google adding specialized capabilities to its Gemini app, like the combination of deep research and web browsing.

According to Microsoft, consumers will lose access to Group Chats, AI-generated podcasts in Copilot, Copilot Labs experimental features, and Deep Research, by August 18, 2026. For paying professional users, Researcher will offer a replacement for the latter, at least.

The company will also ditch its goofy animated character for Copilot, named Mico, a floating blob that felt like an AI-ified version of Clippy. Other features may temporarily disappear during the transition, Microsoft warns, and files generated by the stand-alone Copilot app will be migrated to OneDrive.

While the company says the goal is to make Copilot a “simpler, more cohesive experience,” it’s also an admission that Copilot has lost its way. In July, The Information reported that Microsoft EVP Jacob Andreou, who oversees Copilot, said in an internal memo that the app needed to earn “the right to exist” in its customers’ lives, which required moving on from features that didn’t work.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s new $500B plan is risky but brilliant, especially for aging GPUs
Tech.content:
Nvidia announced this week that Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR were willing to commit up to $500 billion to build AI data centers. That eye-popping figure got a lot of the attention, but the bigger story is Nvidia’s effort to create a secondary market for aging GPUs.

To convince those big-name financial companies, Nvidia has agreed to guarantee, with its own money, that its chips used as collateral in these deals will retain their value.

Many have now commented on how unusual, smart, and dangerous this plan is. It is all of those things. The bond markets got so spooked that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took to X and business TV to better explain how Nvidia’s risk would be limited.

But underneath the financial maneuvering to fund AI data centers (and keep revenue for Nvidia flowing), is something, perhaps, far more interesting for startups and enterprises: Huang wants to ensure an ecosystem of used AI hardware flourishes, helping sustain demand for Nvidia hardware as it ages.

Specifically, Nvidia is promising that if GPUs used as collateral don’t retain their value as expected, the company will cover up to 25% of the difference. So, if a data center owner defaults on a loan and the lender must liquidate, but the chips can’t command the price the books say they should, Nvidia will chip in.

The dangerous part for Nvidia is that this creates something financiers call “wrong way” risk. That is, Nvidia’s obligations will grow as demand weakens. Should that happen, its revenues will likely be squeezed as well.

Still, the scheme is deliberately unlike the comparison to Lucent Technologies that some have been making. Lucent was the telecommunications equipment provider that rose and crashed with the dotcom bubble after lending its customers money to buy its wares.

The Lucent comparison is a shadow over Nvidia, Huang knows. And not an unfair one. Nvidia definitely has committed billions toward those who buy its chips, including frontier AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic, neoclouds like CoreWeave (the originator of using Nvidia chips as collateral), as well as Nebius, Firmus, and Lambda. And it has been working on another $750 billion worth of circular deals this summer, Bloomberg has calculated.

“Is this circular financing?” Huang wrote on X about the new scheme. “This initiative is designed to address that concern. We are bringing independent, long-term institutional capital into the AI infrastructure market.”

That’s true. Unlike Lucent, Nvidia is getting others to shoulder the bulk of the capital and risk, merely by agreeing to protect a portion of its chips’ value in the future.

Should this plan work, Nvidia will have found new sources of money for AI data center builds, after many of the traditional methods have begun to wear thin. For instance, some of the hyperscalers have already taken on a lot of debt (like Oracle), issued new tranches of equity (Google), and burned much cash (Meta).

The situation has become so dicey that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently recommended the book “1873” during his latest earnings call. It’s about the railroad-era financial engineering that crashed the nation’s economy.

The risk is that today’s AI boom, where demand far outstrips capacity, doesn’t continue for much longer. Rather than being in the early innings, what if enterprises and consumers temper AI usage? Or new technologies come along to make existing infrastructure more effective and/or all of today’s AI infrastructure obsolete?

Then, like so many buggy whips in the face of automobiles (to paraphrase Danny Devito’s Lawrence Garfield), demand dries up and everything crashes.

Yet, Huang is arguing that won’t happen by selling a vision of AI as a long-term “investable infrastructure,” as he describes it. That makes his AI servers, which he calls “AI factories” akin to railroads or airlines rather than quickly depreciating assets like PCs.

“When needs change, the factory can be used by another customer, another cloud or another operator. This broad ecosystem gives NVIDIA compute a deep market of potential users and offtakers, helping protect residual value,” he promised.

In that future, Nvidia cares as much about aging architecture as it does the new chips. And perhaps startups, enterprises, and even researchers will tap into a broader variety of hardware, each tuned to different AI needs, just like they are beginning to pick affordable open-weight models alongside the frontier choices.

As the king of AI, Nvidia has the power, and the window of opportunity, to make that happen.

Tech.title: Who really needs a cocktail robot?
Tech.content:
Bartesian’s cocktail makers would be best described like a Keurig or Nespresso machine, but for alcoholic drinks. The Bartesian Duet model that I tested certainly lives up to that description — it’s really easy to serve a bunch of different cocktails with the push of a button, plus your own liquor.

But as I sipped on my raspberry ginger gimlet, I couldn’t shake the nagging question: Who is actually going to buy a $300 cocktail robot?

There’s nothing wrong with the product. And it does exactly what it says! In the sleekly designed machine, you add your spirits of choice (between one and four types of liquor, depending on which model you’re using) and plop in a Bartesian capsule with hyper-concentrated mixes for multi-ingredient drinks like espresso martinis, watermelon margaritas, mai tais, and cosmos. There’s a barcode on the capsule that your machine scans to determine which spirit (or spirits) you need in your drink, and then you can select how strong you want your drink to be, which modulates the amount of water the machine will use to dilute the concentrate. Then, you put the drink in the provided, high-quality cocktail shaker with some ice to cool it down before pouring it into your glass.

When I invited some friends over to test the Bartesian, we enjoyed the inherent novelty of trying out a product we’d never seen or used before. Once we all sat down with our various drinks, we tried to decide who actually makes up the target audience for such an odd product, which also requires the purchase of cocktail capsules at about $2.50 each.

Image Credits:Bartesian

The Bartesian is not for true cocktail lovers — the capsules don’t actually contain any alcohol, which means that if you’re making a drink like an aviation, you’re getting some sort of non-alcoholic approximation of ingredients like crème de violette and maraschino liqueur.

It’s no coincidence that my friends and I all liked the Bartesian’s lemon drop capsules the best, since the only alcoholic ingredient in the drink is the vodka that we bought ourselves to add to the machine. To be fair to Bartesian, it’s not like you’d recommend a Nespresso machine to your friend who owns a Fellow kettle and only buys single-origin beans.

This cocktail robot is also not for anyone who is even remotely worried about the amount of counter space in their kitchen. It’s pretty big for something that you (hopefully?) aren’t using on a daily basis, and if anything, it would probably encourage me to start drinking more often just to justify the $300 expense. Plus, if you have counter space to spare, you probably have a lot of money. And if you have a lot of money and like cocktails, I’d say you are more likely to have a fully stocked bar with fancy liqueurs already. What will the other partners at your law firm say if you serve aviations that don’t use real crème de violette?

Even as someone who thinks Tito’s is top-shelf liquor (I am not that fancy), I could tell that something tasted a little bit artificial about most of these drinks. My friends and I all doctored up our drinks with some seltzer and lemon juice, which made them taste much better. But this kind of post-robot mixing sort of defeats the point of the whole endeavor.

Maybe my tastes just don’t align with the mixologists at Bartesian — my colleague Lauren reviewed a different Bartesian unit last year and told me that she loved it, especially the margaritas.

Drink preferences aside, I still keep coming back to the same question: Who is this product for?

I could see the Bartesian being useful if you host a lot of parties and don’t hire a bartender, since you can make a whole cocktail menu’s worth of drinks without much effort or planning. One friend remarked that this machine feels like the sort of thing that an older couple would keep in their beach house to impress their friends. A colleague suggested that this could really shine in a retirement home. Personally, I could see a Bartesian at a coworking space’s happy hour, where people are just happy to get free drinks… then again, there’s a reason why WeWork stopped offering unlimited beer back in the day.

Tech.title: Apple in talks to pay publishers to provide Siri with current news: report
Tech.content:
In Brief

Apple is in talks to pay publishers to use their content to power the upcoming Siri AI, according to a new report from The Wall Street Journal. The tech giant has reached out to publishers in recent months about using their content to provide Siri with access to current news and information.

Apple has proposed a variable compensation model that would pay publishers when their content is used, rather than through a fixed licensing fee. This marks a departure from the standard industry practice of guaranteed fees, which are generally tied to broad access to content, rather than a pay-as-you-go model. Apple has considered a nine-figure budget for the payments, the report says.

Apple did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

The discussions come as Apple has been working to significantly enhance Siri, years after promising users a smarter and more capable AI assistant.

Siri AI is expected to roll out later this year.

Tech.title: In a first, US will allow some private firms to carry out cyberattacks
Tech.content:
The U.S. government will for the first time allow vetted private companies to launch offensive cyber operations against international criminal gangs and hackers, the White House said on Wednesday.

In a newly published presidential memorandum, the Trump administration said the move will allow the federal government to use “innovative capabilities of the private sector” to combat cybercrime and threats targeting Americans, such as ransomware attacks, financial scams, and sextortion.

The memorandum allows private companies participating in the government’s program to conduct surveillance, like using spyware to collect intelligence, as well as make disruptive attacks aimed at the destruction of criminals’ data or systems.

The policy change marks a seismic shift in the U.S. government’s long-standing position under U.S. federal computer hacking laws, which broadly prohibit private companies from conducting cyberattacks or disruption operations without a court-authorized approval.

Private companies are regulated under the same computer hacking laws as anyone else in the United States, which prohibit people or companies from carrying out cyberattacks. The U.S. government’s position to date, through multiple administrations, has been that the private sector can defend against incoming cyberattacks, but not launch or operate them.

While the presidential memorandum establishes the new policy, it’s still in its early days and the government has not yet fully established how the program will operate. The new policy is likely to face legal challenges and opposition by critics, who have for years argued that private companies should not get involved with government hacking operations.

The government will issue guidance in the next two months outlining the requirements participating companies will have to meet before being allowed into the program. This guidance would consider companies of all sizes, including smaller private companies, which might be better suited for specialized operations, the memorandum reads.

Participating companies must deposit $1 million in escrow, which will be forfeited if the government finds out a company isn’t complying with its rules on how to conduct these operations. The memorandum directs the federal government to create procedures preventing any operation from targeting Americans or U.S.-based systems.

Any operation will require sign-offs from representatives from the Justice Department and Homeland Security before it can be approved. Operations are to be conducted exclusively under the supervision of the federal government.

The policy also requires any participating company to notify the government if it discovers an imminent cyberattack against critical U.S. infrastructure, such as power grids or water providers.

When reached by email, a White House spokesperson did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about whether any private companies are already participating in the program, and referred to the White House’s fact sheet.

The memorandum stops short of allowing companies to “hack back” any cyber threats. Critics have argued that private industry getting involved with government operations may spark diplomatic and international ramifications, such as if a foreign government complains that they were attacked by a U.S. company.
